etym.Lagos: {{ety|en|id=Nigeria|:bor|pt:Lagos<id:Nigeria>|text=+|nodot=1}}, either from {{m|pt|lago|lagos|lit=lakes}} or after the {{l|pt|Lagos|Portuguese city|id=Portugal}}. {{pw dbt|en|Lakes}}.
etym.Gabriel:
{{etymon|en|id=given name|:der|la:Gabriel<id:given name>|tree=1}}
From {{bor|en|la|Gabriel}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Γαβρῑήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|גַּבְרִיאֵל|tr=gaḇrīʾḗl}}, from {{m|hbo|גֶּבֶר|tr=géḇer|t={{sqb|[[strong]]}} [[man]]}} or the triliteral root {{m|hbo|ג־ב־ר||[[strength]], [[manliness]]|tr=g-b-r}}, {{m|hbo|־י||[[me]], [[my]], [[-'s]]|tr=-i}}, and {{m|he|אֵל|tr=ʾēl|t=[[God]], [[god]]}}, from {{der|en|sem-pro|*ʾil-}}. {{doublet|en|Jibril}}.
etym.Abdoulaye: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from {{der|fr|ar|عَبْدُ اللّٰهِ}}, i.e. [[Abdullah]]. Native spellings include Wolof [[Abdulaay]] and Pulaar [[Abdullaye]] etc.
etym.Xavier: Toponymic surname of a 16th-century saint born in the Kingdom of Navarre, Francis de Xavier, from a place name in the Kingdom of [[Navarre]], originally from {{der|en|eu|Xabier}}. Doublet of {{m|es|Echeverría}}.
etym.Fathallah:
Ultimately from {{der|en|ar|فَتْح اللَّٰه}}.
{{root|en|ar|ف ت ح|ء ل ه}}
etym.Zinédine: {{bor+|fr|ar|زين الدين}}, from {{m|ar|زين}} + {{m|ar|الدين}}, from {{m|ar|دين}} + {{m|ar| ال}}. {{transliteration|fr|ar|زين الدين}}. Variant of {{m|fr|Zayn ad-Din}}.
etym.Michael:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Michael|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Michael}}, from {{der|en|fro|Michel}}, {{der|en|ang|Michahel}}, from their source {{der|en|la|Michaēl,Michāhēl}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μιχαήλ|Μῐχᾱήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|מִיכָאֵל|tr=mîḵāʾēl|lit=who is like God?}}. {{dbt|en|Miguel|Mikhail}}.
etym.Daniel: From {{inh|en|enm|Daniel}}, {{m|enm|Daniell}}, from {{der|en|grc|Δᾱνῑήλ}}, from {{der|en|he|דָּנִיֵּאל|tr=daniyél|lit=God is my judge}}, name borne from the prophet whose story is told in the Book of Daniel.<ref>''Oxford Names Companion''</ref>
etym.Aaron:
{{ety|en|:bor|la:Aaron|tree=1}}

From {{bor|en|la|Aaron}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀαρών}}, from {{der|en|he|אַהֲרֹן||tr=ʾAhărōn}}, of unknown meaning, possibly meaning “[[bearer]] of [[martyr]]s”, or perhaps also, or instead, related to the Ancient Egyptian {{m|egy|[[ꜥḥꜣ]] [[rw]]||[[warrior]] [[lion]]}}, though it has been suggested to also mean “[[elevated]]”, “[[exalted]]” or “[[high]] [[mountain]]”. {{doublet|en|Harun}}.
etym.Anthony:
{{etymon|en|:bor|la:Antōnius|:influence|grc:ἄνθος|tree=1}}
From {{bor|en|la|Antōnius}}, name of a Roman gens (with excrescent -h- suggested by an unetymological association with {{noncog|grc|ἄνθος||flower}}). The Roman clan name is of uncertain etymology, but is not Greek or Hebrew; most likely of {{der|en|ett|-}} origin, possibly derived from Ani, the Etruscan god of the sky. {{doublet|en|Antoine}}.
etym.Roy:
From various sources:
* {{der|en|xno|roy|t=king}} a variant of {{der|en|fro|roi}}, from  {{der|en|la|rex|rēx, rēgem}} from  {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₃rḗǵs||ruler, king}}. {{doublet|en|Rey}}.
* {{der|en|gd|ruadh|t=red, red-haired}} from {{der|en|sga|rúad}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*roudos}} from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₁rewdʰ-}}.
* Anglicisation of {{bor|en|bn|রায়|pos=surname}}. {{dbt|en|Rai|rex|rajah}}.
etym.Axel: From {{der|en|da|Aksel}}, first used for the bishop and statesman [[Absalon]] Hvide (1128–1201), from biblical [[Absalom]]. Some sources suggest that the bishop was originally named [[Áskell]], from {{der|en|non|-}} "god" + "cauldron, helmet", and Absalon was chosen as the nearest-sounding Christian equivalent, leading to the exchange of the middle consonants.
etym.Joseph:
{{etymon|en|id=name|:inh|enm:Ioseph<id:name>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Ioseph}}, ultimately from {{der|en|hbo|יוֹסֵף|tr=Yoséf|lit=(God) shall add}}; a son of Jacob. {{dbt|en|Yusuf}}. {{senseno|en|one whose chastity is above temptation|t=one whose chastity is above temptation|cap=1}} is a reference to the story of Joseph and [[Potiphar]]'s wife in [[w:Vayeshev|Genesis 39]].
etym.Samuel:
From {{bor|en|la|Samuēl}}, from {{der|en|grc|Σαμουήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|שְׁמוּאֵל|tr=šəmûʾēl|lit='God has set' or 'God has placed'}}.<ref>{{R:Strong's|H|410}}</ref><ref>{{R:Strong's|H|7760}}</ref>

Taken to mean a contraction of popular folk etymology {{l|he|שְׁאִלְתִּיו מֵאֵל|gloss=I have asked/borrowed him from God}} (Modern: Šəʾīltīv mēʾĒl, Tiberian: Šĭʾīltīw mēʾĒl) by way of {{l|he|שָׁאוּל מֵאֵל|gloss=asked/borrowed from God}}<ref>{{R:Strong's|H|7592}}</ref> from [https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+samuel+1%3A20&version=NIV 1 Samuel 1:20].<ref>{{cite-web |title=Radak on Genesis 5:29:1 |url=https://www.sefaria.org/Radak_on_Genesis.5.29?lang=bi |site=Sefaria|year=1842|publish
etym.Claude: In use from the 16th century. {{bor+|en|fr|Claude}}, from {{der|en|la|Claudius}}, the name of a Roman gens. The clan name is traditionally said to be from {{der|en|la|claudus||lame}}, but is most likely of {{der|en|sbv|-}} origin.
etym.Jean:
Variant of {{m|en|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehane}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}}. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

The unincorporated community in Nevada, originally named Goodsprings Junction, was renamed Jean on 28 June 1905 by postmaster George Arthur Fayle in honor of his wife.
etym.Martin: From {{inh|en|enm|Martin}}, from {{der|en|la|Mārtīnus|t=of or like Mars” or “little Mars}}, {{af|la|Mars|alt1=Mārs, Mārtis|-īnus|pos2=diminutive suffix|nocat=1}}. See {{m|la|Mārs}} for further etymology.
etym.Pascal: From {{uder|en|la|Paschālis}}, from {{m|la|paschālis|t=Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter}}, from {{m|la|pascha|gloss=Easter}} + {{m|la|-ālis|pos=suffix forming adjectives}}, for birth on Easter, or in honor of the 9th-century pope [[w:Pope Paschal I|Paschal I]] (died 824). {{doublet|en|Paschal}}. The programming language was named after French mathematician, philosopher and physicist {{w|Blaise Pascal}} (1623–1662).
etym.Quentin:
{{wp}}
From {{uder|en|fro|-}}. The name of a third century French martyr, from {{der|en|la|Quīntīnus}}, a derivative of the Roman [[praenomen]] {{m|la|Quīntus}}, from {{m|la|quīntus||fifth}}. It was brought to England by the Normans, but never became particularly popular. Compare {{dbt|en|Quinton|notext=1}}.
etym.Patrice: 20th century variant of [[Patricia]], probably borrowed from the {{uder|en|fr|-}} male given name {{m|fr|Patrice}}.
etym.Enzo:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Enzo}} (equivalent to {{cog|en|Hank}}), from {{der|en|de|Heinz}}, a diminutive of {{m|de|Heinrich}} ({{cognate|en|Henry}}), from {{der|en|goh|Heimrih}}, {{m|goh|Haimirich}} ({{m|goh|heim||home}} + {{m|goh|rihhi||ruler}}), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Haimarīks}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|-}} roots.

Rare in the US<ref>Social Security Administration, [https://web.archive.org/web/20180202070118/https://www.ssa.gov/cgi-bin/babyname.cgi Popularity of a Name]</ref> and UK<ref>England & Wales Baby Names: Baby name trends in England & Wales from 1996 to 2018, [http://names.darkgreener.com/#enzo Enzo]</ref> prior to 2003, popularized in the 2000s.
etym.Gaétan: {{bor+|fr|it|Gaetano}}, from {{m|it|gaetano||resident or native of [[Gaeta]]}}, from {{der|fr|la|Caiētānus}}. Name of {{w|Saint Cajetan|a saint}}.
etym.Moshe: {{bor+|en|he|-}}. {{translit|en|he|משה|tr=moshé}}, sometimes conjectured to derive from {{der|en|egy|msj||to give birth to}}, a common element in Egyptian names of the form ‘[name of deity] is the one who bore him’.
etym.Blaise: Borrowed from {{der|en|fro|Blaise}} in the Middle Ages and revived partly due to the modern {{der|en|fr|-}} equivalent, from {{der|en|la|Blasius}}. {{doublet|en|Blasius}}.
etym.Loup: From {{der|en|fr|loup||wolf}}: the language was attested in a notebook titled ''Mots loups'' ("wolf words") compiled by Jean-Claude Mathevet, a priest who worked among the Algonquians.
etym.Isaïe: From the {{der|fr|la|Īsāiās}}, the {{w|Vulgate}} spelling of {{m|la|Ēsāiās}}, from the {{der|fr|grc|Ἠσαΐας}}, from the {{der|fr|hbo|יְשַׁעְיָהוּ|tr=yəšaʿyā́hū}}.
etym.Térence: {{bor+|fr|la|Terentius}}. Itself borrowed from latin goddess Terensis, a goddess who presided over the threshing of wheat. Ultimately from {{m+|la|terō}} linked to the technic to separate cobs and seeds of wheat. Cognate with ancient greek [[τέρην]], to make soft.
etym.Alexandra:
From {{der|en|grc|Ἀλεξάνδρα}}, from {{af|grc|ἀλέξω|t1=to defend|ἀνδρός|alt2=ἀνδρ-|pos2=stem of {{m|grc|ἀνήρ|t=man}}|nocat=1}}. Feminine form of ''[[Alexander]] ''(“the man who repels [enemies]”).

The community in Prince Edward Island is named after {{w|Queen Alexandra}} (1844–1925).
etym.Alexa:
* From {{af|en|Alex|-a}}. A feminine form of {{m|en|Alex}}.
* {{given name|en|female|clipof=Alexandra}}.
etym.Marjorie: Variant of {{m|en|Margery}}, a medieval vernacular form of {{m|en|Margaret}}.
etym.Chloé:
{{root|fr|ine-pro|*ǵʰelh₃-}}
{{bor+|fr|grc|χλόη||young green shoot}}, an epithet of goddess {{l|en|Demeter}}
etym.Dylan: From {{der|en|cy|-}} mythology; possibly from {{der|en|cel|-}} for "son of the sea" or "born from the ocean." Unrelated to the name {{m|en|Dillon}}, although the homophony may result in the two being considered variant spellings of the same name.
etym.Leila: From {{uder|en|ar|لَيْلَى}}. Taken into English usage through nineteenth-century literature. {{root|en|ar|ل ي ل}}
etym.Aïssatou: A French spelling of a West African name ultimately derived from {{der|fr|ar|عَائِشَة|t=Aisha}}.
etym.Aïssata: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from {{der|fr|ar|عَائِشَة|t=Aisha}}. Native spellings include Pulaar ''Aysata''.
etym.Fatimata: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from {{der|fr|ar|فَاطِمَة}}, i.e. [[Fatima]]. Native spellings include Pulaar ''Faatimata''.
etym.Lancelot:
From {{inh|en|enm|Launcelot}}, from {{der|en|fro|Lancelot}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Lanzo}}, hypocoristic form of names beginning in {{m|frk|*Land-}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*landą||land}}, and diminutive Old French endings {{m|fro|-el}} and {{m|fro|-ot}}.

Related to {{cog|ang|Landbeorht}} (modern {{cog|en|Lambert}}).
etym.Dimitri: Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Dimitri}}, a variant of {{m|it|Demetrio}}, from {{der|en|la|Dēmētrius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Δημήτριος}}.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
etym.Fiona:
From {{der|en|ga|fionn||fair, white}}. In use before 1713.<ref>See https://familysearch.org/pal:/MM9.3.1/TH-267-12041-126121-22?cc=1823613&wc=9020216</ref> Popularized by James Macpherson (see 1765 quotation), and perhaps by the 19th-century Scottish writer William Sharp, who chose “Fiona Macleod” as his pen name.
* {{sense|Sara Duterte}} After the fictional character {{w|Princess Fiona}} from the ''Shrek'' series, who transforms from princess to ogre.
etym.Jeanne: From {{bor|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Lorraine: {{inh+|en|enm|Loreyne}}, from {{der|en|fro|Loherraine}}, from {{m|fro|loherenc|t=Lotharingian}}; compare {{cog|la-eme|Lotharingia}} (ultimately named for {{w|Lothair II}}, who ruled it); compare {{doublet|en|Lotharingia|notext=1}}, {{cog|de|Lothringen}}.
etym.Natasha: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ru|Ната́ша}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Ната́лья}}, cognate to [[Natalie]].
etym.Vanessa: {{der|mul|la-new|-}}, from the {{der|mul|grc|-}} deity {{m|grc|Φάνης|}}. Named by {{w|Johan Christian Fabricius}}.
etym.Nadia: Originally the French spelling of {{m|ru|На́дя}}, an [[informal]] Russian [[pet form]] of the virtue name {{m|ru|Наде́жда|t=[[Nadezhda]], [[Nadyezhda]]|lit=[[Hope]]}}, from {{m|ru|наде́жда||[[hope]]}}, entered as a translation of the [[Ancient Greek]] word from {{m|grc|ἐλπίς||[[hope]]}} with the same meaning. See also {{m|grc|Ἐλπίς||[[Elpis]]}}.
etym.Sabrina: Popularity likely inspired from {{bor|id|ar|صَابْرِينَا}} based on Arabic root {{m|ar|ص ب ر}}, folk etymologized form of earlier {{m|ar|سَابْرِينَا}} (now mostly limited to non-Arabs with the name), from {{bor|id|en|Sabrina}}.
etym.Ghyslaine: {{alternative form of|fr|Ghislaine}} (less common spelling variant); {{female equivalent of|fr|Ghislain}}
etym.Yasmine: Variant of {{m|en|Jasmine}}, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding {{uder|en|ar|-}} and {{uder|en|fa|-}} names.
etym.Yasmina: Variant of {{m|en|Jasmine}}, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding {{uder|en|ar|-}} and {{uder|en|fa|-}} names.
etym.Radegonde: From the Germanic given name {{m|gem-pro|*Rēdagunþiz}}, from {{der|fr|gem-pro|*rēdaz||advice}} and {{m|gem-pro|*gunþiz||battle}}.
etym.Mika:
* {{sense|Japanese given name}} Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|みか|tr=Mika}}.
* {{sense|Hebrew given name}} From {{der|en|he|מִיכָה|tr=mīḵāh}}
etym.Aya:
The planetoid was named after the Akkadian goddess, which began with the same first letter as the provisional designation 2002 AW<sub>197</sub>.

{{rfe|en}}
etym.Kumiko: Transliteration of {{bor|en|ja|駒実子|tr=Kumiko}} and many other spellings. See {{ja-l|くみこ}}.
etym.Hitomi: {{bor+|en|ja|ひとみ|tr=Hitomi}}, a given name with numerous possible original kanji.
etym.Kasumi: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|かすみ|tr=Kasumi}}. Compare with the native English name ''[[Misty]]'', which is an equivalent formation.
etym.Victoria: From {{der|mul|la|victōria|t=victory}}, often in honor of {{w|Queen Victoria}}.
etym.Claudia: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from {{borrowed|en|la|Claudia}}.
etym.Erika: Spelling variant of {{m|en|Erica}}, the feminine form of {{m|en|Eric}}, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from {{der|en|non|Eiríkr}}.
etym.Julia: From {{der|en|la|Iūlia}}, feminine form of the Roman gens name {{m|la|Iūlius}}. Further popularized by early Christian saints. {{doublet|en|Julie}}.
etym.Julie:
{{bor+|nb|fr|Julie|t=female given name}}, from {{der|nb|la|Iūlia|t=Roman female given name}}, the feminine form of {{m|la|Iūlius|t=Julius}}. The ultimate origin of the Roman family name is uncertain; see {{m|nb|Julius}}.<ref name="Nordic Names">[https://www.nordicnames.de/wiki/Julie “Julie”], ''Nordic Names''.</ref> {{etydate|18th century}}.<ref name="Nordic Names" /> {{doublet|nb|Julia|t1=female given name}}.

Compare {{cog|da|Julie}}, {{cog|sv|Julie}}, {{cog|fi|Julie}}, {{cog|kl|Julie}}, {{cog|cs|Julie}}, {{cog|en|Julie}}, {{cog|de|Julie}} and {{cog|nl|Julie|t=female given name}}.
etym.Pauline: From {{bor|en|fr|Pauline}}, in turn from {{der|en|la|Paulīna}}; in regular use since the 19th century. {{surf|en|Paul|-ine<pos:feminine suffix>}}.
etym.Delphine: {{uder|en|fr|-}} form of {{uder|en|la|Delphina}}, meaning ''woman from [[Delphi]]'';  [[wikipedia:Delphine_of_Glandèves|Bl. Delphine of Glandèves]] was a 14th century nun from [[Provence]].
etym.Hortense: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} form of the {{der|en|la|Hortēnsia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Hortēnsius||name of a Roman [[gens]]}}, probably derived from {{m|la|hortēnsis||having to do with gardens}} on the basis that the first to bear the name was a gardener.
etym.Carmen: From {{der|en|es|Carmen}}, cognate with {{m+|en|Carmel}}. Made famous outside Spain by the [[opera]] ''Carmen'' (1875) by [[w:Georges Bizet|Georges Bizet]].
etym.Mireille: From {{bor|fr|oc-pro|Mirèio}}/{{m|oc-pro|Mirèlha}}. Invented by the poet {{w|Frédéric Mistral}} for {{w|Mirèio|his poem of the same title}} (1859).
etym.Soraya: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fa-ira|ثریا|tr=sorayyâ}}, from {{der|en|fa-cls|ثریا|tr=surayyā|t=brilliant gem; [[Pleiades]]}}, ultimately from {{der|en|ar|ثُرَيَّا}}.
etym.Yoshiko: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|美子}}, {{m|ja|芳子|tr=よしこ, Yoshiko|lit=good, excellent child}}.
etym.Yoko: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|ようこ|tr=Yōko}}, a female given name with many variant [[kanji]] spellings.
etym.Yuko: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|ゆうこ|tr=Yūko}}, a female given name with many variant [[kanji]] spellings.
etym.Andrew:
{{etymon|en|:der|grc:Ἀνδρέᾱς|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|ang|Andreas}}, from {{der|en|la|Andreas}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀνδρέας}}, cognate with {{m|grc|ἀνδρεῖος|t=manly}}, both from {{m|grc|ἀνήρ|t=man}}. {{doublet|en|André|Andreas|Andrei|Andrey}}.
etym.Alexander:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂lek-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Alexander,Alexandre}}, from {{der|en|la|Alexander}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος}}, from {{m|grc|ἀλέξω||to defend}} + {{m|grc||ἀνδρ-}}, the stem of {{m|grc|ἀνήρ||man}}. {{doublet|en|Alastair|Alejandro|Iskandar|Sikandar|Alessandro|Alexandre}}.
etym.Andreas: From {{bor|en|la|Andreas}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀνδρέᾱς}}, cognate with {{m|grc|ἀνδρεῖος||manly}}, both from {{m|grc|ἀνήρ||[[man]]}}. {{doublet|en|Andrew}}.
etym.Alex: {{clipping|en|Alexander}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος}} 'he who wards off men', i.e. protector, possibly of Hittite origin. Also from {{m|en|Alexius}}, from the same Ancient Greek first element, "helping, defending". These two origins of Alex are [[indistinguishable]] in most languages. The female name has the same root, a {{clipping|en|Alexandra|nocap=1}} or the female name {{m|en|Alexis}}, in some cases also a spelling variant of {{m|en|Alix}}.
etym.Angelus:
* {{sense|given name}} From {{der|en|la|Angelus}} and its etymon {{der|en|grc|ἄγγελος|t=angel}}.
* {{sense|common noun}} From the first word ({{m|la|angelus}}) of its {{bor|en|la|-}} [[incipit]], "Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariæ": "the Angel of the Lord declared unto Mary".
{{doublet|en|angel}}.
etym.Kwame: An ancient and traditional [[Akan]] day-name meaning "born on Saturday". Popularized in the 1960s when {{w|Kwame Nkrumah}} was the Prime Minister of [[Ghana]].
etym.Ambrose: From {{bor|en|la|-}} saints' name {{m|la|Ambrosius}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἀμβρόσιος||immortal, divine}}. Compare {{m|en|Athanasius}}.
etym.Damon:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*demh₂-}}
From {{bor|en|grc|Δάμων}}, a name famous for the story of {{w|Damon and Pythias}}; derivative of {{m|grc|δαμάζω||to tame, subdue}}.
etym.Aegidius: From {{der|en|la-lat|Aegīdius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Αἰγιδιός||kid skin}} (sometimes interpreted as “the protecting”).
etym.Anastasius: From {{lbor|en|la|Anastasius|notext=1}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀναστάσιος}}, from {{m|grc|ἀνάστασις||[[resurrection]]}}. The name and its more common female counterpart, [[Anastasia]], were originally given to children who were born around [[Eastertime]] during the early years of Christianity.
etym.Rami: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|رَامِي}}, masculine singular construct form of [[رام|رَامٍ]] (rāmin). This surname is predominantly found in [[Morocco]] and [[India]].
etym.Anatolius: From {{der|en|la|Anatolius}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἀνατολή||sunrise}}. Name of early saints in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]].
etym.Dritan: From {{suffix|sq|dritë|t1=light|-an}}. Probably the suffix was voluntarily inserted to render it similar to {{cog|xil|*Tritanus}}.
etym.Arcadius: From {{bor|en|la|Arcadius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀρκάδιος||of Arcadia}}. See ''[[Arcadia]]'' for more information.
etym.Kwasi: From {{bor|en|ak|Kwasi}}, from {{m|ak|Kwasiada||Sunday}}, from the day of the week, {{m|en|Sunday}}.
etym.Sarel:
From {{uder|en|enm|Sarlo}}, {{m|enm|Sarle}} and {{m|enm|Serle}}, from [[Anglo]]-[[Scandinavian]] or {{uder|en|nrf|Sarli}} and {{m|en|nrf|Sarle}}, ultimately from [[Old Norse]].<ref name="Surname">{{cite-book|en|author=Percy Hide Reaney, Richard Middlewood Wilson|year=1991|title=A Dictionary of English Surnames|publisher={{w|Routledge}}|isbn=9780415057370|page=2736}}</ref>

The given name sense is derived from {{bor|en|af|Sarel}}.
etym.Cézanne: From {{bor|fr|it|Cesana}}. Nominal usage can be attributed to artist {{w|Paul Cézanne}}.
etym.Agapetus: From {{der|en|la|Agapētus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ᾰ̓γᾰπητός}}, from {{m|grc|ᾰ̓γᾰπητός|t=beloved}}, from {{m|grc|ᾰ̓γᾰπᾰ́ω|t=to love}} + {{m|grc|-τός|t=masculine suffix}}.
etym.Christian:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*gʰrey-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Cristien}}, from {{der|en|fro|chrestien}}, from {{der|en|la|Chrīstiānus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Χρῑστιᾱνός}}, from {{m|grc|Χρῑστός||Christ, anointed [one]}} + {{der|en|la|-}} suffix {{m|la|-ānus}}. The older form is {{m|en|Christen}}. {{doublet|en|cretin}}. {{surf|en|Christ|-ian}}.
etym.Christopher: From {{der|en|la-lat|Christophorus}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Χρῑστόφορος||[[carrier]] of [[Christ]]}}, from {{der|en|grc|Χριστός||[[Christ]]}} + {{m|grc|φόρος||[[carrier]], [[bearer]]}}, from {{m|grc|φέρω|φέρειν|to [[carry]], to [[bear]]}} + {{m|grc|-ος||[[-er]]: ''[[form]]ing [[agent noun]]s''}}, from the legend of [[Saint Christopher]] carrying the infant Jesus across a river.
etym.Eugene: {{bor+|en|fr|Eugène}}, from {{der|en|la|Eugenius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐγένιος||well born}}, from {{suf|grc|εὖ|t1=good, well|γενής|t2=born a certain way|nocat=1}}. Parallel to {{m|en|eugenics}}. {{doublet|en|Yevgeny|Eugenius|Owen}}.
etym.Dennis: From {{inh|en|enm|Denis}}, from {{der|en|fro|-}} saint's name {{m|fro|Denis}}, brought to England by Normans; from Latin {{m|la|Dionysius}}, a masculine name literally meaning “follower of (the wine god) [[Dionysus]]”.
etym.Basil: Name of several early saints, particularly in the [[Orthodox Church]], from {{uder|en|la|Basilius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Βασίλειος}}. {{doublet|en|Vasilios|Vasily}}.
etym.Demetrius:
From {{der|en|grc|Δημήτριος|lit=belonging to {{l|grc|Δημήτηρ}}, the earth goddess}}; from {{m|grc|Δή}}, an early form of {{m|grc|γῆ|t=earth}} + {{m|grc|μήτηρ|t=mother}}. {{doublet|en|Dimitris|Dmitry}}.
{{wp}}
etym.Erasmus: From {{bor|en|la-med|Erasmus}}. The EU student exchange programme is named after {{w|Erasmus|Erasmus of Rotterdam}}, and also a {{glossary|backronym}} for “European [Community] Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students”.
etym.Dion: Borrowed from {{bor|en|grc|Δίων}}. Also a medieval English and French diminutive of [[Dionysius]] ([[Dennis]]).
etym.Damian: From the {{uder|en|grc|-}} name {{m|grc|Δαμιανός}} which was derived from {{m|grc|δαμάω||to tame}} (see {{m|grc|δαμάζω}}). Name known in Ancient Greece, later borne by Christian saints.
etym.Claus: From {{bor|en|nl|-}} and {{bor|en|de|Claus}}, a contraction of {{m|de|Nicolaus||[[Nicholas]]}}. The spelling {{m|en|Klaus}} is from more modern {{m+|de|Klaus}} and other Germanic languages.
etym.Collin: {{suffix|en|Coll|in}}. A spelling variant of {{m|en|Colin}}. From a medieval diminutive of {{m|en|Coll}}, a diminutive of {{m|en|Nicholas}}.
etym.Dorian: Constructed like the {{der|en|fr|Doriens}}. From the {{der|en|la|-}} root of {{m|la|Dōres}} + {{m|en|-ian}}. Compare {{cog|grc|Δωριεύς||of [[Doris]]}}.
etym.Cosmo:
{{wp|+ (name)}}
Borrowed by Scotland from Italy in the 18th century. An {{der|en|it|-}} variant of {{m|it|Cosimo}}, from the name {{m|und|Cosmas}} of a saint (martyred with his brother [[Damian]] in the fourth century), from {{der|en|grc|κόσμος||order, ordered universe}}.
etym.Cosmas: From {{bor|en|la|Cosmas}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κοσμᾶς}}, from {{m|grc|κόσμος}}. {{doublet|en|Cosmo}} and related to {{m|en|cosmos}}.
etym.Athanasius: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|Athanasius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀθανάσιος}}, from {{m|grc|ἀθανάσιος|t=immortal}}, from {{m|grc|ἀθάνατος|t=immortal}}. {{doublet|en|Athanasios|Afanasy}}. Compare {{m|en|Ambrose}}.
etym.Cleo:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ḱlew-}}
Shortened from {{m|en|Cleopatra}} or a variant of {{m|en|Clio}}. The rare male name derives from names of Ancient Greek origin such as {{m|en|Cleon}} and ''Cleopas''.
etym.Cletus: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|Clētus}}, short form of the papal name {{m|la|Anaclētus}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἀνάκλητος|t=invoked|pos=from {{af|grc|ἀνακαλέω|-τός|nocat=1}}}}.
etym.Cassander: From {{der|en|grc|Κάσσανδρος}}, from  {{m|grc|κέκασμαι|κέ'''κασ'''μαι|t=to shine; excel over}} and {{m|grc|ἀνήρ||man}}. In turn, the name means "one who excels over man."
etym.Leon: Ultimately from {{bor|en|la|Leo}} and {{m|la|leo||[[lion]]}}, from {{der|en|grc|Λέων}} and {{m|grc|λέων||[[lion]]}}, likely ultimately from a non-Indo-European language. Sometimes via other related languages such as {{der|en|fr|Léon}} and sometimes as a diminutive of related names such as {{m|en|Leonard}} and {{m|en|Leonardo}}.
etym.Orion: From {{inh|en|enm|Orioun}}, from {{der|en|la|Ōrīōn}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ὠρίων}}, speculatively from {{der|en|akk|𒌋𒊒𒀭𒈾|tr=Uru-anna||heaven's light}}, though without any firm evidence.
etym.Jason: From the {{der|en|grc|Ἰάσων|}}, from {{m|grc|ἰάομαι||I heal}}. The Jason mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 17:5-9, Romans 16:21) is probably a Greek rendering of [[Joshua]].
etym.Jerome: From the {{der|en|fro|-}} vernacular form of the saint's name [[Hieronymus]], from {{der|en|grc|Ἱερώνυμος}}. {{doublet|en|Geronimo|Hieronymus}}.
etym.Jacques:
{{ety|fr|:slbor<unc>|la:Iācōbus|tree=1}}
From {{der|fr|la|Iācōbus}}, possibly a semi-learned borrowing (compare inherited {{cog|fro|James}}, source of {{cog|en|James}}), from {{der|fr|grc|Ἰάκωβος}}, from {{m|grc|Ἰακώβ}}, from {{der|fr|hbo|יַעֲקֹב|tr=Yaʿăqōḇ}}. {{doublet|fr|Jacob}}, a learned borrowing. Note {{uder|fr|fro|Jasque}}.
etym.Orpheus: From {{bor|en|grc|Ὀρφεύς}}, built from an uncertain root with the {{m|grc|-εύς}} suffix. Perhaps root-cognate to {{cog|grc|ὀρφανός|t=orphan}}.
etym.Hercules:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ḱlew-}}
From {{bor|en|la|Herculēs}}, from {{der|en|ett|𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἡρακλῆς}}, apparently cognate of {{m|grc|Ἥρα||Hera}} and, according to Haudry, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*yóh₁r̥|t=year, season}} + {{m|grc|κλέος||glory}}. {{doublet|en|Heracles}}.
etym.Gregory: Via {{der|en|la|Grēgorius}}, from post-classical {{der|en|grc|Γρηγόριος|t=watchful, vigilant}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἐγείρω|t=awaken, arouse}}.
etym.Hyacinth: From {{uder|en|la|Hyacinthus}}, a saint's name from {{uder|en|grc|Ὑάκινθος}}, the name of a mythological character.
etym.Galen:
[[File:Galenus.jpg|thumb|A 17th-century [[engraving]] of Galen ''({{senseno|en|Roman and Greek physician}})'' by Georg P. Busch]]

From {{inh|en|enm|Galen}}, from {{der|en|la|Galēnus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Γαληνός}}, from {{m|grc|γαλήνη|gloss=calm, tranquillity}}.<ref>{{R:OED Online|pos=n|id=3298469322}}</ref>
etym.Isidore: {{uder|en|fr|-}} form of the name of early {{der|en|es|-}} saints, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰσίδωρος|}}, meaning "gift of (the goddess) [[Isis]]".
etym.Giles: Medieval English form of {{der|en|fro|-}} saints' name {{m|fro|Giles}}, modern {{m|fr|Gilles}}, an altered form of {{der|en|la|Aegīdius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Αἰγίδιος}}, derivative of {{m|grc|αἰγίδιον||kid, young goat}}.
etym.Eustace:
From the {{der|en|fro|-}} form of {{der|en|la|Eustathius||}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐστάθιος||ancient name, also of Christian Saint}}, from  {{der|en|grc|εὐσταθής||steadfast, stable}}.
Or from {{m|grc|εὔστᾰχῠς||fruitful|lit=abundant in grain}}, from {{m|grc|εὖ}} + {{m|grc|στάχυς}}. {{doublet|en|Ostap}}.
etym.Klaus: From {{der|fi|gmh|}} (compare {{cog|de|Klaus}}), a short form of {{der|fi|la|Nicolaus}}. Attested in Finland since the Middle Ages. Also later associated with the saint's name {{ncog|la|Claudius}}.<ref>{{R:fi:Etunimet}}</ref>
etym.Isadore: A [[non-standard]] variant of [[Isidore]], possibly inspired by the well-known feminine variant [[Isadora]] of [[Isidora]].
etym.Iskander:
{{dercat|en|grc}}
{{bor+|en|ar|الإسْكَنْدَر|t=Alexander}}. This surname is mostly found among [[Copt]]s in [[Egypt]]. {{doublet|en|Alexander}}
etym.Nicander: {{bor+|en|la|Nicander}}, itself a borrowing from {{der|en|grc|Νίκανδρος}}. Cognate with {{cog|fr|Nicandre}}.
etym.Paris: From {{bor|mul|la||herba Paris (Herba Paris), Paris herba}}, from {{der|mul|la|herba}} and {{der|mul|la|par||equal}}, in reference to the regularity of its leaves, petals, etc. See image.
etym.Peter: From {{inh|en|enm|Peter}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Petrus}}, from {{der|en|la|Petrus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Πέτρος}}, from {{m|grc|πέτρος|t=stone, rock}}. {{doublet|en|Pedro|Piers|Boutros}}.
etym.Steven:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*stegʷʰ-}}
{{inh+|en|enm|Stevene}}, {{m|enm|Steven}}, from {{der|en|xno|Estievne}}, {{m|xno|Estievene}}, from {{der|en|la|Stephanus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Στέφανος}}, from {{m|grc|στέφανος||crown, wreath}}, from {{m|grc|στέφω||to put round, to surround}}.
etym.Philip:
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:Philip}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Philip}}, ultimately from {{der|en|grc|Φίλιππος|}}, name of ancient kings of Macedonia, from {{m|grc|φίλιππος||fond of horses}}, from {{af|grc|φιλέω|t1=to love|ἵππος|t2=horse|nocat=1}}.
etym.Theo: Short form of [[Theodore]], or of the rare given names [[Theobald]], [[Theophilus]] or [[Theodoric]], or of [[Theodora]].
etym.Sebastian: From {{der|en|la|Sebastiānus}}, name of an early [[Christian]] saint, from ancient city of {{w|Sebaste}} in [[Asia Minor]] (modern {{w|Sivas}}, Turkey), from {{der|en|grc|Σεβαστός||august, venerable, exalted}}, itself a translation of the Roman title {{m|la|Augustus}}.
etym.Phineas: From {{bor|en|grc|Φινέας}}, alternative form of {{m|grc|Φινεύς}}. See ''{{w|Phineus}}''. Alternative source from {{uder|en|he|(פִינְחָס)}}. See ''[[Phinehas]]''.
etym.Phinehas: Uncertain. From {{bor|en|hbo|פִּינְחָס|tr=Pīnəḥās}}; further derivation is uncertain. {{m|hbo|פִּינְחָס|tr=Pīnəḥās}} has been suggested to derive from {{der|en|egy|pꜣ-nḥsj|lit=the [[Nubian]]}}, from {{m|egy|pꜣ}} + {{m|egy|nḥsj}}. Alternatively, within Judaism the name has been suggested to be a compound of the elements {{m|hbo|פה|tr=mouth}} and {{m|hbo|נחש|tr=intuitive knowledge}}, and so meaning "[[oracle]]", but this has been suggested to be an example of [[folk etymology]] made after the fact.
etym.Rastus: Thought to be derived from {{m|en|Erastus}}. Despite paucity of actual usage, the name became associated with African-American men because of a character in the first ''Uncle Remus'' book by Joel Chandler Harris.
etym.Sophus: A less common spelling of [[Sofus]], from the {{der|da|la|-}} cognomen {{m|la|Sophus}}, from {{der|da|grc|-}} meaning "wisdom"; a masculine equivalent of [[Sophia]].
etym.Strephon: From {{bor|en|grc|στρέφων}}, the active present participle of {{der|en|grc|στρέφω|t=to [[twist]], to [[avert]]|pos=verb}}, chiefly from its use as the name of a rustic lover in Sir Philip Sidney's 1593 pastoral romance [[w:The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia|''The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia'']].
etym.Petre: From a medieval spelling variant of [[Peter]].
etym.Procopius: Via {{der|en|la|Procopius}} from {{der|en|grc-koi|Προκόπῐος}}, from {{der|en|grc|προκοπή|t=progress forward to prosperity; advancement toward success; improvement by diligence}}, with Latin suffix {{m|la|-ius}} equivalent to Greek suffix {{m|grc|-ῐος}}.
etym.Theodore: {{etymon|en|id=given name|:lbor|la:Theodōrus|tree=1|text=++}} The name was popularized in reference to the prominent {{w|St Theodore of Amasea}}. Unrelated to {{m|en|Theodoric}}.
etym.Abdulaziz: {{bor+|en|ota|عبد العزیز|tr=ʼabd ül-ʼaziz}}, from {{der|en|ar|عَبْد العَزِيز|lit=the servant of Aziz}}, one of the 99 names for Allah.
etym.Adel: Ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|*aþalaz}}. The female name is a rare variant of {{m|en|Adele}}. The surname is borrowed from {{bor|en|de|Adel}}.
etym.Ali:
{{root|en|ar|ع ل ي}}
From {{bor|en|ar|عَلِيّ|lit=high, exalted}}, from the Arabic root {{ar-root|ع ل ي|nocat=1}}.
etym.Abbas: From {{bor|en|ar|عَبَّاس||one who frowns a lot; untamed lion}}, from {{m|ar|عَبَسَ||to frown}}, the title of the eightieth [[sura]] of the [[Qur'an]]. {{root|en|ar|ع ب س}}
etym.Abdinasir: From {{der|en|ar|عَبْد النَّاصِر||servant of the Protector}}. {{root|en|ar|ع ب د|ن ص ر}}
etym.Ahmad: {{bor+|en|ar|أَحْمَد}}, elative of {{m|ar|حَمِيد||praiseworthy}}; or from {{bor|en|fa|اَحْمَد<tr:ahmad>}}. {{root|en|ar|ح م د}}
etym.Abdullatif: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|عَبْد اللَّطِيف|t=servant of the Kind}}. {{root|en|ar|ع ب د|ل ط ف}}
etym.Abdunnasir: From the {{der|en|ar|عَبْد النَّاصِر||servant of the Protector}}. {{root|en|ar|ع ب د|ن ص ر}}
etym.Theophilus: From {{inh|en|enm|Theophilus}}, from {{der|en|la|Theophilus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Θεόφιλος}}, meaning "love of God" or "friend of God".
etym.Zeno:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*dyew-}}
Via {{bor|en|la|Zēnō}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ζήνων}}, an ancient derivative of {{m|grc|Ζεύς}}, from {{der|en|grk-pro|*dzéus}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*dyḗws}}. Modern scientific and philosophical use derives from {{w|Zeno of Elea}}, poser of {{w|Zeno's paradoxes}}.
etym.Abu Bakr:
{{root|en|ar|ء ب و|ب ك ر}}
{{translit|en|ar|أَبُو بَكْر|lit=father of a young camel; father of a person named Bakr}}.
etym.Timaeus: From {{bor|en|la|Tīmaeus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Τῑ́μαιος}}, from {{der|en|grc|τῑμάω|t=honour|pos=verb}}. Appears as the name of one of [[Plato]]'s dialogues. It is also the name of a person mentioned in the [[New Testament]] (Mark 10:46).
etym.Amirul:
{{root|en|ar|ء م ر}}
Ultimately from {{bor|en|ar|أَمِير||commander, prince}}. A case of rebracketing, the ''-l'' probably comes from {{der|en|ar|ال}}, through it being a shortening of {{der|en|ar|أمير المؤمنين|tr=ʔamīr al-muʔminīn}}. {{doublet|en|admiral}}.
etym.Ahmaud: Apparently a variant of [[Ahmad]], from {{der|en|ar|أَحْمَد}}, from {{m|ar|حَمِدَ||to thank or to praise}}. {{root|en|ar|ح م د}}
etym.Hasan:
From {{bor|en|ar|حَسَن|t=fine, good, good-looking, handsome, manly; strong}}.
{{root|en|ar|ح س ن}}
etym.Hassan:
From {{bor|en|ar|حَسَن|t=fine, good, good-looking, handsome, manly; strong}}.
{{root|en|ar|ح س ن}}
etym.Hany: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|هَانِيّ}}, meaning "one who lives in happiness and tranquillity"; "the embellisher"; or "luscious".
etym.Barack: Anglicized spelling, used by [[Luo]] speakers, of {{m|en|Barak}}, ostensibly as an [[Old Testament]] name. A cognate of the biblical {{m|en|Baruch}}.
etym.Baha:
{{root|en|ar|ب ه ي|ب ه و}}
From {{der|en|ar|بَهَاء|t=splendor, glory}}.
etym.Burhan:
From {{der|en|ar|بُرْهَان||proof}}, an epithet of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]].
{{root|en|ar|ب ر ه ن}}
etym.Basheer:
From {{der|en|ar|بَشِير||bringer of good news}}
{{root|en|ar|ب ش ر}}
etym.Hamza:
From {{bor|en|ar|حَمْزَة|lit=[[lion]]}}, from the [[Arabic]] root {{ar-root|ح م ز|nocat=1}}.
{{root|en|ar|ح م ز}}
etym.Hakim:
{{bor+|en|ar|حَكِيم|tr=ḥakīm|t=wise}}. This surname is mostly found in [[Indonesia]].
{{root|en|ar|ح ك م}}
etym.Bilal: From {{der|en|ar|بِلَال}}, specially {{w|Bilal ibn Rabah|Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ}}.
etym.Hashim:
From {{der|en|ar|هَاشِم|t=Hashim}}. The name signifies “breaker of bread”, from {{m|ar|هَشَمَ|t=to destroy, smash}}.

{{root|en|ar|ه ش م}}
etym.Bismillah:
From {{bor|en|ar|بِاسْمِ اللّٰه|tr=bismi llāh|t=in the name of God}}
{{root|en|ar|س م و|ء ل ه}}
etym.Elham: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fa|الهام|tr=elhâm}}, itself borrowed from {{der|en|ar|إِلْهَام|t=inspiration}}. Related to ''{{l|en|Ilham}}''.
etym.Ghassan: Said to be named after a nearby lake of the same name.
etym.Lulu: A {{reduplication|en|Lu|nocap=1}}, a {{clipping|en|nocap=1}} of given names with the first syllable of ''Lu'', ''Lou'', such as {{m|en|Lucy}}, {{m|en|Lucille}}, {{m|en|Louise}}, {{m|en|Louisa}}.
etym.Husayn:
{{translit|en|ar|حُسَيْن}}, from the root {{ar-root|ح س ن|nocat=1}}.
{{root|en|ar|ح س ن}}
etym.Mohammad:
{{bor+|nb|ar|مُحَمَّد|tr=muḥammad|t=praised, commendable}}, through a Latin-script transliteration of the Arabic name. The Arabic form is the passive participle of {{der|nb|ar|حَمَّدَ|tr=ḥammada|t=to praise, commend}}, from the root {{m|ar|ح م د|tr=ḥ-m-d|t=praise}}.

Related Arabic names include {{m|ar|أَحْمَد|tr=ʔaḥmad|t=more praiseworthy}} and {{m|ar|مَحْمُود|tr=maḥmūd|t=praised}}.
etym.Mahmud: {{translit|en|ar|مَحْمُود|lit=praised, laudable}}, the {{ar-passive participle|nocat=1|noderived=1}} of the {{ar-form|I}} verb {{m|ar|حَمِدَ|t=to praise}}, from the triconsonantal root {{ar-root|ح م د|nocat=1}}. The name {{m|en|Muhammad}} comes from the same root, and has a similar meaning. {{root|en|ar|ح م د}}
etym.Jafar: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|جَعْفَر}}. A transliteration of an Arabic and Persian male [[given name]].
etym.Masoud: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|مَسْعُود}}; this surname is predominantly found in [[Tanzania]] and [[Egypt]]. {{root|en|ar|س ع د}}
etym.Irfan:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|عِرْفَان|tr=ʕirfān|t=knowledge}}. This given name is mostly found in [[Pakistan]].
{{root|en|ar|ع ر ف}}
etym.Mashallah: From {{bor|en|ar|مَا شَاءَ ٱللَّه}}. {{root|en|ar|ش ي ء|ء ل ه}}
etym.Labib: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|لَبِيب|lit=sensible, reasonable}}; this surname is predominantly found in [[Egypt]]. {{root|en|ar|ل ب ب}}
etym.Muhammad:
{{translit|en|ar|مُحَمَّد|t=[[praise]]d, [[commendable]], [[laudable]]}}, the passive participle of {{m|ar|حَمَّدَ||to [[praise]], [[commend]], [[laud]], [[extol]]}}. From the same triconsonantal root {{ar-root|ح م د|nocat=1}} as, but distinct from, {{pwd|en|Mahmud|notext=1}}. {{dbt|en|Mahound|mammet}}.
{{root|en|ar|ح م د}}
etym.Musa: {{bor+|mul|la-med|musa}}, from {{der|mul|ar|مَوْزَة||banana}}, from {{der|mul|pal|𐭬𐭅𐭆|tr=mwc|ts=mōč}}, from {{der|mul|sa|मोच}}; see there for more.<ref>{{cite-web |last=Blench |first=Roger|authorlink=Roger Blench|title=Things your classics master never told you: a borrowing from Trans New Guinea languages into Latin |url=https://www.academia.edu/25619010/Things_your_classics_master_never_told_you_a_borrowing_from_Trans_New_Guinea_languages_into_Latin |work=Academia.edu |publisher=Academia, Inc. |year=2016}}</ref>
etym.Rahim: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|رَحِيم|t=[[kind]], [[compassionate]]}}. The surname is predominantly found in [[Bangladesh]]. {{root|en|ar|ر ح م}}
etym.Osman: {{inh+|en|enm|-}}, from {{uder|en|non|Ásmundr}},<ref>{{cite book|en|1901|first=Charles Wareing|last=Bardsley|entry=Osman|title=A Dictionary of English and Welsh Surnames|location=London|page=574|pageurl=https://books.google.com/books?id=GkAHAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA574}}</ref> from {{m|non|áss|t=a god|id=god}} + {{m|non|mund|t=protection, hand}}.
etym.Nuh: Ultimately from {{bor|en|ar|نُوح}}, sometimes through other languages.
etym.Radhi: From {{bor|en|ar|رَاضِي}}.<!--{{root|en|ar|ر ض و}} or ر ض ي?-->
etym.Muhammed: Borrowed from {{bor|fi|ar|مُحَمَّد|tr=muḥammad}}; the Finnish transliteration and spelling are most likely influenced by German {{m|de|Mohammed}} and Swedish {{m|sv|Muhammed}}.
etym.Omari: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|عمري}}. The surname is predominantly found in [[Tanzania]].
etym.Reza: {{bor+|en|fa-ira|رِضَا}}, from {{m+|fa-cls|رِضَا}}, borrowed from {{m+|ar|رِضَا}}, from {{m|ar|رِضًا||satisfaction, fulfillment}}, verbal noun of {{m|ar|رَضِيَ||to be pleased; to be satisfied}}. {{root|en|ar|ر ض و}}
etym.Nasrallah: From {{bor|en|ar|نَصْر اللَّٰه}}. {{root|en|ar|ن ص ر|ء ل ه}}
etym.Najibullah:
From {{bor|en|ar|نجيبالله|lit=distinguished servant of the god Allah}}, from {{m|ar|نجيب||{{m|en|Najib}}}}+{{m|ar|الله||{{m|en|Allah}}}}.
{{root|en|ar|ن ج ب|ء ل ه}}
etym.Riza: {{bor+|en|fa|رِضَا<tr:rizā>}}, borrowed from {{m+|ar|رِضَا}}, from {{m|ar|رِضًا||satisfaction, fulfillment}}, verbal noun of {{m|ar|رَضِيَ||to be pleased; to be satisfied}}. {{root|en|ar|ر ض و}}
etym.Sami:
{{etymon|en|id=ethnonym|:der|se:Sápmi|tree=1}}
From {{der|en|se|Sápmi}},<ref>{{R:New English Dictionary}}</ref> from one of the {{der|en|smi}} languages, of uncertain origin/meaning, but possibly related to {{der|en|ine-bsl-pro|*źémijāˀ||land}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|Finn}} (the direct descendant is {{m|en|Finn||person from Finland}}). More at [[w:Sápmi#Etymology|Sápmi]] and [[w:Sámi people#Etymologies|Sami]].
etym.Tariq:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|طَارِق|t=[[messenger]], nocturnal [[visitor]], or [[morning star]]}}, from {{m|ar|طَرَقَ|t=to [[knock]], to [[rap]]}}.
{{root|en|ar|ط ر ق}}
etym.Sabir: {{bor+|en|pml|sabir||know}}, in [[w:Molière|Molière]]'s ''{{w|Le bourgeois gentilhomme}}'', probably from {{der|en|es|saber}}, ultimately from {{der|en|la|sapio|sapere}}.
etym.Zahir:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|ظَاهِر}}, {{m|ar|ظٰهِر}}. The surname is mostly found in [[Afghanistan]] and [[Pakistan]].
{{root|en|ar|ظ ه ر}}
etym.Saleh: From {{bor|en|fa-ira|صالح|tr=sâleh}} or directly from {{bor|en|ar|صَالِح|lit=[[pious]]}}. {{root|en|ar|ص ل ح}}
etym.Salah: As an Islamic/{{der|en|ar|-}} surname, as well as a Jewish adoption of it, from {{m|ar|صَلاة|t=prayer}} or {{m|ar|صَلاح|t=righteousness}}. {{root|en|ar|ص ل و}} {{root|en|ar|ص ل ح}}
etym.Usman: Via an intermediary language, such as {{bor|en|fa-cls|عُثْمَان}}, or {{bor|en|ms|Usman}}, from {{der|en|ar|عُثْمَان}}.
etym.Shakur: {{bor+|en|ar|شَكُور|t=thankful, grateful}}. This surname is predominantly found in [[India]]. {{root|en|ar|ش ك ر}}
etym.Sajid: {{bor+|en|ar|سَاجِد|tr=sājid}}. This surname is mostly found in [[Pakistan]]. {{root|en|ar|س ج د}}
etym.Jesus: From {{inh|en|enm|Jhesus}}, {{m|enm|Iesus}}, from {{der|en|la|Iēsūs}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰησοῦς}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יֵשׁוּעַ|tr=yēšū́aʿ}}, a contracted form of {{m|he|יְהוֹשֻׁעַ|tr=yəhōšúaʿ|gloss=[[Joshua]]}}, meaning "the Lord saves". The form {{m|he|יֵשׁוּעַ|tr=yēšū́aʿ}} is attested in some of the later books of the Hebrew Bible ([[w:Ezra–Nehemiah|Ezra–Nehemiah]]), and translated as [[Jeshua]] or [[Yeshua]] in some English editions (the former appearing in the [[King James Version]]). The Greek texts make no distinction between Jesus and [[Joshua]], referring to them both as {{m|grc|Ἰησοῦς}}. In the Wycliffe Bible (Middle English), the forms used are {{m|enm|Jhesus}} and {{m|enm|Jhesu}}.
etym.Thomas:
{{inh+|en|enm|Thomas}}, from {{der|en|la|Thōmās|g=m}} (as in the Vulgate), from {{der|en|grc|Θωμᾶς|g=m}}, the Biblical Greek transcription of {{der|en|arc|תאומא}} or {{m|arc|תאמא||twin}}, the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles.

In the gospel of John (11:16, 20:24), the Aramaic nickname is also translated into Greek, as {{m|grc|δίδυμος|g=m}}. Used as a given name since the Middle Ages, e.g. {{w|Thomas the Presbyter}} (7th century), {{w|Thomas the Slav}} (8th century), {{w|Thomas of Bayeux}} (died 1100).

{{sense|infidel or doubter}} In reference to the doubting Apostle.
etym.Alan: From {{der|en|obt|Alan}}, name of early {{der|en|br|-}} saints, of disputed origin and meaning; brought to England by [[Norman]]s.  It may have been the name of a Celtic deity, the brother of ''Bran'', {{cog|cy|Alawn}}, {{m|cy|Alun}}. As an early Irish name, perhaps connected with {{m|ga|ail||noble}}. Compare {{cog|fr|Alain}}.
etym.Joan:
A clipped or [[hypochoristic]] form of {{m|en|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}}.
{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Zia: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|ضِيَاء||light}} via Spanish. {{root|en|ar|ض و ء}}
etym.Bartholomew:
From {{bor|en|la|Bartholomaeus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Βαρθολομαῖος}}, from {{der|en|arc|בר תלמי|tr=bar tolmai|t=son of [[Talmai]]; son of [[Ptolemy]]}}, from {{m|arc|בר|tr=bar|t=[[son]]}} and {{m|arc|תלמי|tr=tolmai|t=[[Talmai]]; [[Ptolemy]]}}. It has long been unclear whether the Apostle's father was named after the biblical Talmai, king of Geshur, or one of the Greek Ptolemies, as the two originally unrelated names were conflated in [[w:Judeo-Aramaic languages|Jewish Aramaic]].

The name's pronunciation was changed to match the spelling; contrast {{cog|fr|Barthélemy}} from the same source.
etym.Anirban: From {{der|en|bn|অনির্বাণ}}, from {{der|en|sa|अनिर्वाण}}, meaning an eternal or inextinguishable flame (of life), from {{der|en|sa|अ-||un-}} + {{m|sa|निर्वाण||dying}}.
etym.Manasseh: From alteration of {{der|en|la|Manasses}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Μανασσῆς}}, from {{der|en|hbo|מְנַשֶּׁה|tr=M'nashé}} + {{der|en|grc|-ς|pos=''[[form]]ing [[noun]]s''}}, to more closely match the original Hebrew form. The biblical etymology for the name connects it to {{m|hbo|נִשָּׁה}} or {{m|hbo|נישה||[[causing]] to [[forget]]|tr=nishá}}.
etym.Zinedine: {{bor+|en|ar|زين الدين}}, from {{m|ar|زين}} + {{m|ar|الدين}}, from {{m|ar|دين}} + {{m|ar| ال}}. {{transliteration|en|ar|زين الدين}}. {{lit|beauty of the faith}}. Variant of {{m|en|Zayn ad-Din}}.
etym.Gavin:
{{dercat|en|cel|cel-bry|cel-bry-pro|cel-pro}}
Medieval variant of {{m|en|Gawain}}, the name of an [[Arthurian]] knight, first recorded as {{m+|fro|Gauvain}}. The form ''Gavin'' survived in Scotland and spread to other English-speaking countries in the 1960s. {{doublet|en|Gawain}}.<ref>Bolton, Lesley (2009). The Complete Book of Baby Names. Sourcebooks, Inc</ref>
etym.Harvey:
From ''Haerviu'', name of a Breton saint, from {{der|en|obt|hoiarn||iron}} + {{m|obt|viu||blazing}}. Cognate with modern {{cog|br|Haerviu}}.

In Ireland, used as an anglicisation of {{der|en|ga|Ó hAirmheadhaigh}} and {{m|ga|Ó hEarchaidh}}.

The civil parish in New Brunswick is probably named in honour of British colonial administrator {{w|John Harvey}} (1778 - 1852).
etym.Tristan: {{uder|en|fro|-}}, the name of a knight, lover of [[Iseult]] in medieval romance [[w:Tristan and Iseult|Tristan and Iseult]], from {{uder|en|cel|-}} ''[[Drystan]]'' derived from ''[[drest]]'' meaning "riot" or "tumult".
etym.Percival:
From {{der|en|fro|Perceval}}, name of a knight in a twelfth century Arthurian romance by the French poet Chrétien de Troyes. Shaped like {{cog|fro|percier||pierce}} + {{m|fro|val||valley}}, but probably representing some {{der|en|cel-gau|-}} or {{der|en|owl|-}} name, possibly related to {{der|en|cy|Peredur}}, from {{m|cy|ber||spear, lance}} (from {{der|en|wlm|ber}}, from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*ber}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*beru||spit}}) + {{m|cy|dur||hard metal, steel}} (see {{cog|la|durus}}).

Cognate with {{cog|de|Parzival}} and {{m|de|Parsifal}}.
etym.Brice: From {{uder|fr|la-lat|Brictius|Bri(c)tius}}, {{m|la|Bricius}}, possibly from {{uder|fr|cel-gau|Briccus}}, {{m|cel-gau|*Brikkos}}, from {{uder|fr|cel-pro|*brikkos||speckled}}. The name of a 5th-century French saint.
etym.Schuyler:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*seǵʰ-}}
A {{bor|en|nl|-}} surname{{rfv-etym|en}} (cf. {{m|nl|scholier}}) from {{der|en|de|Schüler||scholar, student}};<ref>{{cite-web|author=Kuiken, Kees|work=''Digitaal Vrouwenlexicon von Nederland''|title=Schuyler, Alida (1656–1727)|publisher=[http://huygens.knaw.nl Huygens ING]|date=13 Jan. 2014|titleurl=http://resources.huygens.knaw.nl/vrouwenlexicon/lemmata/data/Schuyler|accessdate=14 Jul. 2018}}.</ref> brought to America by seventeenth-century Dutch immigrants. {{doublet|en|scholar|schooler}}.
etym.Jewell:
{{ety|en|:der|enm:-<ety:bor<obt:Judicaël<ety:af<iudd><cael>>>>|tree=+}}
Medieval/{{der|en|enm|-}} form of a {{der|en|br|-}} saint's name, from {{der|en|obt|Judicaël}} "lord" + "generous." The second element is from {{m|obt|hael|t=generous, bountiful}} and identical to {{cog|cy|hael|t=generous}} (see that entry for details).
etym.Joost: From earlier {{m|nl|Joos}}, from {{der|nl|la-med|Iodocus}}, {{m|la|Iudocus}}, from Old {{der|nl|br|Iodoc}}. Cognate with {{cog|en|Joyce}}.
etym.Onuphrius: From {{bor|en|la|Onuphrius}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ὀνούφριος}}, from {{der|en|egy|wnn-nfr|{{egy-h|E34:n:n-nfr-A40}}|tr={{l|egy|wnn-nfr}}|He who is Continually Good}}, an epithet of [[Osiris]].
etym.Petrock: Name of an obscure early saint, of {{uder|en|kw|-}} or {{uder|en|cy|-}} origin. Possibly related to [[Peter]].
etym.Galahad: From {{der|en|fro|Galahad}}, of obscure origin and meaning. Suggestions include Old Welsh, or biblical [[Gilead]].
etym.Coen:
* {{sense|Jewish}} Variant of {{m|en|Cohen}}.
* {{sense|given name}} As a modern given name, also a variant of {{m|en|Koen}}.
etym.Deacon:
* English occupational surname for someone working in the household of a {{m|en|deacon}}.
* Also as an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Dicken}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Deocáin}}, "descendant of {{m|ga|Deocán}}."
etym.Diederik:
{{etymon|en|:bor|nl:Diederik}}
Of {{der|en|nl|-}} origin, from {{der|en|dum|Diederic}}, from {{der|en|odt|*Thiodarīk}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Theodarīk}}, ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Þeudarīks}}. Compare with {{m|en|Derek}}, {{m|en|Theodoric}}.
etym.Imhotep: From {{der|en|egy|jj-m-ḥtp|lit=(the one) coming in peace, (the one) returning home safely}}: {{egy-h|M18-G17-R4:X1*Q3}} from the perfective active participle of {{m|egy|jj||to come, to return}} + {{m|egy|m ḥtp||in peace, safely}}.
etym.Jinping: From the {{bor|en|cmn-pinyin|-}} romanization of the {{bor|en|cmn|金平}}.
etym.Anil:
{{etymid|en|Indian}}
{{bor+|en|hi|अनिल}}, {{bor|en|mr|अनिल}}, {{bor|en|kn|ಅನಿಲ್}}, {{bor|en|ta|அனில்}}, {{bor|en|ml|അനിൽ}}, {{bor|en|bn|অনিল}}, {{bor|en|ne|अनिल}}, {{bor|en|ur|اَنِیل}}, or {{bor|en|si|අනිල්}}, from {{der|en|sa|अनिल||Hindu god of the wind}}.
etym.Adrian: From {{der|en|la|Hadrianus||from the Roman harbor Hadria}} a place name ultimately from {{der|en|ett|𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀}}. {{doublet|en|Hadrian}}. See {{w|Adria}}.
etym.Handy: Originating as a nickname for a [[handy]] person.
etym.Ivy: From {{m|en|ivy}}, the name of a plant. An ivy branch used to be hung outside an establishment to advertise that it sold alcohol, so it may originally been an occupationational surname for the proprietor of such an establishment. {{rfv-etym|en}}
etym.Laurel:
From {{bor|ceb|es|Laurel}}, from {{m|es|laurel}}. {{Catálogo alfabético de apellidos|ceb}}. {{doublet|ceb|laurel}}.

The municipality in Batangas is named after {{w|Jose P. Laurel}}, 3rd President of the Philippines.
etym.March:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:March|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|March}}, {{m|enm|Marche}}, borrowed from {{der|en|xno|marche}}, from {{der|en|fro|marz}}, from {{der|en|la|mensis Mārtius|gloss=the Martian month}}, from earlier {{m|la|Mavors}}.
etym.Olive: Medieval form of the {{uder|en|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Oliva}} "olive"; revived in the 19th century when flower and plant names became fashionable. The surname is topographical, often representing an Anglicization of continental European surnames such as {{uder|en|es|Oliva}}.
etym.Pearl:
From {{m|en|pearl}}.
* {{sense|river in China}} From {{der|en|zh|珠江||Pearl River|tr=Zhūjiāng, Zyu1 Gong1}}; {{calque|en|zh|珠||pearl|tr=zhū, zyu1|nocap=1}}.
* {{sense|haven in Hawaii}} From {{der|en|haw|Wai Momi|t=pearl water}}; {{calque|en|haw|momi||pearl|nocap=1}}.
etym.Sage:
* As an English and {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, from {{m|en|sage|id=wise person}}, a nickname for a wise person. The given name, in general use since the 1990s, is also associated with the {{l|en|sage|id=Salvia officinalis}} plant. Compare {{m|en|Desage}}, {{m|en|Lesage}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Savage}}.
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, from a placename derived from the noun {{m|de|sege|t=sedge}} (see {{m|en|sedge}}).
etym.Silver: As a surname, anglicised from the {{bor|en|de|-}} Jewish ornamental surname {{m|de|Silber}}.
etym.Algernon:
From {{der|en|fro|als gernons||having [[mustache]]s}}, from {{m|fro|als}} (contraction of {{m|fro|a}} and {{m|fro|les}}) + {{m|fro|gernon}}, variant of {{m|fro|grenon||mustache}}, from {{der|en|la-vul|*granonem||facial hair, mustache}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*granō||[[awn]], beard-hair, hair-tips, mustache}}, related to {{cog|goh|grana}}, {{m|ang|granu||mustache}}, {{cog|non|grǫn||mustache, (upper) lip}}, {{cog|ang|granu||mustache}}.

Mustaches were often a prominent cultural component for men of  some early medieval [[Germanic]] societies (contrary to popular culture, [[beard]]s were uncommon), whence the name originates from. However, the particular distinction owing this name [[vis-a-vis]
etym.Royal: A [[habitational]] surname, shaped by [[folk etymology]], from places in England, [[Riehale]], [[Righale]], [[Ryhill]] and [[Ryall]], {{inh|en|ang|ryge||rye}} + {{m|ang|hyll||hill}}, and [[Royle]], {{m|ang|rā||roe}} + {{m|ang|hyll||hill}}.
etym.Rowan:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₁rewdʰ-}}
Anglicised from the {{der|en|ga|-}} saints' name {{m|ga|Ruadhán||little red one}}, or as a surname from {{m|ga|Ó Ruadháin||descendant of Ruadhán}}.
etym.Rudyard:
{{inh+|en|ang|Rudierd}} (name of the village in Staffordshire, recorded in the [[Domesday Book]]), from {{der|en|ang|rude}} {{m|ang|geard|t=rue yard}}, first mentioned in
1002.<ref>{{cite book|last =Mills|first =A.D.|author=A.D. Mills|title =A Guide to English Place-Names|publisher =Oxford University Press|year=1998|location =Oxford}}</ref>
etym.Ivory: The surname is habitational from {{m|fr|Ivry}} in Normandy, and in some cases patronymic from a diminutive of {{m|en|Ivor}}. The modern given name is associated with {{m|en|ivory}}.
etym.Talon: The surname derives from {{der|en|fro|talon||heel}} as a nickname for a deformity, or for a swift runner; also diminutive of {{m|en|Talbot}} and {{m|fr|Talleyrand}}. The modern given name is associated with English {{m|en|talon}}.
etym.Juniper: A [[topographic]] surname from {{m|en|juniper}}. In some cases [[matronymic]] from an equivalent of {{m|en|Jennifer}} influenced by [[folk etymology]].
etym.Childebert: {{bor+|en|fr|Childebert}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Childebertus}}, ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Hildiberhtaz}}, from {{af|gem-pro|*hildiz|t1=battle, fight|*berhtaz|t2=bright, shining|nocat=1}}.
etym.Chlothar:
{{bor+|en|la-med|Chlōtharius}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Hlōdhari}}, ultimately from
From {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} {{af|gem-pro|*hlūdaz|t1=loud, famous|*harjaz|t2=commander, warrior|nocat=1}}. Cognate with {{cog|ang|Hloþhere}}, {{cog|de|Lothar}}.
etym.Joe:
{{etymon|en|id=Joseph|:clipping|Joseph<id:name>}} <!--for a particular person-->
{{etymon|en|id=name|:clipping|Joseph<id:name>|Joel|Josiah|Josias|tree=1}} <!--for broader use-->
{{U|short form}} ([[diminutive]] form) of various names beginning with ''Jo...'', particularly the male names [[Joseph]] and, less often, [[Joel]], [[Josiah]] and [[Josias]]. The spelling {{m|en|Jo}} is used more often for diminutives of similar female names.
etym.Noel:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ǵenh₁-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Nowel}}, borrowed from {{der|en|fro|Noel||Christmas}}, from {{der|en|la|natalis|'''nātālis [diēs''' Dominī]|'''birth[day''' of the Lord]}}. {{doublet|en|nada|natal|Natal|née}}.
etym.Bo: Either borrowed from modern {{bor|en|da|Bo}} or {{bor|en|sv|Bo}}, or a spelling variant of the male given name {{m|en|Beau}}.
etym.Jo:
[[clipping|Clipping]] or [[hypochoristic]] form of various female given names beginning with ''Jo...'', primarily {{m|en|Joan}}, {{m|en|Joanna}}, etc. but also {{m|en|Josephine}} and {{m|en|Jolene}}.

{{dbt|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} in reference to the first derivation.
etym.Henri: 20th-century given name from {{der|fi|en|Henry}}<ref>{{R:fi:Etunimet}}</ref> or {{der|fi|fr|Henri}}, akin to {{m|fi|Henrik}}.
etym.Michel:
{{etymon|en|:bor|fr:Michel|:inh|enm:Michel|tree=1}}
Either a [[reborrowing]] of {{bor|en|fr|Michel}} or a continuation (with pronunciation influenced by Modern French) of {{inh|en|enm|Michel}}, both from {{der|en|fro|Michel}}, from {{der|en|la|Michāēl}}, borrowed from {{der|en|grc-koi|Μῐχᾱήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|מִיכָאֵל|tr=mîḵāʾēl|lit=who is like God?}}. {{dbt|en|Michael|Miguel|Mikhail}}.
etym.Gaston: First recorded for medieval French aristocracy, of disputed origin, possibly from Germanic ''[[gast]]'' "guest". ("A man from [[Gascony]]" has also been suggested, compare [[Gascon]].)
etym.Germain: A [[patronymic]] from a medieval [[given name]], identical with the French one; or from an ethnic term for a [[German]].
etym.Esmé: First recorded as a male given name in Scotland in the sixteenth century, {{unk|en|title=probably}} from {{uder|en|fr|esmé||esteemed}}, or confused with {{m|fr|Aimé}} / {{m|fr|Aimée}}.
etym.Florent: Name of early Christian saints, from {{uder|fr|la|Florens|Florentem}} "flourishing".
etym.Caillou: From {{uder|en|fr|-}}; see {{m|fr|caillou}}. Nickname of the eponymous boy of the Canadian book and TV series ''{{w|Caillou}}''.
etym.Albert:
{{etymon|en|:inh|ang:Æþelbeorht|:der|fro:Albert<ety:der<la:Albertus>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|ang|Æþelbeorht}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Aþalaberht}}, a compound of {{m|gem-pro|*aþalaz||noble}} + {{m|gem-pro|*berhtaz||bright, famous}}, or from {{der|en|fro|Albert}}, from {{der|en|la|Albertus}}, itself from the Germanic name. Regardless of the exact route, it is a {{doublet|en|Ethelbert|nocap=1}}. It became popular in 19th-century England due to Queen Victoria’s consort, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.
etym.Abelard: From {{der|en|fr|Abélard}}, an extension of the {{m|fr|Abel}} with an {{der|en|gem|}} suffix ''-(h)ard''. Possibly also regarded a variant of the German {{m|de|Eberhard}} "boar" + "hard", equivalent to English {{m|en|Everett}}.
etym.Anne: From {{bor|en|fr|Anne||[[Ann]]}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[Vulgate]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα}} in the [[New Testament]], from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. Occasionally reborrowed from languages who adopted the name from English. Very infrequently from {{bor|en|et|-}} abbreviation of {{m|et|Anna}} instead. {{doublet|en|Ann|Ana|Anna|Hannah}}. Compare {{m|en|John}}.
etym.Ludwig:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ḱlew-|*weyk-|id2=contain}}
Borrowed from {{bor|en|de|Ludwig}}, which see for more information. {{doublet|en|Louis}} etc.
etym.Alf: From {{inh|da|non|Alfr}}, {{m|non|alfr|t=elf}}, with an identical meaning in modern Danish. Also a medieval contraction of {{m|da|Adolf}}, and later used as a pet form of {{m|da|Alfred}}.
etym.Johann:
{{bor+|nb|de|Johann|t=male given name}}, a short form of {{m|de|Johannes|t=male given name}}, ultimately from {{der|nb|la|Iōhannēs|t=male given name}}, from {{der|nb|grc|Ἰωάννης|tr=Iōánnēs|t=male given name}}, from {{der|nb|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān|t=Yahweh is gracious}}.

Compare {{cog|da|Johann}}, {{cog|sv|Johann}}, {{cog|fi|Johann}}, {{cog|is|Jóhann}} and {{cog|fo|Jóhann|t=male given names}}.
etym.Alger:
* As an English surname, when pronounced with a soft ''g'', from the {{der|en|enm|-}} personal name {{m|enm|Alger}}, borrowed from {{der|en|fro|Aug(i)er}}, of {{der|en|gem|-}} origin, from {{m|frk|*Adalgari}}, composed of {{m|frk|*aþal|t=noble}} + {{m|frk|*gaiʀ|t=spear}}. Compare {{m|en|Auger}}.
* When pronounced with a hard ''g'' it is a variant of {{m|en|Elgar|Algar}}. As a Scottish and English surname, it may be a variant of {{m|en|Algeo}}.
etym.Hermann: From the {{der|en|de|-}} and Jewish surname, from {{m|de|Hermann}}. Compare {{m|en|Harman}}, {{m|en|Herman}}.
etym.Engelbert: First attested as ''egniberde'' and ''eginberde'' in 1323. Compound of {{der|nl|ofs|Egge|pos=a personal name}} and {{m|ofs|bert|t=settlement}}.
etym.Amory: Medieval personal name from {{der|en|gem-pro|*amalą||vigor, bravery}} + {{m|gem-pro|*rīks||ruler}}. For the first element, compare {{m|gem-pro|*ammōną|t=to bother, irritate}}.
etym.Ludolph: Borrowed from {{der|en|de|Ludolf}}, an ancient personal name composed of the {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} elements {{af|gem-pro|*liudīz|t1=people|*wulfaz|t2=wolf|nocat=1}}.
etym.London:
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:Londoun|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Londoun}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Lunden}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|-}} via {{der|en|la|Londinium}} – see for details. {{doublet|en|Londinium}}.
etym.Devon: From {{inh|en|ang|Defenas}}, which meant both "Devonians" and "Devon," exemplifying the common [[w:Anglo-Saxons|Anglo-Saxon]] practice of naming a place after the people who inhabit it.
etym.Kerry:
* As an English surname, from a personal name derived from {{der|en|non|Kári}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Ciardha|t=descendant of Ciardha}}, from {{m|ga|ciar|t=black}}.
etym.Essex:
[[File:Flag of Essex.svg|thumb|Flag of Essex]]
{{inh+|en|ang|Ēastseaxan|lit=East [[Saxon]]s}}, which stood for both Essex and the people of Essex.
etym.Boston: The US city is named after the English town (from which several prominent colonists had come), which itself is sometimes said to be named as a contraction of {{m|en|[[w:St. Botolph|Botolph]]'s [[town]]}} or {{m|en|[[w:St. Botolph|Botolph]]'s [[stone]]}} (the name {{m|en|Botolph}} itself coming from {{der|en|ang|Botwulf}}, from {{m|ang|boda}} + {{m|ang|wulf}}). However, this is uncertain.
etym.Clyde: From {{der|en|gd|Cluaidh}}, the name of a river in Scotland, of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by ''clut'' (“the cleansing one”).
etym.Ceylon:
{{ety|en|:bor|pt:Ceilão|tree=1}}
{{bor+|en|pt|Ceilão}}, from {{der|en|fro|Seilan}} ({{w|Marco Polo}}), from {{der|en|fa|سیلان|tr=saylān}}, ultimately from {{der|en|pi|sīhaḷa}}, from {{der|en|sa|सिंहल}}. {{doublet|en|Sinhala}}.
etym.Augusta:
{{ety|en|:der|la:Augusta}}
From {{der|en|la|Augusta}}, feminine of {{m|la|Augustus}}. The places are mostly named for British royalty.
etym.Dallas:
# The Texas city was named after {{w|George M. Dallas}}, vice president to Polk; family name is evolved from ''dalhous'' (13th c.), meaning "dweller at the house in the dale," from {{m|en|dale}} + {{m|en|house}}.
# The Scottish place-name is from {{der|en|xpi|-}}, equivalent to {{cog|cy|dôl||meadow, haugh}} + {{m|cy|gwas||abode}}.
etym.Denver:
{{ety|en|:af<lit:crossing or passing of the Danes>|ang:Dene|ang:fær|:af<lit:valley-bank>|ang:denu|ang:ofer}}
{{named-after|en|James W. Denver|wplink==}}. The surname ''Denver'' ultimately derives from {{der|en|ang|-}} ''Dene-fær'' {{gloss|"crossing or passing of the Danes"}}, from {{m|ang|Dene}} + {{m|ang|fær}}; or alternatively from ''den-ōfer'' {{gloss|"valley-bank"}}, from {{m|ang|denu|}} + {{m|ang|ofer}}.
etym.Kimberley:
English place name "wood or clearing of [[w:Kyneburga|Kyneburga]] (a seventh century female saint)", from {{der|en|ang|cyne-||royal}} + {{m|ang|burh||fortress}} + {{m|ang|leah|lēah|[[leigh]], clearing}}.
{{wp}}
etym.Orville: Invented by Fanny Burney for the hero of her novel ''Evelina''. It has been suggested that it is based on the very old {{der|en|cy|-}} forename of {{m|cy|Eurfyl}}, meaning 'gold'.
etym.Fayette: After {{w|Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette}}
etym.Neo: Recent coinage from the prefix {{m|en|neo-||new}}. Popularized by a character in the science-fiction film ''{{w|The Matrix}}'' (1999), where it is explained as an anagram of "(the) One".
etym.Brixton: {{sense|district of London}} Thought to originate from ''Brixistane'', meaning "the stone of Brixi (a Saxon lord)".
etym.Mekhi: An African-American coinage, popularized by the actor {{w|Mekhi Phifer}}.
etym.Ronin: From modern films and comics, perhaps literally "a {{m|en|ronin}}". Compare also {{m|en|Ronan}}.
etym.Raiden: Possible a modern variant of {{m|en|Rayden}}, or a coinage rhyming with {{m|en|Braiden}}, {{m|en|Jaiden}}, etc.
etym.Texas: {{bor+|en|es|Texas}} (also {{m|es|Tejas}}), from Hasinai {{der|en|cad|táyshaʔ||friend, ally}}, used to refer to the [[Caddo]] nation.
etym.Addison: A [[Appendix:Glossary#patronimic|patronymic]] surname from a medieval diminutive form of {{suffix|en|Adam|son}}.
etym.Allison: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} diminutive form of {{m|en|Alan}}, {{m|en|Alexander}} or {{af|en|Alice|-son}}.
etym.Bailey: {{sense|English topographic surname}} {{cln|en|surnames from Old French}} See {{m|en|bailey||outer castle wall}}
etym.Ashley: From {{inh|en|ang|*Æsċlēah}}, composed of {{m|ang|æsċ|t=[[ash]] tree}} + {{m|ang|lēah|t=[[wood]], [[clearing]]}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|ash|alt1=Ash|-leigh|alt2=-ley}}.
etym.Blake: A surname derived from either {{der|en|ang|blæc||black}} or from {{der|en|ang|blāc||pale, fair, shining, white}}, or as an anglicisation of {{der|en|ga|Ó Bláthmaic}}.
etym.Abbott: An occupational surname for someone employed by an {{l|en|abbot}}. In the U.S., sometimes an anglicization of {{der|en|it|Abate}}, {{der|en|es|Abad}} or {{der|en|de|Abt}}. {{doublet|en|Abad}}.
etym.Boyd: From {{der|en|gd|-}}, either {{m|gd|buidhe||blond, yellow, fair}}, or a [[habitational]] surname from the [[w:Isle of Bute|Isle of Bute]] in Scotland.
etym.Trenton:
Originally named "Trent's town" in the 17th century, after a [[Quaker]], William [[Trent]].

The town in Nova Scotia is named after the capital of New Jersey.
etym.Beaumont: Inherited from {{inh|en|enm|}}, borrowed from {{der|en|xno|}}, from {{com|fro|bel|mont|alt1=beau|t1=beautiful|t2=mountain|nocat=1}}. Cognate with {{cog|fr|Beaumont}}. {{dbt|en|Belmont}}.
etym.Braden: Anglicised from an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname {{m|ga|Ó Bradáin||descendant of Bradán}}, from a personal name meaning "salmon," from {{m|ga|bradán|t=salmon}}.
etym.Becker: From {{m|de|Beck||baker}} (from {{der|de|gmh|becke}}), or a variant spelling of southern German {{m|de|Bäcker||baker}}.
etym.Anson: From {{suffix|en|Ann|son}} (the former word is a diminutive).
etym.Bing:
====Proper noun====
{{en-proper noun}}

# {{surname|en|from=Old English}} of {{inh|en|ang|-}} origin and unknown meaning.
# {{given name|en|male|from=surnames}}.
# {{given name|en|male|dimof=Bingley,Bingham}} (see also {{w|Bing Crosby}}).
etym.Alvis: First recorded as a given name of Latvians in early 20th century. Possibly of {{uder|lv|goh|-}} origin, from {{m|goh|al||all}} + {{m|goh|wīsī||wise}}, or from names beginning with Alv-, also as a masculine form of {{m|lv|Alva}}.
etym.Berry: Variant of [[Bury]] and (in dialects with Mary-marry-merry merger) [[Barry]]. The given name is also a pet form of names beginning with Ber-.
etym.Bellamy: Of Norman origin, from {{der|en|fro|bel||fair}} + {{m|fro|ami||friend}}. Could also be a locational surname from the Norman town of [[Bêlleme]] ([[Belesme]]).
etym.Bodie:
* As a Scottish surname, variant of {{m|en|Body}}, {{m|en|Boddy}}, {{m|en|Boddie}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Bodi}}, see {{m|en|Beaudin}}.
etym.Ainsley: Habitational surname for someone from [[Annesley]], [[Nottinghamshire]] or [[Ansley]], [[Warwickshire]], both from {{der|en|ang|anne||alone, solitary}} or {{m|ang|ānsetl||hermitage}} + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland, clearing}}.
etym.Blakeley: Habitational surname from several minor places in [[England]], from {{der|en|ang|blæc||black}} + {{m|ang|leah|lēah|woodland clearing}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|black|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
etym.Brent: English surname from placenames in [[Devon]] and [[Somerset]], from {{der|en|ang|brant|t=steep}}, referring to hills. Compare {{m|en|Brents}}.
etym.Bruce: From a Norman place name, [[w:Brix, Manche|Brix]], of disputed meaning.
etym.Brook:
* As an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|brook|id=body of water}}.
* As a north {{der|en|de|-}} surname, from {{der|en|nds|-}} {{m|nds-de|Brook|t=swamp, marsh}}, related to the above.
* As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Broek}}, from {{m|nl|broek|id=marsh}}, also related to the above.
* As a Jewish and German surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Bruck}}, {{m|en|Bruch}} (from {{m|de|Bruch|id=wetland|t=wetland, marsh}}).
etym.Browning:
From {{der|en|ang|Brūning}}, a [[Appendix:Glossary#patronymic|patronymic]] for a person nicknamed {{m|ang|Brūn||brown}} (see {{m|en|Brown}}).

For the first half-century of their manufacturer, the majority of semi-automatic handguns in Europe were designed by John M. Browning.
etym.Brock: From {{inh|gmw-cfr|goh||*brūd}}, northern variant of {{m|goh|brūt}}. The word underwent the regular Ripuarian velarization ''-ūd-'' → ''-ugd-'' → ''-og-''.
etym.Byron: A habitational surname from {{inh|en|ang|byrum||at the [[byre]] or cattleshed}}.
etym.Bradford:
* Various place names in England, from {{der|en|ang|brād||broad}} + {{m|ang|ford||ford}}.
* {{sense|shaken martini}} {{rfe|en}}
etym.Calvin: Latinization of Norman-Picard ''Cauvin'', a nickname for a {{m|fr|chauve|gloss=bald}} person.
etym.Braxton: Perhaps a habitational surname from the village of {{m|en|Branxton}}, in [[Northumberland]].
etym.Campbell:
* As a Scottish surname, from {{bor|en|gd|Caimbeul}}, from {{m|gd|cam|t=crooked}} + {{m|gd|beul|t=mouth}}. Compare {{m|en|Cameron}}, from {{m+|gd|cam|t=crooked}} + {{m|gd|sròn|t=nose}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Mac}} {{m|ga|Cathmhaoil|t=son of Cathmhaol}}, see {{m|en|Caulfield}}, {{m|en|Cowell}}.
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Camel}}, probably influenced by the above.
* {{sense|duck breed}} Developed by Adele Campbell.
etym.Cade:
* As an English surname, from an old personal name {{m|ang|Cada}}, from a {{der|en|gem|-}} root meaning "lump, swelling" and perhaps related to the next sense.
* Also as an English occupational surname for a cooper, from {{der|en|fro|cade|t=barrel, cask}}, from {{der|en|la|cadus}}.
* Also as an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|cade#Etymology 1|cade (sense 1)|t=domestic animal}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, spelling variant of {{m|fr|Cadé}}, from {{m|en|cade#Etymology 3|cade|t=juniper}}.
etym.Carey:
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Gehrig}}, {{m|en|Gehring}}.
* As a {{der|en|cy|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Carew}}.
* As an English surname, from placenames derived from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*karɨd|t=to love}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|mac}} {{m|ga|Fhiachra|t=descendant of [[Fiachra]]}}, from {{m|ga|préachán|t=crow}}.
* Also as an Irish surname, from the root of the name {{m|en|Kerry}}.
etym.Brodie: {{named-after|en|Steve Brodie|wplink=Steve Brodie (bridge jumper)|born=1861|died=1901}}, who made a disputed claim to have jumped off the Brooklyn Bridge and survived.
etym.Brennan: From {{bor|en|ga|Ó Braonáin||descendant of [[Braonán]]}}, a diminutive of {{m|ga|braon||moisture, drop}}. Alternatively, from {{bor|en|ga|Ó Branáin||descendant of [[Branán]]}}, a diminutive of {{m|ga|bran||raven}}.
etym.Callahan: From {{der|en|ga|Ó Ceallacháin}}, from {{m|ga|Ceallachán}}, diminutive of the given name {{m|ga|Ceallach}}. {{doublet|en|Kelly|Kellogg}}.
etym.Casey: Anglicisation of an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname {{m|ga|Ó Cathasaigh|lit=descendant of (a person named) Watchful}}.
etym.Claire: {{bor+|en|fr|Claire}}, also a spelling variant of the {{cog|en|Clare}}.
etym.Cole:
The surname is variously from:
# A nickname from {{der|en|ang|col||coal, coal-black}},
# A patronymic from {{m|en|Nicholas}} (see also {{m|en|Coles}}, {{m|en|Colson}}, {{m|en|Colle}}).
# A variation of {{m|en|Cowell}} (which itself has several origins).
# As an {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gd|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|McCool}}.
# As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Kohl}}.
# As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Kool}}.
# As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, Americanized/calqued from {{m|en|Charbonneau}}, influenced by the first sense.
etym.Clifford: From {{inh|en|ang|clif||cliff}} + {{m|ang|ford||ford}}, ''a dweller at the ford by the steep bank''.
etym.Corbin: An {{der|en|xno|-}} nickname from {{m|fro|corb||crow}}, or shortened from the Corbinian, the name of a Frankish eighth-century saint, probably from {{der|en|la|corvus||crow, raven}}.<ref>{{R:SUKCED |page=92 |column=1 |entry=Corbin, Corbyn |text=(Fr.-Lat.) the {{smc|Raven}} [O.Fr. ''corbin'', Lat. ''corvin-us''—''corv-us'', a raven]}}</ref>
etym.Carter: As an English name, from the occupation {{m|en|carter}}. As an Irish name, from {{der|en|ga|Mac Artúir|lit=son of Arthur}}.
etym.Collins:
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Colin}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gv|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Coileáin||t=descendant of [[Coileán]]}}, see {{m|en|Cullen}}, {{m|en|McQuillan}}, and {{m|en|McCallion}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Collin}} and {{m|en|Colette}}.
* As a {{der|en|sl|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Kolenc}}, from {{m|sl|koleno|t=knee}} and the obsolete {{m|sv|kolenc|t=nipplewort}}.
etym.Clifton:
*Literally meaning "town by a cliff." From {{der|en|ang|clif||cliff}} + {{m|ang|tūn||town}}. Analyzable as {{suffix|en|cliff|ton}}.
*In Oregon County, Missouri, from {{suffix|en|Cliff|ton}}. From being named after a {{m|en|Cliff}}, or which may be clipped to ''Clif''.
etym.Chester:
From {{inh|en|enm|Chestre}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ċeaster}}, from {{m|ang|ċeaster|t=a town or city, especially a Roman one}}.

The village in Nova Scotia is likely named after the city in Pennsylvania.
etym.Cassidy: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, Anglicized from {{m|ga|Ó Caiside|t=descendant of Caiside}}, from {{m|ga|cas|t=curly-haired}}.
etym.Clarence: Originally a ducal title of the English and British royal family, from {{m|la|Clārensis|t=from the town of Clare}}, (the town of Clare, Suffolk), although it has also been associated with {{der|en|it|Chiarenza}}, {{m|it|Clarentza}}, &c., a former fortress and settlement in the medieval [[Frankish]] [[principality|Principality]] of [[Achaea]] in [[Greece]].
etym.Carson: Could originate from the Gaelic name "Carr" or "Carra", meaning "rock" or "fort," combined with "son", thus "son of Carr.".
etym.Clinton:
* {{sense|English habitational surname}} A habitational surname, derived from places named {{w|lang=en|Glinton, Cambridgeshire|Glinton}} ("town on a hill") or {{w|lang=en|Glympton}} ("settlement on the River Glyme"), from {{der|en|ang|}} + {{m|ang|tun|gloss=enclosure, homestead, town}}, equivalent to the modern {{af|en|-ton}}.
* {{sense|given name}} Derived from the surnames.
* {{sense|DeWitt County}} Named after {{w|lang=en|DeWitt Clinton}}.
etym.Clayton: From {{inh|en|enm|Claytone}}, {{m|enm|Cleyton}}, from {{der|en|ang|clǣġ|t=clay}} + {{der|en|ang|tūn|t=enclosure, settlement; town}}. Analyzable as {{suffix|en|clay|ton}}.
etym.Chauncey: From the {{der|en|nrf|-}} name based on several locations in France called {{m|nrf|Chancé}}.  See {{cog|fro|chance}}.
etym.Colby: From either the {{der|en|non|-}} personal name {{m|non|Koli}} or {{m|non|kol||charcoal}} + {{m|non|býr||settlement}}.
etym.Cass:
* As an English surname, from a pet form of {{m|en|Cassandra}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Cais|t=descendant of the curly-haired one}}, from {{m|ga|cas|t=curly}}.
etym.Colbert: From a Germanic personal name, composed of {{der|en|gem-pro|*kōlaz||cool, cold; calm}} and {{m|gem-pro|*berhtaz||bright}}.
etym.Clay: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} occupational name for a clay worker, or a habitational name, from {{inh|en|ang|clǣġ||clay}}.
etym.Clancy: Reduced Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Mac Fhlannchaidh||descendant of a person named Red Warrior}}, from {{m|ga|flann||blood-red}}.
etym.Cash: Variant of {{m|en|Case}}. In the US adopted by German immigrants named {{m|de|Kirch}} and {{m|de|Kirsch}}.
etym.Cason: As an English surname, a corruption of the place name {{m|en|Cawston}} in Norfolk. Also borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Cason}}, from a [[Venetan]] form of {{m|it|casa||house}}.
etym.Colt: From {{m|enm|colt}}, as a nickname or occupational name for someone who looked after horses and asses. The given name may also be short for {{m|en|Colton}}. The revolver is {{named-after|en|Samuel Colt|wplink==|born=1814|died=1862|nat=American|occ=inventor|nocap=1}}.
etym.Darwin: From {{inh|en|enm|Darwin}}, {{m|enm|Derwin}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Dēorwine|gloss={{non-gloss|a given name}}}}, composed of {{m|ang|dēore|gloss=dear}} + {{m|ang|wine|gloss=friend}}. The city in Australia is named after {{w|Charles Darwin}}.
etym.Dane: From {{inh|en|enm|Dane}}, from {{der|en|non|danir}} or {{der|en|ang|Dene}}. Both forms ultimately descend from {{der|en|gem-pro|*daniz}}.
etym.Cory: From {{bor|tl|en|Cory}}, [[diminutive]] of {{der|tl|es-PH|Corazón}}, from {{der|tl|es|corazón|t=heart}}, short for {{m|es|María Corazón}}, a reference to the Immaculate Heart of [[Mary]] (''Inmaculada Corazón de María'' in Spanish).
etym.Dana: Of {{unc|en|nocap=1}} origin. Possibly from {{m|en|Dawnay}}, or else an altered form of {{m|en|Dan}} or {{m|en|Daniel}}.<ref>{{cite-book |last=Hanks |first=Patrick |title=[https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780190245115.001.0001/acref-9780190245115 Dictionary of American Family Names] |year=2022 |publisher={{w|Oxford University Press}} |isbn=9780190245115 |edition=second}}</ref>
etym.Darlington: From {{inh|en|enm|Dearnington}}, {{m|enm|Derlinton}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Dēornōþingtūn}}, supposedly “the settlement of {{l|ang|Dēornōþ}}'s people”, from an unclear root + {{m|ang|-ing}} + {{m|ang|tūn}}. Compare {{cog|ang|dīerling}}. The transistor configuration is named for its inventor, {{w|Sidney Darlington}}.
etym.Corrie: From {{der|en|gd|coire||cauldron, boiler; corrie}}, which denotes a bowl-shaped geographical feature similar to a [[cirque]].
etym.Drake:
* As an English surname, from both senses of the noun {{m|en|drake}} meaning "male duck" and "dragon."
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, from {{der|en|nds|drake|t=dragon}}, related to the above.
* As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, Americanized/{{der|en|vls|-}} variant of {{m|en|Draak}}, also related to the above.
etym.Darrell: Derived from [[d'Airel]], name of a [[Norman]] family that came from a place called [[Airelle]] in [[Calvados]].
etym.Courtney: Variant of {{m|en|Courtenay}}, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from {{der|en|la|Curtenus}}, a personal name from {{m|la|curtus||short}}.
etym.Devin:
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}}, English, and {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, spelling variant of {{m|en|Devine}}. Also see {{m|en|Devon}}.
* Also as a French surname, from {{m|fr|devin|t=fortuneteller}}.
* As a {{der|en|ru|-}} surname, from {{m|ru|дева|t=maiden}}.
etym.Dillon: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{der|en|br|Leon}} and {{der|en|nrf|Léon}}, named after Sir Henry de Leon of the {{w|Viscounty of Léon}}.<ref>Grenham, John (1994). The Little Book of Irish Clans. Dublin, Ireland: John Hinde. p. 19.</ref> Related to the surname {{m|en|Lyon}}. Unrelated to the name {{m|en|Dylan}}, although the homophony may result in the two being considered variant spellings of the same name.
etym.Duane:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*dʰewbʰ-}}
Anglicized form of the {{bor|en|ga|-}} name {{m|ga|Dubhán}} (from {{der|en|pgl|ᚇᚑᚃᚐᚌᚅᚔ}}), from {{m|ga|dubh||black, dark}}; or transferred from the surname, which is from {{der|en|ga|Ó Dubháin|lit=descendant of Dubhán}}.
etym.Dewey: Possibly from a place name in Northern France, ''Douai''. Welsh origin from [[Dewi]] ([[David]]) has also been suggested.
etym.Donovan: From {{bor|en|ga|Ó Donndubháin||descendant of (a person named) brown & black}}, from {{m|ga|donn||brown}} and {{m|ga|dubh||black}}.
etym.Darcy: Originally from {{w|Bois-d'Arcy, Yvelines}} in Northern France. Related to archaic {{der|en|fr|ardre||to burn, consume}}.
etym.Davion: The modern American usage is possibly transferred from the {{der|en|fr|-}} surname ''Davion'', based on a {{der|en|oc-pro|-}} diminutive of [[David]]. It is not used as a given name in France.
etym.Deane:
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, Anglicized from {{m|ga|Mac}} {{m|ga|an}} {{m|ga|Deagánaigh|t=son of the Deacon}}, see {{m|en|Deacon}}.
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Dean}}.
etym.Darby: From the English place name [[Derby]], from {{der|en|non|djúr||deer}} + {{m|non|býr||settlement}}.
etym.Digby:
From {{der|en|ang|dīc||dyke}} + {{der|en|non|býr||settlement}}.

The town in Nova Scotia is named after admiral {{w|Robert Digby}} (1732 - 1815).
etym.Crusoe: Perhaps from {{der|en|fr|Crusiaux}}, a topographic surname from a diminutive of {{m|fr|creux||hollow}}, or alternatively a variant of {{m|fr|Croiseau}}, a habitational surname.
etym.Dewitt: From {{bor|en|nl|de Witt}}. The verb sense alludes to the 17th-century assassination by lynching of Dutch politicians {{w|Cornelis de Witt}} and {{w|Johan de Witt}}.
