etym.Delmar: Contraction of {{m|en|Delamare}} and {{m|en|de la Mare}}, from places in [[Normandy]] named {{m|fro|La Mare||the pond}}. In the US, also borrowed from {{bor|en|ca|del Mar||of the sea}}.
etym.Errol: Transferred from a rare Scottish surname derived from a place name, of unknown meaning. Later interpreted as a variant of [[Earl]] in the U.S.
etym.Franklin: From {{der|en|enm|frankelein||freeholder}}, see {{m|en|franklin}}. The place names are mostly {{named-after|en|Benjamin Franklin|nat=American|occ=statesman|born=1706|died=1790|wplink==|nocap=1}}.
etym.Fletcher: English occupational surname from the noun {{m|en|fletcher|t=arrow-maker}}. Sometimes confused with {{m|en|Flesher}}.
etym.Foster: English surname, reduced from {{m|en|Forster}}; also from the noun {{m|en|foster}}.
etym.Gage: An [[occupational]] surname from {{der|en|enm|gage|gage, guage|measure}} for an [[assayer]], or {{m|enm|gage||pledge}} for a moneylender.
etym.Garland: English surname, from the noun {{m|en|garland}}. Also derived from Garland in [[Devon]], from an ancestor of the noun {{m|en|gore|id=triangular land|t=triangular piece of land}} + {{m|en|land}}.
etym.Gill:
* As an English surname, converged from variants of {{m|en|Giles}} (sometimes through {{der|en|nl|-}}), {{m|en|Julian}}, and {{m|en|William}}.
* As a northern English surname, from {{der|en|enm|gil|t=ravine, glen}}, from {{der|en|non|gil}}. The Old Norse is also a source of the {{der|en|no|-}} surname.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gd|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|McGill}}.
* Also as an Irish surname, variant of {{m|en|Gall}}.
* As a Jewish/Israeli given name, as well as surname, from {{der|en|he|גיל|t=joy}}.
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Gilger}}.
* As a Sikh {{der|en|pa|-}} surname originating in India, from {{m|pa|ਗਿੱਲ|tr=gill|t=moisture}}.
etym.Fleming: From {{inh|en|enm|flameng}}, from late {{der|en|non|Flæmingi}}, from {{der|en|non|Flǽmingr}}, {{der|en|dum|Vlaminc}}, {{m|dum|Vleminc}}, from {{der|en|ofs|-}} (unattested) (compare {{cog|fy|Flaming}}), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*flaumaz|t=flowing, current (water)}} and the patronymic suffix {{m|gem-pro|*-ingaz|t=belonging to, descended from}}. More at {{l|en|Flanders}}.
etym.Evelyn: From {{inh|en|enm|-}} forms of the {{der|en|fro|-}} female name {{m|fro|Aveline}}, diminutive of the {{der|en|gem|-}} root {{m|gem-pro|*avi-}}, of uncertain meaning, possibly “desired, wished for“ (compare {{cog|la|aveo|avēre}}, "to wish for") or ''aval'' “strength”. By {{glossary|folk etymology}} also misunderstood as a diminutive of the feminine given name {{m|en|Eve}}, q.v. {{doublet|en|Eileen}}. Also compare {{m|en|Ava}}.
etym.Dudley: From {{der|en|ang|-}}, literally "wood or clearing of {{m|ang|Dudda}} (a personal name of unknown meaning)".
etym.Gaylord: Derived from the {{der|en|fro|-}} surname {{m|fro|Gaillard}} (from {{m|fro|gaillard||strong}}), via {{der|en|xno|-}}. Compare {{cog|es|Gallardo}} (from {{m|es|gallardo||dashing, strapping, gallant}}. Shaped by {{lg|folk etymology}} into {{com|en|gay|lord|nocat=1}}.
etym.Fraser: Scottish surname thought to be from {{der|en|nrf|-}}, but not corresponding to any obvious places in France; perhaps a corrupted transcription of a {{der|en|mga|-}} name.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref> More at [[w:Clan Fraser#History|Fraser]].
etym.Forrest: English surname, from the noun {{m|en|forest}}. Also adopted and translated from the word for "forest" in various other languages by settlers.
etym.Floyd:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*pelH-}}
Anglicisation of the Welsh name {{lang|cy|Lloyd}}, from {{der|en|cy|llwyd||[[grey]], grey-haired}}.
etym.Dwight: Probably from a {{inh|en|enm|-}} female name [[Diot]], a pet form of [[Dionysia]], the feminine form of [[Dionysius]].
etym.Emmett: From a {{der|en|enm|-}} diminutive of the female given name [[Emma]].
etym.Emmitt: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} diminutive of the female given name {{m|en|Emma}}.
etym.Farley: From {{der|en|ang|fearn||fern}} + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|fern|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}} and doublet of {{doublet|notext=1|en|Farnley}}.
etym.Emmet: From a {{der|en|enm|-}} diminutive of the female given name [[Emma]].
etym.Fallon: Reduced Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Ó Fallamhain||descendant of Fallamhan}}, a personal name related to {{m|ga|follúnaitheoir||ruler, governor}}.
etym.Finnegan: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ga|Ó Fionnagáin||descendant of {{m|ga|Fionnagán}}}}. {{m|ga||Fionnagán}} is a given name that descends from [[Old Irish]] {{m|sga|Finnacán}}, which is typically anglicised as Finnegan itself.
etym.Edson: From {{suffix|en|Ed|son}}; originally given to the {{l|en|son}} of a man named Ed.
etym.Haskell:
* The programming language is {{named-after|en|nat=American|occ=logician|Haskell Curry|wplink==|born=1900|died=1982|nocap=1}}.
* As an English surname, from the {{der|en|enm|-}} personal name {{m|enm|Askell}}, from {{der|en|non|Áskell}}. Compare {{m|en|Axtell}}, {{m|en|Askin}}, {{m|en|Haskin}}, {{m|en|Hasty}}, {{m|en|Astin}}.
* As a surname in the Isle of Man, a variant of {{m|en|Castell}}, itself related to the above.
* As a Jewish surname, from {{m|en|Khaskl}}, a {{der|en|yi|-}} form of {{m|en|Yeḥezqel}}, see {{m|en|Ezekiel}}.
etym.Hamilton: From {{inh|en|ang|*Hameldūne}}, from {{m|ang|hamel||blunt, flat-topped}} + {{m|ang|dūne||hill}}. The Scottish surname is from the place in Leicestershire. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of {{w|Alexander Hamilton}} featured on it.
etym.Grant:
{{etymon|en|id=surname|:bor|gd:Grannd<id:surname>}}
From {{bor|en|gd|Grannd}}, from {{der|en|xno|graunt|t=big, large}}, from {{der|en|fro|grant}}, from {{der|en|la|grandis}}. {{doublet|en|grand}}. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of {{w|Ulysses S. Grant}} featured on it.
etym.Holly:
{{wp|+ (name)}}
{{swp|<dab!>}}
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, calque of {{m|ga|mac}} {{m|ga|cuilinn|t=holly}} (see {{m|en|McCullen}}) and sometimes {{m|en|McQuillan}}.
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Holley}}.
* As a {{der|en|cs|-}} and {{der|en|sk|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Holý}}, {{m|en|Holy}}.
* Also as a locational English surname, from {{der|en|ang|hol}} {{m|ang|leah|t=wood, clearing, meadow}}, compare {{m|en|Hollywood}}.
* Also as an English surname, short form of {{m|en|Holiday}}.
* Also as an English surname, after the {{m|en|holly}} tree.
* As a feminine given name popularized by Truman Capote's {{w|Breakfast at Tiffany's}} (especially the 1961 film adaptation star
etym.Hunt:
{{ety|de|:from|Hund}}
Originated as a metaphorical application of {{m|de|Hund||dog}} to small minecarts (16th c.), with final lenition generalized across all forms, though unlenited forms also still exist.
etym.Hayley: Localities in England, from {{inh|en|ang|-}} {{m|ang|hēg||hay}} + {{m|ang|lēah||wood, clearing}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|hay|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
etym.Houston: Originally from a place near [[Glasgow]], from the {{inh|en|enm|-}} equivalent of "[[Hugh]]'s town". Analyzable as {{affix|en|Hugh|-s-|-ton}}
etym.Hammond:
A patronymic surname from the {{der|en|xno|-}} given name {{m|fro|Hamo}}, {{m|fro|Hamon}}, from {{der|en|gem}} names beginning with a derivative of {{der|en|gem-pro|*haimaz||home}}, such as descendants of {{m|gem-pro|*Haimarīks||Henry}}.

The river in New Brunswick is named after British politician and colonial governor {{w|Sir Andrew Hamond, 1st Baronet}} (1738–1828). The civil parish is named after a settlement, named in turn after the river.
etym.Hampton:
Variously from:
* {{inh|en|ang|Hāmtūn}}, from {{m|ang|hām}} and {{m|ang|tūn}} (equivalent to {{m|en|home}} + {{m|en|town}});
* {{inh|en|ang|hēantūn}}, from {{m|ang|hēah}} and {{m|ang|tūn}}  (equivalent to {{m|en|high}} + {{m|en|town}}).<ref>https://www.ancestry.com/name-origin?surname=hampton</ref>

The town in New Brunswick may have been named after one of several towns in New England. The civil parish is named after the town.
etym.Howe:
* As an English surname, from {{der|en|enm|hoʒe|t=steep ridge}}, a late variant of {{m|enm|hōge}}, dative case of {{der|en|ang|hoh|t=hock, heel}}, with likely influence from {{der|en|non|haugr|t=hill}}.
* Also as an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Hugh}}, pronounced to rhyme with {{m|en|how}}.
* As a {{der|en|no|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Hove}}, from the dative singular of {{cog|non|hof|t=place of worship}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Haugh}}; also a variant of {{m|en|Hoey}}.
* As a {{der|en|zh|-}} surname, variant romanization of {{m|zh|侯}}, see also {{m|en|Hou}}.
* Also as a Chinese surname, possibly from {{der|en|yue|-}} form of the names {{m|zh|豪}},
etym.Graham: The surname derives from ''[[Grantham|Gra(nt)ham]]'', the name of a place in [[Lincolnshire]], from {{inh|en|ang|*grand||gravel}} + {{m|ang|hām||homestead}}.
etym.Hayden: Originally a place name, from {{inh|en|ang|heg||hay}} + {{m|ang|denu||valley}}. Alternatively, from {{der|en|dum|heiden||heathen}}.
etym.Granville: The commune of France is from {{der|en|fro|Granville}}, {{m|fro|Grandvilla}}, {{m|fro|Grande Villa}}, {{m|fro|Grandivilla}}, from {{m|fro|grant||grand}} + {{m|fro|ville||settlement}}. The surname is of {{der|en|nrf|-}} baronial origin, from {{w|Grainville}}, a former commune in Normandy, from the given name {{m|nrf|Guarin}} + {{m|nrf|ville}}, meaning “Guarin's town”. ''Guarin'' ultimately derives from {{der|en|gem-pro|*warduz||guard}}.
etym.Hayes:
*As an English locational surname, from {{inh|en|ang|hæs||brushwood}} (see {{m|ang|hris}}) and {{inh|en|enm|hay||enclosure}}, {{m|enm|heye}}.
*As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó hAodha||descendant of [[Aodh]]}}.
etym.Hutchison: From a medieval diminutive of the given name {{m|en|Hugh}} {{suffix|en||son}}.
etym.Gore: From any of various places named {{w|Gore#Places|Gore}}, from {{m|en|gore|id=triangular land|t=a triangular piece of land where roads meet}}.
etym.Hamlin: From the {{der|en|xno|-}} personal name {{m|xno|Hamlin}}, a double diminutive of {{der|en|fro|Haimon}}.
etym.Hardie: Scottish variant of {{m|en|Hardy}}. Also shortened from {{m|en|McHardie}}, Anglicized from {{der|en|gd|mac}} {{m|gd|C(h)ardaidh|t=son of the craftsman}}, from {{m|gd|ceardaí}}.
etym.Halsey: Places in England, from {{inh|en|ang|hals||neck of land}} + {{inh|en|ang|ieg|īeġ|island}}
etym.Goody: From {{inh|en|enm|Godeve|pos=female given name}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Godġifu|pos=female given name}}, from {{com|ang|god|ġifu|nocat=1}}. {{dbt|en|Godiva}}.
etym.Kent:
{{dercat|en|cel-bry-pro}}
{{inh+|en|enm|Kent}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Cent}}, from {{der|en|la|Cantium}}, from {{der|en|cel-bry|-}} {{m|cel-bry-pro|*Cantio}} (compare {{cog|sga|céite||gathering, folkmoot, hillock}}), from {{der|en|cel-pro|*kantos||corner, rim}}.
etym.Irving: Variant of the Scottish habitational surname {{m|en|Irvine}}, probably from a {{der|en|cel|-}} word cognate with {{cog|cy|ir}}, {{m|cy|yr||fresh}} + {{m|cy|afon||river}}.
etym.Johnson:
A [[patronymic]] surname from {{suf|en|John|-son}}, literally “son of John”.
* In the U.S. the name Johnson has been adopted by numerous European immigrant families originally named [[Johansson]], [[Johnsson]], [[Johansen]], [[Jonsson]], etc.
* {{dbt|en|Johansson|Johansen|Jansen|Hansen}}.
etym.Kelvin:
Of {{der|en|cel|-}}/{{der|en|gd|-}} origin, possibly from {{m|gd|caol||narrow}} or {{m|gd|coille||wooded}} + {{m|gd|abhainn||river}}.  The surname is derived from the river.

The surname was also possibly influenced by {{m|en|Calvert}} ({{cog|enm|calfhirde}}).
etym.Kim: {{clipping|en|Kimball}} and {{m|en|Kimberley}} as a male name, and of {{m|en|Kimberley}} and {{m|en|Kimberly}} as a female name.
etym.Kirk:
{{etymon|en|id=original proper noun|kirk|tree=1|text=++}} {{dbt|en|Church}}.

The sense meaning [[fellatio]] as well as the verb are derived from the [[w:shooting of Charlie Kirk|shooting of Charlie Kirk]], as he was shot in the {{m|en|neck||fellatio}}.
etym.Irwin: From a medieval given name [[Erwin]], from {{l|ang|Eoforwine}}, from {{der|en|ang|eofor||boar}} + {{m|ang|wine||friend}}, the latter of which is from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*wini}}.
etym.Jefferson: From {{suffix|en|Jeffrey|son}}.  The placenames in the United States are named for {{w|Thomas Jefferson}}.
etym.Johns: Variant of {{m|en|John}} with [[genitival]] or [[excrescent]] {{affix|en|-s<id:patronymic>}} or a variant of {{m|en|Jones}}.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
etym.Huxley: From the {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|*Hucc}} + {{m|en|-s-}} + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland clearing, glade}} {{cln|en|terms suffixed with -leigh}}. The first element could also be {{m|ang|husc||insult, scorn, mockery}}.
etym.Keeley: Reduced Anglicized from {{der|en|ga|Ó Caollaidhe||descendant of Caollaidhe}}, a personal name based on the adjective {{m|ga|caol||slender, graceful}}.
etym.Kendall: From the placename {{m|en|Kendal}} in [[Cumbria]], "valley of the river {{m|en|Kent}}", and {{m|en|Kendale}} in [[Humberside]], from {{der|en|non|kelda|t=spring}} + {{m|non|dalr|t=valley}}.
etym.Irvine: Probably from {{der|en|cel|-}} words cognate with {{cog|cy|ir}}, {{m|cy|yr||green, fresh}} + {{m|cy|afon||water}}.
etym.Judson: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} short form of the given name [[Jordan]] + [[son]].
etym.Keaton: A variant of {{m|en|Caton}} or {{m|en|Keeton}}, or a [[habitational|habitational name]] from Keaton in [[Ermington|Ermington, Devon]], possibly derived from {{der|en|cy|cae|t=hedge, enclosure}} + {{der|en|enm|toun|t=farmstead, settlement}}.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
etym.Kenton: From either the {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|Cena}} or {{m|ang|cyne-||royal}} + {{m|ang|tūn||enclosure; settlement, town}}.
etym.Jagger: Occupational surname from Yorkshire, {{m|en|jagger||peddler}}. The modern given name use is partly after {{w|Mick Jagger}}.
etym.Jax: Shortened from {{m|en|Jackson}}, {{m|en|Jaxon}} or fanciful spelling of the surname {{m|en|Jacks}}.
etym.Lane: As an English surname, from {{m|en|lane}}; as an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from several origins, including {{m|ga|Laighin}}.  See [[w:Lane (surname)|Lane]].
etym.Lincoln:
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:Lincolne}}
{{inh+|en|enm|Lincolne}}, from {{der|en|ang|Lincolle}}, {{m|ang|Lindcolen}}, {{m|ang|Lindcylene}}, from {{der|en|la|[[Lindum]] [[colōnia|Colōnia]]|t=the Roman settlement {{w|Lindum Colonia}}}}, from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*llɨnn||pool}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*lindos||lake, liquid}}, in reference to the [[w:Brayford Pool|Brayford]].  In the United States, many of the places established since 1865 are named after {{w|Abraham Lincoln}}.
etym.Kyle: From several [[place]]s in [[Scotland]] and [[Northern Ireland]], derived from [[Gaelic]] ''[[caol]]'' (“[[narrows]]”).
etym.Leslie: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally ''Lesslyn'', {{der|en|gd|[[lios]] [[cuileann]]|t=garden of hollies}}.
etym.Lowell: A {{inh|en|enm|-}} diminutive of {{der|en|fro|lou}} + {{m|fro|-el|pos=diminutive suffix}}, meaning "little wolf". Akin to {{m|en|Wolfie}}.
etym.Lesley: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally ''Lesslyn'', {{der|en|gd|[[lios]] [[cuileann]]|t=garden of hollies}}.
etym.Lindsey: From {{der|en|ang|Lindesege}}, ultimately from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*llɨnn||pool}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*lindos||lake, liquid}} (as in {{m|en|Lincoln}}) + {{m+|ang|ēġ||island (of land)}}.
etym.Leroy: Transferred from the common {{der|en|fr|-}} surname {{m|fr|Leroy}}, meaning "the king".
etym.Lester:
* As an English surname, from the placename {{m|en|Leicester}}.
* Also as an English surname of {{der|en|nrf|-}} origin, from {{m|en|Lestre}} in Normandy, from {{der|en|fro|Lestra}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Laxtra}}, perhaps from {{m|la|extera|t=exterior (part of a property)}}.
* As an English and Scottish surname, variant of {{m|en|Lister}}.
* Also as an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Laster}}.
* As a Scottish and {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, shortened from {{m|en|McLester}}.
etym.Leigh: From the nominative case of {{inh|en|ang|lēah||wood, meadow}}, 'dweller by the wood or clearing'.
etym.Lennon: From {{der|en|ga||Ó Leannáin|descendant of Lover ({{m|ga|leannán|Leannán}})}} and from {{m|ga||Ó Lonáin|descendant of Blackbird ({{m|ga|lonán|Lonán}})}}.
etym.Kyler:
An American anglicization of Dutch [[Cuyler]] "archer" and German [[Keiler]] "wild boar".
* The surname is quite rare. The given name may be a recent coinage based on [[Kyle]] and [[Tyler]].
etym.Lindsay: From [[Lindsey]] in [[Lincolnshire]], from {{inh|en|ang|Lindesēġe}}, {{m|ang|Lindesīġe|t=Isle of Lind}}, the Old English name of the city of [[Lincoln]], Lincolnshire, in which "Lind" comes from the Common Brittonic form of the name of Lincoln and "isle" refers to Lincoln being surrounded by fenland; from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*llɨnn||pool}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*lindos||lake, liquid}}, in reference to the [[w:Brayford Pool|Brayford]] + {{m+|ang|ēġ||island}}; cf. modern {{cog|cy|llyn}} and [[Dublin]].
etym.Leighton: Various place names in England, {{inh|en|ang|leac||leek}} + {{m|ang|tun||settlement}}, also in the sense of a herb garden. <ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Dictionary of Surnames. Oxford University Press 1988.</ref>
etym.Linden:
* As a {{der|en|nl|-}}, {{der|en|de|-}} and Jewish surname, plural form of {{m|en|Linde}}.
* As a Dutch and {{der|en|vls|-}} surname, from several placenames called {{m|en|Linden}} or {{m|en|Lienden}}. Also shortened from {{m|en|Vanderlinden}}.
* As a {{der|en|sv|-}} surname, from {{m|sv|lind|t=lime tree}}. Compare {{m|en|Lindeen}}.
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Lindon}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, shortened from {{m|en|McLinden}}, itself a variant of {{m|en|McClinton}}.
etym.Leeroy: A less common spelling variant of {{m|en|Leroy}}.
etym.LeeRoy: A less common spelling variant of {{m|en|Leroy}}.
etym.Lee Roy: A less common spelling variant of {{m|en|Leroy}}.
etym.Lamar: From a placename in [[Normandy]], which was derived from {{der|en|fro|la}} {{m|fro|mare||the pool}}.
etym.Leland: Shortened from {{m|en|McLeland}}, {{m|en|McClellan}}, from {{bor|en|ga|Mac}} {{m|ga|giolla|Giolla}} {{m|ga|Fhaoláin}}, "son of servant of (Saint) {{m|ga|Faolán}} (=Little Wolf)".
etym.Milton: The English place names are from {{der|en|ang|mylen||mill}} or {{m|ang|middel||middle}} + {{m|ang|tun||settlement}}.
etym.Murray: Scottish surname derived from the place name {{m|en|Moray}} in northeastern Scotland, from {{der|en|la-med|Moravia}}, {{m|la|Morauia}}, from {{der|en|gd|Moireibh}}, {{m|gd|Moireabh}}, {{m|gd|Moreb}}, ultimately from {{der|en|cel-pro|*mori||sea}} + {{m|cel-pro|*trebā||settlement}}.
etym.Neville:
* A {{der|en|nrf|-}} baronial surname, {{m|nrf|de Neville}}, from place names in [[Normandy]], {{m|fr|Néville}}, from {{der|en|fro|Neville|lit=Néel's estate}} or {{m|fro|Neuville|lit=new settlement}}, equivalent to {{m|fro|nuef|id=new}} + {{m|fro|ville}}.
* Also as an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Niadh}} (see {{m|en|Nee}}) or {{m|ga|Ó Cnaimhín}} (see {{m|en|Nevin}}).
etym.Macaulay: From Scotland, an [[Appendix:Glossary#anglicisation|anglicisation]] of the {{uder|en|gd|-}} [[Gaelic]] ''Mac Amhalghaidh'' ("son of Amhalghaidh"). From [[Ireland]], an anglicisation of the Gaelic ''Mac Amhlaoibh'' ("son of Amhlaoibh") or ''Mac Amhlaidh'' ("son of Amhlaidh"). These Gaelic names are derived from the {{uder|en|non|-}} personal name [[Áleifr]] and [[Óláfr]].
etym.Mandel:
* {{bor|en|gem}} surname ({{bor|en|nl|Mandel}}, {{bor|en|de|Mandel}}, {{bor|en|yi|מאַנדל|tr=Mandl}}, all meaning "almond"). Also found in {{cog|sl|-}} as {{m|sl|Mandelj}}.
* As a south German and Austrian surname, variant of {{m|en|Mandl}}, from {{suf|de|Mann|l|nocat=1}}.
* As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, from {{m|nl|mandel|t=sheaf of wheat}} (see {{m|de|Mandel|id=sheaf}} below).
* As a Jewish surname, variant of {{m|en|Mendel}}.
etym.Mills: From {{m|en|mills}}, in reference to mill owners and mill workers.
etym.Marshall:
* As an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|marshal}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Mercier}}.
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Marschall}}.
etym.Mitchell: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} vernacular form of the {{der|en|fro|-}} given name {{m|fro|Michel||[[Michael]]}}, or in some cases from a {{inh|en|enm|-}} nickname {{m|enm|muchel||big}}.
etym.Miller: English surname, capitalization of {{m|en|miller}}. {{doublet|en|Muller}}. Also compare {{m|en|Milner}}, {{m|en|Millward}}, {{m|en|Müller}}, {{m|en|Mueller}}, {{m|en|Mulder}}, {{m|en|Molenaar}}, {{m|en|Muenier}}, {{m|en|Molinaro}}, {{m|en|Molinero}}, {{m|en|Molnár}}, {{m|en|Mlinar}}, {{m|en|Mlynarczyk}}.
etym.Murphy: From {{der|en|ga|Ó Murchadha|t=descendant of Murrough}}, {{l|ga|Mac Murchaidh|t=Son of Murrough}}, etc. See {{l|sga|Muircath}}.
etym.Maxwell: From an earlier form [[Mackeswell]], meaning "Mack's well or spring", from {{inh|en|ang|welle||well}}.
etym.Marion: From {{inh|en|enm|Marion}}, from {{der|en|fro|Marion}}, a diminutive of [[Marie]], used in England since the Middle Ages.
etym.Madison: Usually derived from [[Mathieson]] ({{m|en|Matthew}} + {{m|en|-son}}), occasionally from {{der|en|enm|Maddy||[[Maud]]}} + {{m|en|-son}}. <ref>P. H. Reaney and R. M. Wilson, ''A Dictionary of English Surnames'', Oxford University Press, 1997, page 293.</ref> In the movie ''Splash'', its use as a given name derives from Manhattan’s [[Madison Avenue]].
etym.Norris: An {{der|en|xno|-}} surname, from {{der|en|fro|norreis||a northerner, a migrant from the north}}. More at French {{m|fr|norois}}.
etym.Mortimer: A {{l|en|habitational}} surname from ''{{w|Mortemer, Seine-Maritime|Mortemer}}'' in {{l|en|France}}, from {{der|en|fro-nor|-}}, literally meaning “dead pond”.
etym.Montgomery: From a {{uder|en|nrf|-}} surname, from a place in Normandy ({{uder|en|fro|-}} for "Gomeric's hill"). Gumaric was a {{uder|en|gem|-}} personal name composed of {{m|gem-pro|*gumô||man}} and {{m|gem-pro|*rīks||ruler}} (whence the modern French surnames ''Gomery'', ''Gommery'' and ''Gumery''<ref>Patrick Hanks, Flavia Hodges, ''A Concise Dictionary of First Names'' (Oxford University Press, 2001)</ref> or the [[Galician]] [[placename]] [[:w:gl:Gomariz|Gomariz]]).
etym.Monroe: From {{inh|en|ang|mann||g=m|human being, person, man}} + [[Roe]], a river in [[Northern Ireland]], meaning "man from the River Roe".
etym.Norton:
From {{der|en|ang|norþ||north}} + {{m|ang|tūn||enclosure; settlement, town}}.

The parish in New Brunswick is named after Norton, Massachusetts.
etym.Mallory: From an {{der|en|xno|-}} nickname for an unfortunate person, from {{der|en|fro|maleure}}, {{m|fro|malheure||unhappy, unlucky}}<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref> (whence {{cog|fr|malheur}}), from {{af|fro|mal|t1=bad|eur|t2=fortune|nocat=1}}.
etym.Melvin:
Variant of the Scottish surname [[Melville]], from a place name [[Malleville]] in Normandy, from {{der|en|la|mala||bad}} + {{der|en|fro|ville||settlement}}.
* Used to Anglicize {{m|gd|Mac Gille Beathain}} in Scotland and {{m|ga|Ó Maoil Mhín}} in Ireland.
etym.Nelson:
From {{der|en|enm|-}} {{suffix|en|Neil|son}} and {{suffix|en|Nell|son}}.
* In the United States, also an Anglicisation of {{der|en|gmq|-}} {{gloss|[[Scandinavian]]}} surnames such as [[Nilsen]], [[Nielsen]], and [[Nilsson]], equivalent to "son of [[Nicholas]]".
etym.Nolan: Anglicized from {{bor|en|ga|Ó Nualláin|lit=descendant of {{l|ga|Nuallán}}}}, diminutive of {{m|ga|nuall||chariot-fighter, champion}}.
etym.Marley: From several different places in England, from {{der|en|ang|mære||boundary}} or {{m|ang|myrig||pleasant}} or {{m|ang|mearþ||marten}}  + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland clearing}}. In the first case, equivalent to {{suf|en|mere#Etymology_2|alt1=mere|t1=boundary|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
etym.Meade:
Two main origins:
* A variant of {{m|en|Mead}}, a topographic or occupational surname.
* Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Midheach}}, superseded spelling of {{m|ga|Míoch||Meathman, a native of Meath}}.
etym.Mayson: As a surname, {{inh|en|enm|May}}'s son, personal name shortened from {{m|en|Matthew}} and many other origins. The modern given name is mostly a spelling variant of {{m|en|Mason}}.
etym.McKinley: Anglicized from {{bor|en|gd|Mac}} {{m|gd|Fhionnlaoich}}, "son of {{m|gd|Fionnlaoch}} (=Fair Warrior)". The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of {{w|William McKinley}} featured on it.
etym.Melanchthon: Translation of the old German surname [[Schwartzerdt]], meaning "black earth" into Greek.
etym.Rhodes: From {{bor|en|fr|Rhodes}}, from {{der|en|la|Rhodus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ῥόδος}}, of uncertain etymology. Possibilities include a pre-Greek name (cf. {{cog|phn|𐤄𐤓𐤏𐤃}}, "[[snake]]"), {{m|grc|ῥόδον||[[rose]]}}, and {{m|grc|ῥόα|ῥοιά|[[pomegranate]]}}.
etym.Richmond: From {{inh|en|enm|Rychemund}}, from a name cognate to {{cog|fr|Richemont|t=town in Normandy}}. Equivalent to {{af|en|rich|mound}}.
etym.Reilly: From {{der|en|ga|Ó Raghallaigh}}, a surname meaning "descendants of {{l|ga|Raghallach}}".
etym.Read: English and Scottish surname, variant of {{m|en|Reed}}.
etym.Reed:
* As an English and Scottish surname, from the adjective {{m|en|red}}.
* Also as an English surname, from {{der|en|ang|rēodan|t=to clear out}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*reudan|id=clear}}.
* Also as an English surname, from several places in England, such as Reed, Lancashire (from {{der|en|ang|ra|t=roe deer}} or Rede, Suffolk (see {{m|en|Rede}}).

Compare {{m|en|Rider}}, {{m|en|Reader}}.
etym.Ridley: Place names in England, {{inh|en|ang|hrēad||reeds}} or {{m|ang|rydde||cleared land}} + {{m|ang|lēah||wood, clearing}}. <ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref> Thus, equivalent to {{m|en|reed}} or {{suf|en|rid|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
etym.Rock:
* As an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|rock}}. Compare {{m|en|Roach}}.
* Also as an English surname, misdivision of {{der|en|enm|atter}} {{m|enm|oke|t=at the oak}}. Compare {{m|en|Nock}}.
* As an English occupational surname, from {{der|en|non|rokkr|t=distaff}}. Compare {{m|en|Rocker}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, translated from names like {{m|ga|Mac}} {{m|ga|Conchairge|t=son of the hound of the rock}}, from {{m|ga|cú}} + {{m|ga|carraig}}, see also {{m|en|McHarg}}.
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname {{m|de|Röck}}, variant of the personal name {{m|en|Rocco}}, see {{m|en|Roche}}.
* Also as a German surname, from the noun {{m|de|Rock|t=skirt gown}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, shor
etym.Percy: From {{der|sv|en|Percy}}. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1845. By [[folk etymology]] associated with {{m|sv|Per||Peter}}.
etym.Oakley:
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:<ety:inh<ang:Āclēa>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|ang|Āclēa}}, from {{m|ang|āc||oak}} + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland clearing, glade}}, thus a clearing in an oak forest; equivalent to {{suf|en|oak|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}. Compare {{m|en|Ackley}}, {{m|en|Akeley}} and {{m|en|Oakleigh}}, which have the same origin.
etym.Riley:
* From {{l|en|Ryley}} in [[Lancashire]], from {{der|en|ang|ryge||rye}} + {{m|ang|leah||clearing, meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|rye|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
* A variant of {{m|en|Reilly}}, from {{der|en|ga|Ó Raghallaigh}} (see {{m|en|O'Reilly}}).
etym.Quinn: The surname is {{bor+|en|ga|Ó Coinn||descendant of Chief|nocap=1}}.
etym.Paige: Variant of {{m|en|Page}}, from {{m|en|[[page#Noun_2|page]]||}}, from {{der|en|fro|page}}, possibly via {{der|en|roa-oit|paggio}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|pagius||servant}}, probably from {{der|en|grc|παιδίον||boy, lad}}, from {{m|grc|παῖς||child}}; some sources consider this unlikely and suggest instead {{der|en|la|pagus||countryside}}, in sense of "boy from the rural regions".
etym.Quincy:
A [[Norman]] surname of {{der|en|fro|-}} origin, from a place name Quincy or [[Quincey]] in France, ultimately from {{der|en|la|Quintus||[[fifth]] [born]}}.

Use in reference to toilets derives from President [[w:John Quincy Adams|John Quincy Adams]], who was the first to have one installed at the [[White House]].
etym.Roosevelt: From a {{bor|en|nl|-}} name of a farm, either {{m|nl||Rozenveld}} (one in [[Zeeland]]) or {{m|nl||Ruiseveld}} (one in [[Brabant]]), from {{der|en|dum|-}}; the former could be a compound of {{m|dum|rose||wild rose / poppy?}} + {{m|dum|velt||open country; field}} or like the latter of {{m|dum|rusch|t=rush reed}} + {{m|dum||velt}}, {{m-g|open land growing with rushes}}.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
etym.Payton: Habitational surname from a minor place in [[Sussex]], from the {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|Pǣga}} + {{m|ang|tūn||enclosure; settlement, town}}.
etym.Reagan: Anglicized from {{uder|en|ga|-}} Gaelic {{m|ga|Ó Riagáin|t=descendant of Riagán}}, a personal name possibly derived from {{m|ga|ríodhgach|t=impulsive, furious}}, an alternative form of [[ríogach]].
etym.Ogden: Places in England, from {{inh|en|ang|āc||oak}} + {{m|ang|denu||valley}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Dictionary of Surnames. OUP 1988.</ref>
etym.Remington: The surname is from {{w|Rimington}}, from {{der|en|ang|rima||edge, border}} + {{m|ang|-ing}} + {{m|ang|-tun|lit=settlement by the boundary stream}}.
etym.Oakland: By [[proprialization]] of {{af|en|oak|-land}}, as likewise with {{m|en|Oakwood}} from {{m|en|oakwood}}.
etym.Ripley: From the {{inh|en|ang|-}} folk name for the Anglian tribe, {{m|ang|*Hrype}} + {{inh|en|ang|lēah||woodland clearing}}.
etym.Parnell: Matronymic from a medieval spoken form of {{m|en|Petronella}}.
etym.Rhett: Name of a South Carolina family, anglicized from {{bor|en|nl|de Raedt}}, from {{der|en|dum|raet||advice}}.
etym.Scot:
{{inh+|en|enm|Scot}}, from {{der|en|ang|Sċottas|t=people from Ireland, Irishmen}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Scōttī}} (see {{m|la|Scōtī}} for more).

See {{w|Scoti#Etymology|Scoti}}.
etym.Stancel:
Possibly from:
* Old English ''stane cell'', which means "stone chamber". Or it could be from Stancil, a village in England.
* German Stenzel.
* Polish-Jewish Stencel
* Polish {{m|pl|Stanisław}}, or Russian {{m|ru|Станислав}}
* Romanian {{m|ro|stâncă}}, meaning rock or cliff
etym.Sidney: From {{der|en|ang|*Sīdaneġ}}, the name of a place in Surrey, from {{m|ang|sīd||wide}} + {{m|ang|eġ||island}}.
etym.Rutland: {{unk|en|title=Unclear}}. Attested in {{inh|en|ang|-}} as {{m|ang|Roteland}} and {{m|ang|Ritelanede}}. Perhaps {{m|ang|hrīþer||cattle}} + {{m|ang|land||land}}, or from the personal name {{m|ang|Rota}} + {{m|ang||land}}.
etym.Scott: From {{der|ang|la|Scōtī}}, or from the same source.
etym.Shirley: English place name from {{der|en|ang|sċīr||county}} + {{m|ang|lēah||meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|shire|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}. More at {{m|en|shire}}, {{m|en|leigh}}.
etym.Smith: From {{m|en|smith}} or {{der|en|enm|Smith||a surname}}, alternative form of {{m|enm|Smyth}}, itself from {{m|enm|smyth||smith}}. {{doublet|en|Schmidt|Smid|Smit}}.
etym.Stanford:
Various placenames from {{der|en|ang|stān||stone}} + {{m|ang|ford||ford}}.

* {{sense|The university}} Named after the son of railroad magnate {{w|Leland Stanford}}.
etym.Sawyer:
* As an English occupational surname, from {{m|en|sawyer|t=one who saws}}. Senses loaned from various languages include Jewish/{{der|en|de|Seger}} and {{m|en|Sager}}, {{der|en|sl|Žagar}}.
* As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Seguin}}.
etym.Spencer: An occupational surname from {{inh|en|enm|-}} {{m|enm|Spenser}}, {{m|enm|Spencer}}, {{m|enm|Spensier}}, from the common noun {{m|enm|spenser||[[spencer]]}}, denoting someone who works in a {{m|enm|spense||[[spence]]}}, or as a butler or steward.
etym.Sigourney: According to Ernest Nègre in his book ''Toponymie générale de la France'' (1990), the French placename ''Sigournais'' comes from Old French ''Segurniaci'', which itself has been derived from Latin ''Secorinus'' + ''-acum''. So it appears that the resemblance to Germanic dithematic names starting with *''segaz'' is superficial.
etym.Seymour: From a {{der|en|nrf|-}} surname from a place in [[Normandy]], from {{der|en|fro|Saint-Maur}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Sanctus Maurus|t=[[Saint]] [[Maurus]]}}. <ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref> The name is cognate to {{m|en|Murry}} and {{m|en|Maurice}}.
etym.Stafford:
From {{inh|en|ang|stæþ||landing place}} + {{m|en|ford}}. 

As a surname, occasionally derived from {{der|en|ga|-}} (see {{m|en|Stocker}}).
etym.Sinclair: Derived from [[Saint Clare]], to whom the clan's churches were dedicated.
etym.Shelby: From a medieval name, of {{unk|en|title=obscure}} origin, yet likely an alteration of {{inh|en|enm|Selby}}, {{m|enm|Salibi|t=dweller of the willow place}}, from {{m|enm|salwe|t=willow, sallow}} + {{af|en|-by|t1=settlement, farm}}.
etym.Rylan: Possibly a variant of [[Ryland]], meaning "rye field" and from {{inh|en|ang|-}}.
etym.Rutherford:
{{etymon|en|:af|ang:hrīþer<alt:hryþer>|ang:ford|tree=1}}
From {{der|en|ang|-}} {{m|ang|hryþer||cattle}} + {{m|ang|ford||ford}}. The first element is from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*hrunþaz}}.
etym.Sherlock:
Supposedly from an {{der|en|ang|[[scir]]-[[locc]]||bright-lock}}.
One of a group of surnames originally denoting hair colour, parallel to ''Blacklock'', ''Harlock'' ({{noncog|ang|har||grey}}), ''Silverlock''.

In the sense of {{m-g|a detective}}, from {{m|en|Sherlock Holmes}}.

In the computing verb sense, refers to the software {{w|Sherlock (software)|Sherlock}}, which in 2002 came to replicate some of the features of an earlier complementary program called {{w|Karelia Watson|Watson}}.<ref>{{cite-web|en|date=July 13, 2012|url=http://www.economist.com/blogs/babbage/2012/07/operating-systems-0|work=The Economist|title=You've been sherlocked}}</ref>
etym.Sanders: From the {{der|en|enm|Sander}}, a shortened form of [[Alexander]] + suffix {{m|enm|-s}}.
etym.Royce: Derived from the {{der|en|enm|-}} given name {{m|enm|Rose}}. See {{cog|en|Rose}}.
etym.Royston: From a place name in [[Hertfordshire]], from the medieval given name [[Royce]] + {{der|en|ang|tūn||settlement}}.
etym.Siddiq: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|صِدِّيق|tr=ṣiddīq|t=truthful}}. This surname is mostly found in [[Pakistan]]. {{root|en|ar|ص د ق}}
etym.Saint Clare: A [[calque]] of {{bor|en|la|sancta|Sancta}} {{m|la|Clara||[[holy]] [[Clara]]}}, chiefly in reference to {{der|en|it|Chiara}} {{m|it|Offreduccio}}, St. Clare of Assisi.
etym.Sydney: For the surname and given name, see {{m|en|Sidney}}. The cities in Australia and Canada are named after British politician {{w|Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney}} (1733–1800).
etym.Washington:
{{etymon|en|:inh|ang:Hwæssingatūn<ety:af<*Hwæssa><-ing><tūn>>|tree=1}}
{{m|en||Washington}} (the town in [[Tyne and Wear]], northeast [[England]]): probably from the {{inh|en|ang|-}} place name {{m|ang||Hwæssingatūn|lit=a settlement of the household of {{m|ang||*Hwæssa}}}}, from {{affix|ang|*Hwæssa|pos1=a Saxon chieftain's name|-ing|t2=belonging to|tūn|t3=homestead, settlement|nocat=1}}. It was attested in 1096 as {{m|ang||Wasindone}}. ''*Hwæssa'' is of uncertain origin, said to possibly correspond to {{m|ang|waþ|t=hunt}} + {{m|ang|sige|t=victory}},<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref> or possibly related to {{m|ang|hwæte|t=wheat}}. There are other theories; more on [[w:Washington, Tyne and Wear#Toponymy
etym.Tyson:
* A variant of {{m|en|Tison}}. A nickname from {{der|en|fro|tison||firebrand}}.
* A {{l|en|patronymic}} English surname, variant of {{m|en|Dyson}}, from {{suffix|en|Dennis|son}}.
* In the US, adopted by a German family who came to America (Germantown, PA) in 1683, originally named {{der|en|de|Teisen}} "son of {{m|de|Theiss}}", which was short for {{m|de|Matthias}}. Original spellings were {{m|de|Theisen}}, {{m|de|Theissen}}, {{m|de|Teisen}}, {{m|de|Teison}}.
etym.Vernon: From {{der|en|xtg||uerna|alder}} (from {{der|en|cel-pro|*wernā}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*wern-}}) + {{m|cel-gau||-o}}, {{m|cel-gau||-onis|pos=locative suffix|lit=place of alder trees}}.
etym.Wesley: Several places in England, from {{inh|en|ang|west||west}} + {{m|ang|lēah||wood, clearing}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|west|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
etym.Stanley:
From places in England, {{der|en|ang|stān||stone}} + {{m|ang|lēah||meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|stone|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.
* The given name has also been used as an anglicisation of [[Stanisław]], [[Stanislav]] and related names.

The coastal town in Hong Kong is {{named-after|en|Edward Henry Stanley, 15th Earl of Derby|wplink==|nocap=1}}.
etym.Wayne: An occupational surname for a [[cartwright]], {{der|en|ang|wægen||wagon}}. Cf. {{m|en|wain}}.
etym.Tanner: From {{from|fi|tanner||field, ground}}, but with different declension. Mostly adopted as a surname during the Fennicization of surnames in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.<ref>{{R:fi:Sukunimet}}</ref>
etym.Wile: From {{inh|en|enm|wile}}, an occupational surname for a [[trapper]] or a nickname for a [[wily]] person.
etym.Wells: From {{inh|en|ang|wella}}, genitive plural of {{m|ang|well||spring}}, in reference to a residence near a group of springs. The original use of the genitive case here would've indicated origin. The -s ending of the modern form would be added later on upon reanalysis after the breakdown of the case system (outside of pronouns) that occurred in the development of English.
etym.Wallace: An {{der|en|ang|-}} byname for a [[Welshman]] or [[Breton]], from {{der|en|xno|waleis||foreign}}; see {{m|ang|wǣlisċ}}.
etym.Vance: From a Southern English dialectal form of {{der|en|ang|fenn||marsh, bog}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Dictionary of Surnames. Oxford University Press 1988.</ref>
etym.Warner:
* English, {{der|en|nrf|-}}, and {{der|en|de|-}} surname, all corresponding to {{cog|de|Werner}}. Also see {{m|en|Warrener}}.
* As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, Anglicized from {{m|ga|Ó Murnáin|t=descendant of Murnán}}; see {{m|en|Murnane}}.
etym.Stirling: {{bor+|en|gmw-msc|Stirveling}}, from {{der|en|enm-esc|Strivelin}}, {{m|enm|Strivelyn}}, likely from {{der|en|sga|sreb}}, {{m|sga|srib||stream}}<ref>{{R:DIL|38760|sreb, srib}}</ref> + {{m|sga|linn||pool, lake}}.<ref>{{R:DIL|30274|1 linn}}</ref> Cognate with {{cog|fro|Estrivelin}}, {{cog|wlm|Ystriflin}}.<ref>{{cite-journal|last=Clancy|first=Thomas Owen|title=The Etymologies of Pluscarden and Stirling|date=26 July 2021|journal=The Journal of Scottish Names Studies|volume=17|url=https://clog.glasgow.ac.uk/ojs/index.php/JSNS/article/view/143|issn=2054-9385}}.</ref>
etym.Travis: From an {{der|en|fro|-}} word meaning "to cross over," related to {{m|en|traverse}}. Probably a name for a gatekeeper or the toll collector of a bridge. {{etystub|en|Please specify the Old French root if it is known.}}
etym.Tracy: A Norman baronial surname from places in France, derived from the Gallo-Roman given name ''[[Thracius]]'' which referred to ''[[Thrace]]'' + the Celtic suffix ''*-āko'' (place, property). As a female given name, it is also known as a diminutive of ''[[Theresa]]''.
etym.Wilbur: From an {{inh|en|ang|-}} female given name {{m|ang|Wilburg}}, from {{m|ang|wil||will}} + {{m|ang|burh||fortress}}.
etym.Tasman:
{{ety|en|:bor|nl:Tasman|tree=1}}
{{bor+|en|nl|Tasman}}, from {{der|en|nl|tas||purse, pouch}} + {{m|nl|man||person, man}}.<ref>{{R:Patronymica Britannica|entry=Tasman|page=339|column=2}}</ref> The places are named after [[w:Abel Tasman|Abel Tasman]].
etym.Tatum: From {{m|en|Tatham}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Tāta}}, a personal name of unknown meaning + {{m|ang|ham|hām}}.
etym.St. Clair: An abbreviation of {{m|en|Saint Clair}}, variant of {{m|en|Saint Clare}} under influence from {{der|en|fr|Claire}}, a [[calque]] of {{bor|en|la|sancta|Sancta}} {{m|la|Clara||[[holy]] [[Clara]]}}, chiefly in reference to {{der|en|it|Chiara}} {{m|it|Offreduccio}}, St. Clare of Assisi. The placenames listed below are typically spelt ''St. Clair''{{mdash}}abbreviated with punctuation{{mdash}}following North American practice.
etym.St Clair: An abbreviation of {{m|en|Saint Clair}}, variant of {{m|en|Saint Clare}} under influence from {{der|en|fr|Claire}}, a [[calque]] of {{bor|en|la|sancta|Sancta}} {{m|la|Clara||[[holy]] [[Clara]]}}, chiefly in reference to {{der|en|it|Chiara}} {{m|it|Offreduccio}}, St. Clare of Assisi. The placenames listed below are typically spelt ''St Clair''{{mdash}}abbreviated without punctuation{{mdash}}following Commonwealth practice.
etym.Alexandria: From {{inh|en|enm|Alexandria}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Alexandria}}, from {{der|en|la|Alexandrīa}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλεξάνδρεια}}, from {{m|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος||[[Alexander]]}} + {{m|grc|-εια||[[-ia]]: ''[[form]]ing [[place name]]s''}}, initially chiefly places founded by {{w|Alexander the Great}} of [[Macedonia]] and subsequently usually with reference to Alexandria in Egypt, a major Hellenistic cultural center, center of early Christianity, and continuing major international port. Compare {{l|en|Antioch}}, {{l|en|Seleucia}}, and {{l|en|Ptolemais}}. {{doublet|en|Kandahar|Iskenderun|Scandaroon|Alexandretta}}.
etym.Amaryllis: From {{der|mul|la|Amaryllis||a country girl in [[Virgil]]'s {{w|Eclogues}}}}, from {{der|mul|grc|Ἀμαρυλλίς|pos=from {{m|grc|ἀμαρύσσω||to shine}}}}.
etym.Anastasia: From the name of a 4th-century martyr, {{translit|en|grc|Ἀναστασία|notext=1}}, from {{m|grc|ἀνάστασις||resurrection}}. The name, and its male counterpart [[Anastasius]], were originally given to children who were born around Eastertime during the early years of Christianity.
etym.Chloe:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ǵʰelh₃-}}
{{bor+|en|grc|χλόη||young green shoot}}, an epithet of goddess [[Demeter]].
etym.Catherine: {{bor+|en|fr|Catherine}}, from {{der|en|grc|Αἰκατερίνη}}, {{m|grc|*Ἑκατερίνη}}, of debated meaning, possibly from {{m|grc|ἑκάτερος||each of the two}}, or from the name of the goddess [[Hecate]]. The {{glossary|apheresis}} of the first syllable as well as the spelling with ⟨th⟩ in Latin languages, German and English, is due to a [[folk etymology]], dating from Roman times, which associated the name with the Ancient Greek {{m|grc|καθαρός||pure}}. The name belonged to a 4th-century [[saint]] and [[martyr]] from [[Alexandria]] who was tortured on the wheel from where the term [[Catherine wheel]] originates.
etym.Angela: Feminine form of Church {{der|en|la|Angelus}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἄγγελος||messenger, angel}}.
etym.Ariana:
Modern simplification of [[Arianna]], [[Ariane]] and [[Arianne]], all forms of the [[Greek]] name [[Ariadne]] ("most holy"; Cretan Greek ''αρι'' (ari) "most" and ''αδνος'' (adnos) "holy"). There has been some confusion with the similar sounding [[Adriana]] and [[Adrienne]].
* By [[folk etymology]] also associated with Welsh {{m|cy|arian||silver}}.
etym.Windsor: {{inh+|en|enm|Wyndelsore}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Windlesōra|t=Windsor|lit=bank with a windlass, winch by the riverside}}, from {{m|ang|*windel}} {{gloss|"reel, winch"; > {{cog|enm|windel|t=reel, spool}}}} + {{m|ang|ōra|t=bank, shore}}.<ref> South S.R., The Book of Windsor, Barracuda Books, 1977</ref> See {{m|en|windlass}}.
etym.Aglaia: From {{der|en|grc|Ἀγλαΐα|pos=from {{m|grc|ἀγλαΐα|t=[[splendour]], [[beauty]]}}}}. It has the same Indo-European root as {{l|grc|γελάω||to laugh}}.
etym.Zane:
* The usage seems to date from the American writer Zane Grey (1875-1939), born Pearl Zane Gray. It was the surname of his mother's family, of unknown meaning.
* Sometimes explained as a form of {{m|en|John}} because of the resemblance to {{m|en|Shane}}, or because Italian surnames such as {{m|it|Zanelli}} and {{m|it|Zanetto}} derive from the equivalent name {{m|it|Giovanni}}.
* In some cases, a respelling of {{m|en|Zayn}}, which is of {{der|en|ar|-}} origin.
etym.Berenice: Borrowed from {{bor|mul|grc|Βερενῑ́κη||bringer of victory}}, itself a borrowing from {{der|mul|xmk|-}} (compare the native word {{m|grc|Φερενῑ́κη}}), from {{m|grc|φέρω||to bear, to carry, to bring}} + {{m|grc|νῑ́κη||victory}}.
etym.Candace:
From {{bor|en|la|Candacē}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κανδάκη}}, from {{der|en|xmr|𐦲𐦷𐦲𐦡|ts=kandakə}}, a hereditary title of ancient queens of [[Napata]] (northern [[Sudan]]).
<!--It said here: "The name is also associated with Late Latin {{m|la|candida||whiteness}} via {{glossary|folk etymology}}." Please source. Haven't found any evidence of this association. It also said: "The [[silent e]] at the end might be a result of this association." The final -e is already in the Latin form. Maybe it refers to the fact that this -e is not pronounced. But what does this have to do with "candida"?? Besides: If anything, I think contemporary speakers may associate it with "candy".-->
etym.Candice: A variant of {{m|en|Candace}} associated with Late Latin {{m|la|candida||whiteness}} via {{glossary|folk etymology}}.
etym.Charmian: Diminutive form of {{uder|en|grc|χάρμα||joy}}. According to [[Plutarch]], the name of a servant and advisor of [[Cleopatra]].
etym.Athanasia: From {{bor|en|la|Athanasia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀθανασία}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἀθανασία||[[undying]], [[immortal]]}}. Probable doublet of {{m|en|Tansy}}.
etym.Alexondra: Variant of {{m|en|Alexandra}} to explicate /-ɑ(ː)-/ 〈-o-〉, as opposed to /-æ-/ 〈-a-〉.
etym.Cleopatra:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ḱlew-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Cleopatra}}, from {{der|en|la|Cleopatra}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κλεοπάτρα}}, meaning "glory of her father", from {{m|grc|κλέος||glory}} + {{m|grc|πατήρ||father}}.
etym.Dorcas: From {{uder|en|grc|Δορκάς||gazelle}}, translation of {{m|en|Tabitha}} in the Bible.
etym.Ellen: Medieval English variant of {{m|en|Helen}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἑλένη}}; also used as a variant of {{m|en|Eleanor}} or a feminine counterpart to {{m|en|Elliot}}.
etym.Denise: From {{uder|en|fr|Denise}}, from {{der|en|la|Dionȳsia|pos=feminine form of {{m|la|Dionȳsius}}, a male name of {{uder|en|grc|-}} origin meaning “follower of [[Dionysus]]”}}. Dionysus is the mythological Greek god of wine responsible for growth of the vines and the originator of winemaking. {{doublet|en|Dionysia}}.
etym.Christina: Name of an early martyr, shortened from {{der|en|la|Chrīstiāna||Christian (woman)}}. {{doublet|en|Kirsten}}.
etym.Dora: A diminutive of {{m|en|Dorothy}} used since early 19th century. Sometimes also short for {{m|en|Theodora}} or {{m|en|Isidora}}.
etym.Doris: From {{der|mul|grc|Δωρίς||a nymph, one of the daughters of [[Oceanus]]}}.
etym.Eunice: A biblical name from {{der|en|grc|Εὐνίκη}}, from {{com|grc|εὐ-|t1=good|νίκη|t2=victory|nocat=1}}.<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>
etym.Cynthia: {{bor+|en|la|Cynthia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κυνθία}}, feminine of {{m|grc|Κύνθιος||[[Cynthian]] (of or pertaining to Mount [[Cynthus]], a mountain of [[Delos]], celebrated as the birthplace of [[Apollo]] and [[Artemis]])}}.
etym.Elaine: From {{der|en|fro|Elaine}}, a variant of {{m|fro|Elene}}, cognate to {{m|en|Helen}}, ultimately from {{der|en|grc|Ἑλένη}}. A {{cog|cel}} origin has also been suggested since the name appears in [[Arthurian]] legend. {{doublet|en|Helen}}.
etym.Cora: Apparently brought up in English literature by James Fenimore Cooper in ''The Last of the Mohicans'' (1826), but compare a female heroine of this name in Jean-François Marmontel's ''Les Incas'' (1777) and the {{der|en|grc|-}} epithet {{m|grc|Κόρη}} for {{m|grc|Περσεφόνη}}. It could also refer directly to {{m|grc|κόρη||maiden}}.
etym.Corinne: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} equivalent of ''[[Corinna]]'', from {{der|en|grc|κόρη||girl, maiden, daughter}}.
etym.Eulalie: {{uder|en|fr|-}} from the saints' name [[Eulalia]], from {{uder|en|grc|-}} "sweetly speaking".
etym.Christiana: From {{der|en|la|Chrīstiāna}}; a medieval literate form of the female name [[Christian]]. {{surf|en|Christian|-a}}.
etym.Christa: Contraction of {{m|en|Christina}} and {{m|en|Christiana}}. Rare until the second half of the 20th century, reinforced by the German {{m|de|Christa}}.
etym.Eugenia: {{der|mul|grc|Εὐγενία}}, feminine nominate singular form of {{m|grc|Εὐγένιος||well born}}
etym.Damaris: {{unc|en}}, possibly from {{uder|en|grc|-}} as a variation of {{m|grc|δάμαλις||calf}}.
etym.Cressida: Used by Geoffrey Chaucer, also by Shakespeare in ''{{w|Troilus and Cressida}}'' (1602), from {{der|en|it|Criseida}} (which Boccaccio mistakenly substituted for {{m|it|Briseida||[[Briseis]]}}), from {{der|en|grc|Χρυσηΐς}}, from {{der|en|grc|χρυσός||gold}}.
etym.Eudocia: From {{bor|en|la|Eudocia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐδοκία}}, from {{der|en|grc|εὐδοκία||[[satisfied]] or [[satisfying]] one}}, from {{m|grc|εὐδοκέω||to be [[well-pleased]] or [[well]]-[[pleasing]]}} + {{m|grc|-ία||[[-ia]]: ''[[form]]ing [[adjective]]s''}}, from {{m|grc|εὐ-||[[eu-]]: [[good]]}} + {{m|grc|δοκέω||to [[think]], to be [[thought]], to [[seem]]}}. {{doublet|en|Evdokia}}.
etym.Eudoxia: From {{bor|en|la|Eudoxia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐδοξία}}, from {{m|grc|εὐδοξία||the [[famed]] one, the one of [[good]] [[repute]]}}, from {{m|grc|εὐ-||[[eu-]]: [[good]]}} + {{m|grc|δόξα||[[opinion]], [[judgment]], [[honor]]}} + {{m|grc|-ία||[[-ia]]: ''[[form]]ing [[adjective]]s''}}.
etym.Irene: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Irène}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εἰρήνη||peace}}, name of a goddess of peace, of early Christian saints, and of an 8th-century [[Byzantine]] [[empress]]. {{doublet|en|Eirini}}.
etym.Katherine: {{rfe|en|Variant of {{m|en|Catherine}} with the initial letter changed to ⟨[[K]]⟩ to reflect its {{der|en|grc|-}} origin, or in particular the {{glossary|folk etymological}} connection to {{m|grc|καθαρός||pure}}.}}
etym.Iris: {{der|mul|grc|Ἶρις||the messenger of the gods; a rainbow; the iris (of the eye); the flower}}
etym.Katharine: A variant spelling of [[Catherine]], based on the [[folk etymology]] that it would derive from Greek [[καθαρός]] (''katharos'' "pure").
etym.Hermione: From the {{der|en|grc|Ἑρμιόνη|Ἑρμῐόνη}}. Not related to German {{m|de|Hermine}}.
etym.Karin: From {{bor|en|sv|Karin}} or {{bor|en|da|Karin}}, a medieval form of {{m|sv|Katarina}}, ultimately from {{der|en|grc|Αἰκατερῑ́νη}}. See also {{m|en|Karen}}.
etym.Ilona: From {{der|en|hu|Ilona}}. A rare variant of {{l|en|Helen}} or {{l|en|Helena}}.
etym.Isidora: Name of a fourth-century saint. The feminine equivalent of [[Isidore]], from {{uder|en|grc|Ἰσιδώρα|t=gift of [[Isis]]}}.
etym.Isadora: A variant of {{m|pt|Isidora}}, from {{uder|pt|la|Isidōra}}, {{glossary|feminine}} equivalent of {{m|la|Īsidōrus}}, from {{der|pt|grc|Ῑ̓σῐ́δωρος|t=gift of [[Isis]]}}.
etym.Euphemia: Name of an early Christian [[martyr]], from {{bor|en|grc|Εὐφημία}}, from {{affix|grc|nocat=1|εὐ-|t1=good|φήμη|t2=repute|-ίᾱ}}.
etym.Khloé: A fanciful spelling variant of [[Chloe]], made known in the 2000s by an American TV personality.
etym.Khloe: Variant of {{m|en|Khloé}}, a fanciful spelling variant of {{m|en|Chloe}}, made known in the 2000s by American TV personality {{w|Khloé Kardashian}}.
etym.Jacintha: From {{der|en|la|Hyacintha}} (possibly as a fanciful spelling of {{der|en|es|Jacinta}}), from {{der|en|grc|Ὑακίνθη}}.
etym.Melanie:
{{ety|en|:bor|fr:Mélanie|tree=++}}
From {{bor|en|fr|Mélanie}}, from {{der|en|la|Melania}}, the name of two Roman fifth century saints, from {{der|en|grc|μέλας||black, dark}}.
etym.Margaret:
From the name of 3rd century Saint [[w:Margaret the Virgin|Margaret the Virgin]], from {{inh|en|enm|Margaret}}, from {{der|en|fro|Margaret}} ({{cog|fr|Marguerite}}), from {{der|en|la|Margarita}}, from {{der|en|grc|μαργαρίτης||pearl}}, ultimately from an [[Indo-Iranian]] source.

The same source, through folk etymology, has produced {{cog|ang|meregrot||pearl|lit=stone or pebble of the sea}}, related to {{cog|osx|merigrita}}, {{m|osx|merigriota||pearl}}, {{cog|goh|merigrioz}}, equivalent to {{prefix|en|mer|groat|nocat=1}}.
etym.Lyra: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|Lyra}}/{{m|la|lyra}}, from {{der|en|grc|λύρα||a [[lyre]]; the constellation Lyra}}. {{doublet|en|lira|lyra|lyre}}.
etym.Melissa: {{der|mul|grc|μέλισσα||honey bee}} (compare {{m|en|Melissa}}), which in turn comes from {{m|grc|μέλι||honey}}.
etym.Lydia: {{bor+|en|grc|Λυδία||the region of Lydia}}, from {{m|grc|λυδία||[[beautiful]] one, [[noble]] one}}, a [[feminine]] form of {{m|grc|Λυδός}} ([[Lydus]], from {{m|grc|λυδός}} ([[lydus]])).  The region of Lydia is said to be named for a king {{m|grc|Λυδός}} ([[Lydus]], from {{m|grc|λυδός}} ([[lydus]])); the given name Lydia originally indicated ancestry or residence in the region of Lydia.
etym.Nicola: A feminine version of {{m|en|Nicholas}}, first used in the 20th century.
etym.Kristin: Borrowed in the 20th century from {{uder|en|no|Kristin}}, a variant of [[Christina]].
etym.Ophelia: Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Ofelia}}, coined by the poet {{w|Jacopo Sannazaro}} in his poem ''[[w:Arcadia (poem)|Arcadia]]'' (1504), probably from the {{uder|en|grc|ὠφέλειᾰ||help, aid, succour}}. The name was used by {{w|William Shakespeare}} for the daugher of [[Polonius]] and ill-fated love interest of [[Hamlet]]. The moon (of Uranus) is named after this character. {{dbt|en|anopheles}}
etym.Margery: From Old French; ultimately from Ancient Greek. {{etystub|en}}
etym.Pallas: From {{uder|en|grc|Παλλάς}} (f.) or {{m|grc|Πάλλας}} (m.), from {{m|grc|πάλλω||to poise, sway, or swing}}, but explained here by the ancients as more specifically meaning to brandish something.  In Athena's conventional iconography, she was often depicted with a spear or a shield. Thus the epithet was explained as referring to her brandishing these things.<ref>{{R:grc:Autenrieth|Παλλάς}}</ref>
etym.Lena:
The female name is from the [[Scandinavian]], [[German]] and [[Russian]] pet form of [[Helena]], [[Magdalena]] and [[Yelena]] (also spelled [[Elena]]).

The river in Yakutia is from {{bor|en|ru|Лена}}, from {{der|en|evn|Елюенэ||the Large River}}. Compare to {{cog|sah|Өлүөнэ}}.

{{s|Norwegian river}} Probably related to Old Norse {{m|non|leir||clay}} (see the references).

{{s|Town in Toten}} From {{der|en|non|lein}}.
etym.Krista: A spelling variant of {{m|en|Christa}}, a modern short form of [[Christina]], partly borrowed from {{der|en|de|Christa}}.
etym.Kristen: A spelling variant of {{m|en|Kristin}}, from {{m|en|Christina}}, fairly popular in the latter half of the twentieth century.
etym.Lois: From {{bor|en|grc|Λωΐς}}, of obscure meaning. Unrelated to {{m|en|Louise}} or {{m|en|Louisa}}.
etym.Marita: Borrowed in the late 19th century from {{der|en|no|Marita}}. By [[folk etymology]], explained as a Spanish diminutive of [[Maria]], by analogy with [[Anita]].
etym.Nerissa: Coined by Shakespeare for ''The Merchant of Venice'', apparently from {{der|en|grc|Νηρηΐς||sea-nymph}}.
etym.Teresa: First recorded as the name of a fourth-century Spanish saint. Of obscure origin; suggestions include [[Therasia]] or [[Thera]], ancient name of the [[Greek]] island [[Thira]].
etym.Xena: Possibly a variant of {{m|en|Xenia}}, from {{der|en|la|Xenia}}, from {{der|en|grc|ξενία|t=hospitable}}, the assumed name of a fifth-century saint venerated in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], from {{m|grc|ξένος|t=foreign, strange}}.
etym.Selene: From {{der|mul|grc|Σελήνη}}, name of the goddess of the Moon ([[#English|Selene]]), because the fish resembles a moon.
etym.Sophia: Chiefly from {{bor|en|la|Sophia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Σοφία}}, from {{m|grc|σοφία||[[wisdom]]}}, especially in reference to {{w|Holy Wisdom|holy}} or {{w|sophia (wisdom)|divine wisdom}} under the influence of {{der|en|hbo|חוכמה|tr=khokhmá}}, to the early martyr {{w|Sophia of Rome|St. Sophia}}, and to many figures of European royalty and nobility. Also used as a [[calque]] for the many cognate forms, such as Italian {{m|it|Sofia}}, Ukrainian {{m|uk|Софі́я}}, Russian {{m|ru|Софи́я}}, Polish {{m|pl|Zofia}}, etc. {{dbt|en|Sofia}}.
etym.Rhea:
{{ety|mul|:der|grc:Ῥέα}}
From {{der|mul|grc|Ῥέα}}, the mother of Zeus in Greek mythology. {{coin|mul|Q299547|in=1760}}.
etym.Tina: Short form of {{l|en|Christina}} or of any female name ending in ''-tina'', such as {{l|en|Martina}} or {{l|en|Albertina}}; frequently from {{der|en|la|-ina}}
etym.Theresa: First used in [[Spain]], supposedly derived from {{der|en|la|Thēra}}, from {{der|en|grc|Θήρᾱ}}, name of a city in Santorini, Greece.
etym.Phyllis:
From the masculine {{bor|en|grc|Φύλλις}} or from the feminine
{{m|grc|Φυλλίς}}.
etym.Salome: From {{der|en|grc|Σαλώμη}}, from {{der|en|he|שְׁלוֹמִית|tr=sh'lomít}} (belonging to the same root as {{m|he|שָׁלוֹם|tr=shalóm||peace}}).
etym.Philippa: A Latinate feminine form of [[Philip]], recorded in medieval England, but originally pronounced like the masculine form.
etym.Selena: Either a variant of {{m|en|Selina}}, from {{der|en|la|Caelīna||heavenly|pos=from {{m|la|caelum||sky, heaven}}}}, or from {{m|en|Selene}}, the {{der|en|grc|-}} goddess of the moon.
etym.Veronica: From {{m|en|Veronica||Veronica}}, probably after {{w|Saint Veronica}}, possibly for because of the flowers of some European species resembling the image on the {{w|Veil of Veronica}} in some way.
etym.Zara:
A 20th-century variant of [[Sarah]], or explained as {{bor|en|ar|زَهْرَة||flower}}; given to the daughter of Princess Anne in 1981.
{{root|en|ar|ز ه ر}}
etym.Philomena: From {{der|en|la|Philomēna}}, from {{der|en|grc|Φιλουμένη|lit=beloved}}. Name of an alleged early [[martyr]] whose remains were discovered in 1802 in Rome. {{doublet|en|Philomene}}.
etym.Tryphena: From {{uder|en|grc|Τρύφαινα}}, from {{uder|en|grc|τρῠφή||softness, daintiness}}.<ref>"G5170 - tryphaina - Strong's Greek Lexicon (NIV)." Blue Letter Bible. Web. 27 Apr, 2026. <https://www.blueletterbible.org/lexicon/g5170/niv/mgnt/0-1/>.</ref>
etym.Xenia: From the assumed name of a fifth-century saint venerated in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], {{der|en|la|Xenia}}, from {{der|en|grc|ξενία||hospitable}}. {{doublet|en|Oksana}}.
etym.Rina: Short form of names ending in ''-rina'', such as {{l|en|Katrina}}, {{l|en|Marina}} and {{l|en|Larina}}. Also borrowed from other European languages, such as Italian, in the 20th century.
etym.Fatima:
From {{bor|en|ar|فَاطِمَة}}. {{root|en|ar|ف ط م}}

The name Fatima is from the Arabic root f-t-m (lit. 'to wean') and signifies the Shia belief that she, her progeny, and her adherents (Shi'a) have been spared from hellfire. Alternatively, the word Fatima is associated in Shia sources with Fatir (lit. 'creator', a name of God) as the earthly symbol of the divine creative power.
etym.Zoë:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*gʷeyh₃-}}
From {{uder|en|grc|ζωή||life}}. It was the name of a third century martyr venerated in the [[Orthodox Church]].
etym.Aaliyah: Popularized by American singer {{w|Aaliyah Haughton}} (1979–2001). {{translit|en|ar|عَالِيَة}}. {{root|en|ar|ع ل ي}}
etym.Laila: Variant of [[Leila]] and [[Layla]], from {{der|en|ar|لَيْلَى}}, related to {{m|ar|لَيْلَة||night}}. {{root|en|ar|ل ي ل}}
etym.Layla: One of many {{glossary|alternative form|alternative spellings}} of a name [[transliterate]]d from Arabic; see {{m|en|Leila}} for more information. Since the late 20th century, in English, this given name in this spelling is sometimes bestowed solely because it is considered [[euphonious]], a theme true of many given names; Wikipedia at [[w:Given_name#Popularity|given name § Popularity]]  discusses name choice motivations.
etym.Joumana: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|جُمَانَة}}, meaning a perfect pearl.
etym.Lila: Variant of {{m|en|Leila}} or {{m|en|Lilah}}, depending on pronunciation; also associated with {{bor|en|es|lila||lilac}}.
etym.Farrah: Variant of {{m|en|Farrar}}, from {{inh|en|enm|ferreor||iron worker, smith}}. The given name was popularized by the American actress {{w|Farrah Fawcett}} (1947-2009). Her name is often interpreted as a variant of {{m|en|Farah}}.
etym.Alia:
{{root|en|ar|ع ل ي}}
Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|عَالِيَة}}. The feminine form of {{m|en|Ali}}.
etym.Aleah: Probably a fanciful spelling of {{m|en|Alia}}, {{bor|en|ar|عَالِيَة}}. {{root|en|ar|ع ل ي}}
etym.Hind:
{{wp|[[+ (name)|+]]}}
From {{m|en|hind}}, a nickname for a gentle or timid person.
etym.Sarah: From {{bor|en|hbo|שָׂרָה|tr=śārâ|t=lady, princess}}, from {{w|Sarah|the Biblical figure}} originally named [[Sarai]] ({{m|he|שָׂרָי|tr=śārāy|lit=masters, princes}}).
etym.Martha:
* From {{der|en|la|Martha}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μάρθα|}}, from {{der|en|arc|מָרְתָא|t=mistress|tr=mārtā}}, feminine of {{m|arc|מרא|tr=mārā}}. {{doublet|en|Marfa}}.
* {{sense|humidity chamber}} From the use of {{w|Martha Stewart}}-branded storage closets in the construction of early units.
etym.Sanya: {{translit|en|ru|Са́ня}}, diminutive of {{l|ru|Алекса́ндра}} and {{l|ru|Алекса́ндр}}. In some cases possibly from {{bor|en|sh|Сања}} and {{m|sh|Sanja}}.
etym.Bethany: From {{der|en|grc|Βηθανία}}, from {{der|en|arc|[[בית]] [[עניא]]|tr=beth anya|t=house of wretchedness}}.  This etymology is highly disputed; see {{w|Bethany#Bethany|Bethany}}.
etym.Rabia:
From {{bor|en|ar|رَابِعَة}}, the feminine of {{m|ar|رَبِيع||spring}} as well as {{m|ar|رَابِع||fourth}}, from {{m|ar|أَرْبَعَة||four}}. Hence Rabia means both "spring" and "the fourth female".
{{root|en|ar|ر ب ع}}
etym.Raghda:
From {{der|en|ar|رَغْدَة||pleasant, happy life}}. The name is more common in North African countries.
{{root|en|ar|ر غ د}}
etym.Sahar:
Of {{uder|en|ar|-}} or {{uder|en|fa|-}} origin. In Persian, {{m|fa|سحر|tr=sahar|t=dawn}}. (In Hebrew, {{m|he|סַהַר|tr=sáhar|t=crescent}}.)
{{root|en|ar|س ح ر}}
etym.Zelma: First recorded as a given name of Latvians in 1875. Cognate with English [[Selma]].
etym.Syeda:
{{bor+|en|ar|سَيِّدَة}}. {{root|en|ar|س و د}}
* {{sense|female given name}} From {{bor|en|ur|سیدہ}}, from {{der|en|ar|سَيِّدَة}}
etym.Yasmin: Variant of {{m|en|Jasmine}}, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding {{uder|en|ar|-}} and {{uder|en|fa|-}} names.
etym.Sofana: From {{uder|en|ar|سُفَانَة}}. The name was famously borne by a daughter of the poet {{w|Hatim al-Tai}}.
etym.Rhianna: A variant spelling of {{m|en|Rihanna}}, from {{bor|en|ar|رَيْحَانَة|pos=singulative of {{m|ar|رَيْحَان|t=[[basil]]; [[myrtle]]}}}}. This spelling is possibly influenced by unrelated Welsh names such as {{m|en|Rhiannon}}.
etym.Sariyah: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|سَارِيَة}}, the meaning “a cloud that comes by night”. {{root|en|ar|س ر ي}}
etym.Zahra:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|ar|زَهْراء}}, an epithet of {{l|en|Fatima}}, the daughter of {{l|en|Muhammad}}. As a surname, it is predominantly found in [[Egypt]].
{{root|en|ar|ز ه ر}}
etym.Yasmeen: Variant of {{m|en|Jasmine}}, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding Arabic and Persian names.
etym.Ons: The island's name is from {{uder|gl|la-med|Aunes}}; attested by {{w|Pliny}} as {{der|gl|la-cla|Aunios}}, from {{der|gl|qsb-ibe|-}}, probably from {{der|gl|cel-pro||*au-|t=away, off}},<ref>Falileyev, Alexander (1997). ''Dictionary of Continental Celtic Place-Names'', Aberystwyth University, s.v. ''Aunios''.</ref> perhaps from {{der|gl|ine-pro|*h₂epó}}.<ref>{{cite-book|year=2003|author=Xavier Delamarre|title=Dictionnaire de la langue gauloise: Une approche linguistique du vieux-celtique continental|ISBN=2-87772-237-6|page=60}}</ref>
etym.Bethan: Shortened form of {{m|en|Bethany}}, from {{der|en|grc|Βηθανία}}, from {{der|en|arc|[[בית]] [[עניא]]|tr=beth anya|t=house of wretchedness}}.
etym.Ana: From various languages including {{bor|en|es|-}}, {{bor|en|pt|-}}, {{bor|en|ro|-}}, {{bor|en|bg|-}}, {{bor|en|sh|-}}, {{bor|en|sl|-}}, and {{bor|en|mk|-}}, all derived{{mdash}}sometimes via {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} in the [[Vulgate]]{{mdash}}from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα||[[Anna]]}}, chiefly in reference to {{w|Saint Anne}}, the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]], mother of [[Jesus]], but appearing in the [[New Testament]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. As an Oregonian river, named for Ana Byars, daughter of the surveyor W. H. Byars. {{doublet|en|Ann|Anne|Anna|
etym.Joyce: Medieval ({{der|en|enm|-}}) given name from {{der|en|fro|Josse}}, name of a seventh century saint Latinized as {{m|la|Iodocus}}, from {{der|en|br|Iodoc}}, diminutive of {{m|br|iudh||lord}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*yowdos}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Dictionary of Surnames. Oxford University Press 1988.</ref>
etym.Alanna: A feminine form of {{m|en|Alan}}; variant spelling of {{m|en|Alana}}. Compare also {{m|en|Alannah}}.
etym.Jennifer:
From {{der|en|kw|Gweniver}}, from {{der|en|cnx|Gwynnever}} (cognate with {{cog|cy|Gwenhwyfar}}), from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*Gwɨnnohuɨβar}}<!--, equivalent to ''[[gwen]]'', meaning ''fair, white'', and [g]''[[hwyf]]''[ar], meaning ''smooth''-->. {{doublet|en|Guinevere}}. Compare {{cog|ga|Fionnabhair}}, which may be cognate.

The {{IPAchar|/d͡ʒ/}} consonantism is due to Anglo-Norman influence; compare {{cog|fro|Genievre}} {{IPAchar|/d͡ʒəˈniɛ̯vɾə/|/d͡ʒəˈnjɛvɾə/}}.
etym.Jen: Usually a clipped or hypocoristic form of {{m|en|Jennifer}}, although also used for {{m|en|Jean}}, {{m|en|Jeanette}}, {{m|en|Jeannette}}, etc. {{dbt|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} in these secondary derivations.
etym.Jenna:
A Cornish name, usually as a diminutive form of {{m|en|Jennifer}}.

{{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} when based on {{m|en|Jenny}}'s other derivations.
etym.Olga: Borrowed in the 19th century from {{der|en|orv|О́льга}}, name of a Kievan [[knyaginya]] ({{w|Saint Olga of Kiev}}), a medieval form of [[Helga]], {{der|en|non|heilagr||holy; inviolable, sacred}}. {{doublet|en|Helga}}.
etym.Tabitha: From {{uder|en|arc|sc=Hebr|טביתא|tr=Ṭabītā’||doe, roe, gazelle}}, translated as [[Dorcas]] in the Bible.
etym.Alana: Feminine form of {{m|en|Alan|pos=from {{suffix|en|Alan|-a}}}}. In regular use since the 20th century.
etym.Alannah: Modern variant of {{m|en|Alana}}, the feminine form of {{m|en|Alan}}. Also associated with the affectionate Anglo-Irish term of address {{m|en|alanna||child}}. The spelling is influenced by names of Hebrew origin such as Hannah and Susannah.
etym.Alaina: A variant of {{m|en|Alana}} coined in the 20th century from {{m|fr|Alain}}, the French equivalent of {{m|en|Alan}}.
etym.Imogen: First used by {{w|William Shakespeare}} in ''{{w|Cymbeline}}'', a misprint for [[Innogen]], from {{der|en|gd|inghean||girl, maiden}}
etym.Tamsin: A medieval contraction of {{m|en|Thomasina}}, a feminine form of {{m|en|Thomas}}, revived in the UK in the twentieth century.
etym.Isolde: Borrowed from the {{der|en|de|Isolde}}, German form of {{m|en|Iseult}}.
etym.Patil: {{bor+|en|mr|पाटील||village head}} or through {{bor|en|kn|ಪಾಟೀಲ||village head}}, from {{der|en|omr|𑘢𑘘𑘺𑘩}}, from {{der|en|pra|𑀧𑀝𑁆𑀝𑀇𑀮𑁆𑀮}}, from {{der|en|sa|पट्टकिल}}. {{dbt|en|Patel}}.
etym.Alanis: A feminine form of {{m|en|Alan}} best known for the Canadian singer {{w|Alanis Morissette}} whose father was named Alan.
etym.Alora: From Botswana, it means "my dream" in the [[Bantu]] languages.
etym.Ximena: A female equivalent of {{m|eu|Semeno}}, itself from {{m|eu|seme|t=son}}.
etym.Alaia: Borrowed in the 21st century from {{bor|en|eu|Alaia}}, from {{m|eu|alai||joyful}}. For earlier use among English-speakers, compare {{cog|he|עֲלִיָּה|tr='alīyá||ascent}}, {{cog|ar|عَالِيَة|t=high, exalted}}.
etym.Brianne: A feminine form of {{m|en|Brian}}, taken to regular use in the 1970s.
etym.Alanah: Rare spelling variant of {{m|en|Alana}}, the feminine form of {{m|en|Alan}}.
etym.December:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:December<ety:bor<fro:decembre>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|December}}, {{m|enm|Decembre}}, from {{der|en|fro|decembre}}, from {{der|en|la|december|t=tenth month}}, from {{der|en|la|decem|t=ten}}; + {{der|en|la|-ber}}, from {{m|la|-bris}}, an adjectival suffix; December was the tenth month in the Roman calendar.
etym.April:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Aprill|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|apprile}}, {{m|en|Aprill}}, re-Latinised from {{cog|enm|aueril}}, from {{der|en|fro|avrill}}, from {{der|en|la|Aprīlis||of the month of the goddess [[Venus]]}}, perhaps based on {{der|en|ett|𐌀𐌐𐌓𐌖}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀφροδίτη||Venus}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|ēastermōnaþ|t=April|lit=Easter month}}, see {{m|en|Eastermonth}}.
etym.Bonnie: Originally an American nickname from Scottish {{m|en|bonnie||fine, beautiful}}.
etym.Colleen: From the word {{m|en|colleen}}, from {{der|en|ga|cailín||girl}}, not used as a name in Ireland. Colleen can also be interpreted as a variant of [[Coleen]], which was a product of marketing by the Hollywood film industry (to promote a new starlet in the 1920s).
etym.Apple: From {{m|en|apple}}. As a surname, also an Americanized form of ''[[Appel]]'' or ''[[Apfel]]''.<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
etym.Blue: From the {{der|en|de|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Blau}} or its {{der|en|fr|-}} cognate {{m|en|bleu}}.
etym.Charity:
From {{m|en|charity}} in the Biblical sense of [[Christian]] [[love]]; first used by [[Puritan]]s. In early Christian tradition, [[w:Faith, Hope and Charity|Faith, Hope and Charity]] were the martyred daughters of Saint [[Sophia]]. The names, taken from 1 [[Corinthians]] 13:13 ("And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity") have been translated and used in many languages.

The name of the sura (chapter) is one of several translations of the original Arabic.
etym.Dahlia: The plant genus was named by [[botanist]] Antonio José Cavanilles (1745-1804) after [[Swedish]] botanist {{w|Anders Dahl}} (1751-1789).<ref>{{R:Zander}}</ref><ref>{{R:Plants and their Names}}</ref>
etym.Daisy: From the flower [[daisy]], one of the flower names dating from the 19th century. Also a [[nickname]] for [[Margaret]], since [[Marguerite]] and [[Margarita]] are identical with the French and Spanish word for "daisy".
etym.Diamond:
* As a female given name, from {{m|en|diamond|pos=gemstone}}.
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, Anglicized form of {{m|en|Diamant}}.
* As a {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Ó Diamáin}}.
etym.Ebony: From {{m|en|ebony}}. First used by African Americans in the 1970s.
etym.Karen: From {{bor|en|da|Karen}}, a vernacular form of ''[[Catherine]]'' that arose in medieval Denmark. The sense "middle-aged woman" comes from the popularity of the name among [[baby boomer]]s and [[Gen-Xer]]s. The derogatory usage was popularized via [[African-American Vernacular English]].<ref>{{cite-web|en |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-53588201 |publisher={{w|BBC}} |work=BBC News |date=2020-07-31 |accessdate=2020-07-30 |last=Nagesh |first=Ashitha |title=What exactly is a 'Karen' and where did the meme come from? |passage=Although its exact origins are uncertain, the meme became popular a few years ago as a way for people of colour, particularly black Americans, to satirise the class-ba
etym.Darlene: A 20th-century coinage from {{m|en|darling}} and names like {{m|en|Charlene}} and {{m|en|Marlene}}.
etym.Cheri: A variant of {{m|en|Sherry}} or coined from {{uder|en|fr|chéri}}, {{m|fr|chérie||darling}}, not used as a given name in France.
etym.Daffodil: From the [[daffodil]] flower, used since the end of the 19th century.
etym.Bryony: From the {{m|en|bryony}} plant in the 19th century.
etym.Birdie: From {{m|en|birdie||little bird}}. Also used as a diminutive of {{m|en|Bertha}}.
etym.January:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Januarie<ety:from<Janevere<ety:bor<xno:genever<ety:der<la:Iānuārius>>>>>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Januarie}}, {{m|enm|januari}}, re-latinised forms of {{cog|enm|Janevere}}, {{m|enm|Ieneuer}}, from {{der|en|xno|genever}}, from {{der|en|la|Iānuārius||(month) of Janus}}, a compound of {{com|la|Iānus|-ārius||pos1="[[Janus]]"|pos2=adjectival suffix|nocat=1}}, with the first element perhaps from the [[Proto-Indo-European]] root {{m|ine-pro|*yeh₂-||to go}}. {{doublet|en|Gennaro}}.
etym.June:
{{etymon|en|id=month|:inh|enm:June<id:month><ety:from<Juyn<ety:bor<fro:juin>>>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|June}}, {{m|enm|june}}, re-Latinised variants of earlier {{der|en|enm|Juyn}}, {{m|enm|juyng}}, from {{der|en|fro|juing}}, {{m|fro|juin}}, from {{der|en|la|iūnius}}, the month of the goddess {{m|la|Iuno||Juno}}, perhaps from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂yéwHō}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂óyu||vital force, youthful vigor}}.
etym.July:
{{etymon|en|id=month|:inh|enm:Julie<ety:bor<xno:julie<ety:from<fro:jule<ety:inh<la:iūlius>>>>>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Julie,julius,julye}}, from {{der|en|xno|julie}}, from {{der|en|fro|jule}}, {{m|fro|juil}}, from {{der|en|la|iūlius}} ({{w|Julius Caesar|Gaius Julius Caesar}}'s month), perhaps a contraction of ''*Iovilios'', "descended from [[Jove]]".
etym.Felicity: From the noun {{m|en|felicity}}, and also the English form of {{uder|en|la|Felicitas}}, a name borne by early martyrs.
etym.Ginger: A [[diminutive]] of {{m|en|Virginia}}; also a nickname for someone or something with [[ginger]]-coloured hair.
etym.Grace: From the noun {{m|en|grace}}, first used by Puritans in the 16th century. In Roman Catholic use it may refer to {{w|Our Lady of Graces}}, cognate with Italian [[Grazia]].
etym.Heather: From {{m|en|heather}}; the given name is one of the plant names taken up in the 19th century. The surname is habitational, also meaning someone living on a [[heath]].
etym.Honor: Shortened from {{m|en|Honoria}} and {{m|en|Honora}}; later also interpreted as a [[virtue name]] by [[Puritan]]s.
etym.Jade: From the precious stone {{m|en|jade}}; taken into general use in the 1970s.
etym.Joy: From the noun ''[[joy]]'', first used by [[Puritan]]s in the 17th century.
etym.Lily: A 19th-century flower name, from {{m|en|lily}}. Also a [[diminutive]] of {{m|en|Lilian}} and sometimes {{m|en|Elizabeth}}.
etym.Melody: From the noun {{m|en|melody}}; in regular use since the 20th century.
etym.Mercy: From {{m|en|mercy}} in the 17th century; one of the less common [[Puritan]] [[virtue]] names. In modern use sometimes used to anglicize Spanish {{m|es|Mercedes}}.
etym.Ocean: From {{m|en|ocean||sea}}, inspired by the fashionable French female name [[Océane]].
etym.Patience: From {{m|en|patience}}, a virtue name first used by [[Puritan]]s in the sixteenth century.
etym.Petunia:
{{etymon|mul|id=petunia|:af|fr:pétun|-ia|tree=1}}
From {{af|mul|fr:pétun<t:tobacco>|-ia}}, by comparison of its flowers to the tobacco's.<ref>{{R:BHL|page/3496441#page/251/mode/1up}}</ref> {{coin|mul|Q223963|in=1803}}.
etym.Primrose: The surname derives from a place name in Fife, Scotland; Watson (1926) derived this from {{der|en|xpi|-}}/{{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*prenn||wood, tree}} + {{m|cel-bry-pro|*rros||moor, heath}}. Taylor instead argued for {{der|en|gd|prím||first}} + {{m|gd|ros||promontory}}. Changed by folk etymology because of phonetic resemblance to {{m|en|primrose}}. The given name is one of the 19th-century flower names.
etym.Myrtle: After the plant, {{m|en|myrtle}}; used since the end of the 19th century.
etym.Mavis: Coined at the end of the 19th century from {{m|en|mavis}}, a poetical name for the [[song thrush]].
etym.Misty: From the adjective {{m|en|misty}}, but sometimes also (like {{m|en|Missy}}) used as a nickname for {{m|en|Melissa}}.
etym.Magnolia: {{suffix|mul|{{der|mul|fr|Magnol}}|ia}}. Named by [[botanist]] {{w|Carl Linnaeus}} (1707-1778) after [[botanist]] {{w|Pierre Magnol}} (1638-1715).<ref>{{R:Zander}}</ref><ref>{{R:Plants and their Names}}</ref>
etym.Melodie: From {{inh|de|gmh|melodīe}}, from {{der|de|la|melodia}}, from {{der|de|grc|μελῳδίᾱ}}. Since the 16th century, the inherited form {{m|de||Melodei}} was increasingly readapted to the Latin and to {{der|de|fr|mélodie}}.
etym.Jonquil: From {{m|en|jonquil}}; one of the [[flower]] names invented in the 19th century.
etym.Holley:
* As an English surname, spelling variant of {{m|en|Holly}}.
* Also as an English surname, from {{der|en|ang|hol|t=hollow}} {{m|ang|leah|t=wood, clearing, meadow}} or {{der|en|ang|hol}} {{m|ang|ēage|t=eye}}, perhaps a nickname for someone with a missing eye.
* Also as an English surname, singular variant of {{m|en|Hollis}}.
etym.Melba: Coined by {{w|Nellie Melba}} as a pseudonym; derived from {{m|en|Melbourne}}.
etym.Marigold: From the flower. The rubber gloves are generally bright yellow in colour.
etym.Journey: From {{m|en|journey}} at the end of the 20th century.
etym.Glory: From {{m|en|glory}} as a variant of the more common {{m|en|Gloria}}.
etym.Zinnia: Named for the {{der|mul|de|-}} botanist {{w|Johann Gottfried Zinn}} + [[-ia]], from {{m|de|Zinn||tin}}, from an occupational surname for a [[tinsmith]].
etym.Ann: From {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[Vulgate]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα||[[Anna]]}} in the [[New Testament]], from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. Occasionally reborrowed from languages who adopted the name from English. Very infrequently from {{bor|en|et|-}} abbreviation of {{m|et|Anna}} instead. {{doublet|en|Ana|Anna|Anne|Hannah}}.
etym.Rosemary: A combination of {{compound|en|Rose|Mary}}, referring to the flower as a symbol of [[Virgin Mary]], first recorded in the eighteenth century. It is found in continental Europe as [[Rosemarie]] and [[Rosa]] [[Maria]]. After mid-nineteenth century when flower names became common it may also refer to the herb [[rosemary]], Latin ''ros marinus'' "dew of the sea".
etym.Sapphire: {{rfe|en|Why used for aggressive black women? Character from "Amos 'n' Andy", or some earlier source?}}
etym.Star:
* As a {{der|en|de|-}} and Jewish surname, from {{m|de|Star|t=starling}}.
* Also as a German and Jewish surname, {{semantic loan|en|de|Stern|t=star|nocap=1}}.
* As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, from {{m|nl|star|t=stiff, rigid}}.
* As a {{der|en|sl|-}} surname, from {{m|sl|star|t=old}}.
* As an English given name, from {{m|en|star}}, sometimes originating as a nickname.
etym.Violet: A 19th century flower name from {{m|en|violet}}, sometimes as an anglicisation of the earlier {{uder|en|fr|Violette}}.
etym.Antoinette: From {{der|en|fr|Antoinette}}, feminine diminutive of {{m|fr|Antoine}}, equivalent to {{m|en|Anthony}}.
etym.Aimee: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Aimée||beloved}}. A variation of the English {{m|en|Amy}}.
etym.Annette: From {{bor|en|fr|Annette}}, diminutive of {{m|fr|Anne}}, from {{m|grc|Ἄννα}}, the {{der|en|grc|-}} New Testament form of the {{der|en|he|-}} female name {{m|he|חַנָּה|tr=ḥannâ|t=grace, gracious}} with the French suffix ''<nowiki/>'ette''' meaning cute, adorable or little. So, Annette could mean "Little favor of God", "cute grace" or "little Anne".
etym.Adrienne: From the {{der|en|fr|Adrienne}}, the feminine form of {{m|fr|Adrien}} (equivalent to English {{m|en|Adrian}}).
etym.Alexandrine: Partly from {{bor|en|frm|alexandrin}} and partly from {{bor|en|la|Alexandrīnus}}.<ref>{{R:OED Online|pos=''n.''<sup>1</sup> and ''adj.''<sup>1</sup>|noformat=1|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020010911/https://www.oed.com/dictionary/alexandrine_n1?tl=true}}</ref>
etym.Temperance: From {{m|en|temperance}}. A virtue name first used by [[Puritan]]s in the 16th century.
etym.Tansy: From the plant {{m|en|tansy}}. Probable doublet of {{m|en|Athanasia}}.
etym.Tulip: {{unk|en|title=Unexplained}}, but possibly a late formation from {{m|en|tulip}}.
etym.Sharee: A variant of {{m|en|Sherry}} or coined from {{uder|en|fr|chéri}}, {{m|fr|chérie||darling}}.
etym.Charlotte: From {{bor|en|fr|Charlotte}} in the 17th century, a female diminutive form of {{m|fr|Charles}}, from {{der|en|gmh|Karl}}, which came from the Germanic {{m|gem-pro||*karlaz}}. The civil parish is named after {{w|Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz}} (1744-1818). {{coin|en|Samuel Holland|occ=surveyor|nat=British-Dutch}}.
etym.Blanche: From {{uder|en|fro|blanc|t=white}}. The surname originated as a nickname, or as a [[matronymic]].
etym.Fleur: {{uder|en|fr|fleur||flower}}, name of a character in Galsworthy's ''Forsyte Saga''.
