etym.Gabrielle: {{bor+|en|fr|Gabrielle}}, feminine form of {{m|en|Gabriel}} (see there for more).
etym.Bernadette: From {{uder|en|fr|Bernadette}}, made famous by St. Bernadette of Lourdes.
etym.Chantal: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Chantal}} in the 1960s, from the surname of a French saint Jeanne de Chantal, actually a [[baroness|Baroness]] of Chantal, a place name in France from {{der|en|pro|-}} {{m|pro|cantal||stone, [[moellon]], [[rubblestone]]}}.
etym.Desirée: Introduced to Sweden by the early 19th century {{der|sv|fr|-}}-born queen {{l|fr|Désirée}} Bernadotte. Desirée is the most popular spelling in Sweden.
etym.Eloise: From {{bor|en|fr|Éloïse}}, from the {{der|en|la-med|-}} and French forms that gave rise to its [[Appendix:Glossary#doublet|doublet]] {{doublet|en|Heloise|notext=1}}.
etym.Clarisse: {{bor+|en|fr|Clarisse}}, from {{der|en|it|Clarissa}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Clarissa|t=[[Poor Clare]]}}; see there for more. {{doublet|en|Clarissa|Clarice}}.
etym.Clarice: {{bor+|en|fr|Clarisse}}, from {{der|en|it|Clarissa}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Clarissa|t=[[Poor Clare]]}}; see there for more. {{doublet|en|Clarissa|Clarisse}}.
etym.Genevieve:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ǵenh₁-}}
Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Geneviève}} {{gloss|patron saint of Paris}}, from {{der|en|la|Genovefa}}, {{m|la|Genoveva}}, possibly either of {{der|en|gem}} origin, ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} {{af|gem-pro|*kunją|t1=kin, family|*wībą|t2=woman, wife|nocat=1}}, or of {{der|en|cel}} origin, ultimately from {{der|en|cel-pro|*genos|t=family, clan}}.
etym.Gigi:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Gigi}}. Sometimes a pet form of English names such as {{m|en|Virginia}} or {{m|en|Genesis}}.
Occasionally from initials G.G. (e.g. [[w:George General Grice, Jr|George General 'Gigi' Gryce]]).
etym.Elyse: A rare spelling variant of {{m|en|Elise}}. By folk etymology, connected to {{m|en|Elysium}}.
etym.Elouisa: Alternative form of {{m|en|Eloise}} or {{m|en|Elouise}}, influenced by {{m|en|Louisa}}.
etym.Heloise: From {{der|en|la-med|Heloisa}} under influence from {{der|en|fr|Héloïse}}, probably from {{der|en|fr|Éloi}} + {{m|fr|-esse|-se|[[-ess]]: ''[[feminizing]] [[noun]]s''}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Eligius}}, chiefly after {{w|Saint Eligius}}, from {{der|en|la|ēligō|ēligere|to [[pick]], to [[choose]] from}} + {{m|la|-ius||[[-y]]: ''[[form]]ing [[adjective]]s and [[name]]s''}}. Sometimes alternatively derived from {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} reconstructed as {{m|gem-pro|*Hailawidiz}}, from {{m|gem-pro|*hailagaz||[[holy]]}} or {{m|gem-pro|*hailaz||[[whole]], [[healthful]]}} and {{m|gem-pro|*widuz||[[wood]], [[forest]]}}. As an English name, chiefly after {{w|Peter Abelard}}'s beloved nun {{w|Heloise}}. {{dou
etym.Elois: From {{bor|en|fr|Éloïse}}, from the {{der|en|la-med|-}} and French forms that gave rise to its [[Appendix:Glossary#doublet|doublet]] {{doublet|en|Heloise|notext=1}}.
etym.Jane:
Variant of {{m|en|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}} and earlier use of {{m|en|Joan}} in the same role.

{{dbt|en|Gianna|Ivana|Jana|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Janet:
From {{suffix|en|Jane|et}}, q.v. Chiefly Scottish until the 19th century.

{{doublet|en|Jeanette|Jeannette|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead}}.
etym.Joanne:
From {{der|en|fro|Joanne}}, from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Josephine: From {{bor|en|fr|Joséphine}}, diminutive of {{m|fr|Josèphe}}, feminine form of {{m|fr|Joseph}}. {{surf|en|Joseph|-ine<id:female>}}. Popularized in English by {{w|Josephine Bonaparte}}, the empress of {{w|Napoleonic France}}.
etym.Jacqueline: From {{bor|en|fr|Jacqueline}}, a feminine diminutive form of {{m|fr|Jacques|t=[[James]]}}, from {{der|en|he|יעקב|tr=ya'akóv|t=[[Jacob]]}}, from the root {{m|he|עקב|tr=‘akev|t=[[heel]]}}, because the biblical patriarch {{w|Jacob}} was born just behind {{w|Esau}}, and was grasping Esau’s heel in an effort to prevent him from being born first.
etym.Henriette: From {{bor|en|fr|Henriette}}, feminine form of {{m|fr|Henri|t=[[Henry]]}} coined in the seventeenth century; in English more popular as [[Harriet]] and [[Henrietta]].
etym.Marguerite: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Marguerite}} in the 1860s. {{doublet|en|Margaret}}, ultimately from the {{der|en|grc|μαργαρίτης||pearl}}.
etym.Jeanette:
From {{suffix|en|Jean|ette}} or misspelling of {{bor|en|fr|Jeannette}}, from {{m|fr|Jeanne}} + {{m|fr|-ette}}, q.v. Originally chiefly Scottish.

{{doublet|en|Janet|Jeannette|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead}}.
etym.Janine:
From {{bor|en|fr|Janine}} and {{m|fr|Jeannine}} under influence from {{m|en|Jane}}, from {{m|fr|Jeanne}} + {{m|fr|-ine}}, q.v.

{{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}}.
etym.Monique: Borrowed from {{bor|nl|fr|Monique}}, from {{der|nl|la|Monica}}, probably from {{der|nl|xpu|-}}, though Latin and Ancient Greek etymologies have also been proposed.
etym.Lise: From the {{uder|en|fr|-}}, and possible also from Scandinavian, {{m|fr|Lise}}. Variant of more common English {{m|en|Lisa}}.
etym.Nicolette: Diminutive of {{m|fr|Nicole}}, the feminine form of {{m|fr|Nicolas}}.
etym.Jeannine:
From {{bor|en|fr|Jeannine}}, from {{m|fr|Jeanne}} + {{m|fr|-ine}}, q.v. Sometimes also parsed as a diminutive of English {{m|en|Jean}}, {{m|en|Jeanne}}, etc.

{{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jen|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}}.
etym.Noelle: From {{der|en|fr|Noëlle}}, the feminine form of the male given name {{m|fr|Noël}}.
etym.Stephanie: {{bor+|en|fr|Stéphanie}}. The standard English feminine form of {{m|en|Stephen}}. {{doublet|en|Stephania}}.
etym.Yvonne: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} feminine form of [[Yvon]], variant of [[Yves]], from a {{der|en|gem}} root for "[[yew]]" (see {{cog|ang|iw}}). It might have originally been used of an [[archer]], since yew wood was used to make bows.
etym.Renée: From {{uder|en|fr|Renée}}, meaning [[reborn]], stemmed from {{uder|en|la|-}} [[Renata]]. Feminine form of male [[René]].
etym.Yvette: {{bor+|en|fr|Yvette}}. The politics sense is a reference to the name of a docile young girl in a school textbook, and was popularized by separatist politician {{w|Lise Payette}} (1931–2018).
etym.Paulette: Borrowed in the twentieth century from {{uder|en|fr|-}} [[#French|Paulette]], a diminutive feminine form of {{m|fr|Paul}}.
etym.Rosalie: From {{bor|en|fr|Rosalie}}, from the {{der|en|la|-}} saints’ name {{m|la|Rosālia}}, from {{m|la|rosa||rose}}. {{doublet|en|Rosalia}}.
etym.Elsa:
{{ety|en|:bor|de:Elsa|tree=1}}
From {{bor|en|de|Elsa}}, contraction of {{m|de|Elisabeth}}, occasionally used in English after its appearance in [[Wagner]]'s opera ''Lohengrin'' (1847). The common noun is after [[w:Elsa (Frozen)|the character]] of the ''{{w|Frozen}}'' series of films.
etym.Hildegard: Borrowed from {{bor|en|de|Hildegard}} in the 19th century; ultimately from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Hildigardu}}.
etym.Odette: Diminutive of a short form of {{uder|fr|gem|-}} compound names beginning with the element ''od-, ot-'' "riches," from {{der|fr|gem-pro|*audaz}}.
etym.Brunhilde: From {{inh|de|gmh|Briunhilde}}, from {{inh|de|goh|*Brunnīhilta}}, from {{inh|de|gmw-pro|*Brunnjuhildi}}, from {{inh|de|gem-pro|*Brunjōhildiz}}, from {{m|gem-pro|*brunjǭ|t=breastplate}} + {{m|gem-pro|*hildiz|t=battle, fight}}.
etym.Brunhild: From {{bor|en|de|Brunhilde}}, from {{der|en|gmh|Briunhilde}}, from {{der|en|goh|*Brunnīhilta}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Brunnjuhildi}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Brunjōhildiz|pos=from {{af|gem-pro|*brunjǭ|t1=breastplate|*hildiz|t2=battle, fight|nocat=1}}}}.
etym.Pleasance: From an {{uder|en|fro|-}} female given name {{m|fro|Plaisance}}, from {{m|fro|plaisance||pleasance}}. The surname is partly [[matronymic]], partly [[habitational]] from the {{uder|en|it|-}} town of {{m|it|Piacenza}}.
etym.Lorelei: Borrowed from {{bor|en|de|Lorelei||murmuring rock or lurking rock}}, but not used as a given name in Germany. The Lorelei (or Lorelei, Loreleï, Lore Lay, Lore-Ley, Lurley, Lurelei, Lurlei) is an infamous maritime disaster site because of the Rhine's current and the surrounding terrain. The shipwrecks have been subject to mythological explanation attempts since around 900 AD.
etym.Alberta:
{{ety|en|:af|Albert|-a}}
From {{suffix|en|Albert|a}}. The province was named after [[w:Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll|Princess Louise Caroline Alberta]].
etym.Alice:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Alice<ety:bor<fro:Alys>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Alice}}, from {{der|en|fro|Alys}}, {{m|fro|Alice}}, from {{der|en|goh|Adalheid}}, proposed to derive from {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} {{af|gem-pro|*aþalaz|t1=noble|*haiduz|t2=character|nocat=1}}. {{doublet|en|Adelaide}}.
etym.Alicia: A [[Latinization]] of {{m|en|Alice}}, which is in turn from {{der|en|fro|Adelais}}, {{der|en|gem|-}} {{m|goh|Adalheid}}.
etym.Ada: Short form of {{der|en|gem}} names beginning with {{m|goh|adal||noble}}, such as [[Adelaide]]. Also Latinized form of Hebrew [[Adah]]. The programming language takes its name from [[w:Ada Lovelace|Ada Lovelace]].
etym.Adele: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Adèle}}, equivalent of {{m|en|Adela}}, from a {{der|en|gem|-}} root meaning “noble”. Compare {{m|en|athel}}, {{cog|de|edel}}, {{cog|ang|æþele}}.
etym.Aleshia: One of the modern variations of {{m|en|Alicia}}, meaning "of noble kind".
etym.Amelia: From the feminine given name {{m|en|Amelia}}, used as a Latinized taxonomic name.
etym.Amalia: Derived from {{der|en|gem}} compound names beginning with {{der|en|gem-pro|*amalą||vigor, bravery}}, like Ostrogothic {{m|en|Amalaberga}} and {{w|Amalafrida}}.<ref>{{cite-book|de|title=Deutsche Namenkunde|year=1932|author=Max Gottschald|page=87|year_published=2006|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|location=Berlin, New York|edition=6th|isbn=978-3-11-018031-2}}</ref>
etym.Alison:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Alisoun|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Alisoun}}, from {{der|en|fro|Alison}}, brought to England by the Normans {{gloss|from {{der|en|xno|Alison}}, from {{der|en|nrf|Alison}} }}, diminutive of {{m|fro|Aliz|}}, equivalent to English {{m|en|Alice}}, from {{der|en|goh|Adalhaid||of noble kind}}.
etym.Aletta: From a {{der|en|gml|-}} diminutive form of {{m|de|Adelheid}}, related to English {{m|en|Adelaide}} and {{m|en|Alice}}.
etym.Carly: A feminine form of {{m|en|Carl}} with {{affix|en|-y<id:diminutive>}}, taken to use in the latter half of the 20th century; also a pet form of {{m|en|Carla}}, {{m|en|Carlene}} and {{m|en|Carlotta}}.
etym.Charlene: A feminine form of {{m|en|Charles}} coined in the nineteenth century. Compare {{m|en|Marlene}}, {{m|en|Helene}} and {{m|en|Magdalene}} for the suffix.
etym.Alyssa:
A 20th-century invention. Possible origins:
* From {{suffix|en|alyssum<alt:alyss(um)><t:a plant of the genus {{taxfmt|Alyssum|genus}}>|a}}.
* From {{m|en|Alicia}}, of {{der|en|gem}} origin.
* From {{m|en|Elissa}}.
etym.Verena: Of obscure origin and meaning; from Verena of Zurzach (near [[Zurich]]), a 3rd/4th century saint.
etym.Bertha:
Definitely from {{der|en|ang|Berþa}} as a result of metathesis of h, from earlier {{der|en|ang|Berhte||bright one}}, influence of Latin [[Bercta]].

Alternatively, from {{der|en|goh|berhta||bright one}}, which was an [[epithet]] of the goddess [[Frigg]].
etym.Adeline: From {{der|en|fro|Adeline}}, a diminutive form of {{m|en|Adela}} and {{m|en|Adele}} brought to England by the [[Norman]]s.
etym.Astrid: Borrowed from modern Scandinavian ({{der|en|sv|-}}, {{der|en|no|-}}, {{der|en|da|-}}) {{m|sv|Astrid}} since the 19th century.
etym.Alina: {{bor+|en|it|Alina}}, or a Latinate form of {{bor|en|fr|Aline}}, ultimately from diminutives of the same Germanic name {{m|en|Adela}}, {{m|en|Adele}}.
etym.Albertina: A feminine diminutive form of {{m|en|Albert}}. Latinate variant of {{m|en|Albertine}}. {{surf|en|Albert|-ina}}.
etym.Alesha: One of the modern variations of {{m|en|Alicia}}.
etym.Clotilda: A [[Latinate]] form of the {{der|en|fr|Clotilde}}, of {{cog|gem|-}} origin ({{der|en|gem-pro|*Hlūdahildiz}}).
etym.Alyshia: One of the modern variations of [[Alicia]] meaning ''of noble kind''.
etym.Carlene: A 20th-century coinage from {{m|en|Carl}} and the ending -''ene'', -''lene'', as in {{m|en|Marlene}} and {{m|en|Charlene}}.
etym.Heidi: From Swiss {{der|en|de|Heidi}}, a pet form of {{m|de|Adelheid}}, equivalent of English [[Adelaide]] and [[Alice]]. The name became internationally popular due to the children's book ''{{w|Heidi}}'' (1880). {{C|en|Switzerland}} {{C|en|Fictional characters}}
etym.Henrietta: Latinate form of {{der|en|fr|Henriette}}, derived from the male [[given name]] {{m|en|Henry}}.
etym.Harriet: Anglicized form of {{der|en|fr|Henriette}}, feminine form of {{m|fr|Henri||Henry}}, popular in England in the 18th and 19th centuries.
etym.Geraldine: From {{suffix|en|Gerald|ine}}. c. 1540 by the Earl of Surrey as a poetic name for Lady Elizabeth Fitzgerald, "one of the Fitzgeralds". Taken up as a given name in the 19th century, and used as a feminine form of [[Gerald]].
etym.Gertrude: From {{uder|en|fro}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*gaizaz||spear}} + {{m|gem-pro|*þrūþiz||strength}} or {{m|gem-pro|*trut-||maiden, dear}} ; name of a Belgian seventh century saint.
etym.Emma: Brought to England by the [[Norman]]s; short form of compound given names beginning with a [[Frankish]] [[prototheme]] ''[[Ermin-]]'' or ''[[Irmin-]]'' "entire", from {{der|en|gem-pro|*ermunaz}}.
etym.Edlyn: A 20th-century coinage, apparently a blend of {{m|en|Ed}} + {{m|en|Lyn}}, or a variant of [[Edeline]].
etym.Hilda: Short form of {{der|en|gem|-}} names beginning or ending in {{m|ang|hild||battle}}.
etym.Frida:
* In Scandinavia, Frida mainly derives from the {{der|en|non|-}} name {{m|non|Fríða}}, short for female names ending in {{m|non|fríðr||beautiful, beloved}}.
* In Central and Eastern Europe, Frida is a short form of compound names containing the Germanic element ''[[fried]]'' "peace"; cognate to English [[Freda]].
etym.Ida: Short form of obsolete names beginning with Germanic ''īd'' "work", used for both sexes in medieval England. It was revived in the 19th century, partly mistaken for a Greek name, for the Mount Ida of classical mythology.
etym.Irma: From {{der|en|de|Irma}} in the nineteenth century. Short form of {{der|en|gem}} names beginning with ''irm(en)-, erm(en)'' "whole, entire", from {{der|en|gem-pro|*ermunaz}}. Cognate with {{cog|en|Emma}}.
etym.Freda: A feminine form of [[Frederick]] and [[Fred]], also a short form of [[Winifred]].
etym.Frieda: Short form of names containing the Germanic element ''[[fried]]'' "peace", such as {{m|de|Friederike}} or {{m|de|Elfriede}}.
etym.Frederica: From {{suffix|en|Frederick|a}}.<ref>{{R:behindthename|passage=Usage Portuguese, English {{...}} Feminine form of {{l|pt|Frederico}} or Frederick.}}</ref><ref>{{R:en:DFN|page=103|column=2|passage=Latinate feminine form of ▹Frederick.}}</ref> Compare {{cog|da|Frederikke}}, {{cog|fr|Frédérique}}, {{cog|de|Friederike}}, and {{cog|it|Federica}}.
etym.Evelina: From {{der|sv|en|Evelyn}}, first recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1795. By [[folk etymology]] interpreted as a [[diminutive]] of {{m|sv|Eva}}.
etym.Gerda: Latinate variant of Scandinavian [[Gerd]], from {{der|en|non|Gerðr}}, {{m|non|garðr||protection}}. The name occurs in nineteenth century Swedish poetry and in Hans Christian Andersen's ''Snow Queen'' (1844).
etym.Dagmar: Name of a queen of Denmark (1185–1212), a Czech by descent, originally ''[[Dragomíra]]'' (cf. contemporary Czech {{l|cs|Drahomíra}}), from {{der|da|cu|-}} ''[[Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/dorgъ|dorgъ]]'' "dear" + ''[[Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/mirъ|mirъ]]'' "peace", rendered in medieval Danish under the camouflage of ''[[dag#Danish|dag]]'' "day" + ''[[már#Danish|már]]'' "maid".
etym.Hilma: Used in early 19th-century Scandinavian literature, probably as a variant of [[Wilhelmina]].
etym.Jerilyn:
From {{der|ceb|en|-}}.
Also a {{blend|ceb|Jerry|Lyn|nocat=1|nocap=1}}, {{blend|ceb|Jerome|Lyn|nocat=1|notext=1}}, or a similar construct.
etym.Emmeline: Medieval English form of {{uder|en|fro|Ameline}}, diminutive form of [[Amélie]], cognate to English [[Amelia]].
etym.Elmira: Possibly a feminine equivalent of {{m|en|Elmer}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*aþalaz|t=noble}} + {{m|gem-pro|*mēraz|t=famous}}, as in {{cog|es|Edelmira}}. Introduced through literature (Molière, Goethe).
etym.Huberta: A rare feminine form of {{m|en|Hubert}} (via Latin, or in some cases borrowed from Dutch or German).
etym.Jocelynn: A rare non-standard spelling of {{m|en|Jocelyn}} with {{affix|en|-lynn}}.
etym.Linda:
Latinised short form of {{der|en|gem}} compound names ending in {{m|de|-lind}}, {{m|de|-linde|t=tender, soft}} (English {{m|en|-inda}}), such as {{m|de|Sieglinde}} and {{m|de|Dietlinde}}, and earlier names such as {{cog|goh|Irmilinda}} and {{cog|odt|Frithelind|}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*linþaz|t=gentle, mild}}, whence also {{cog|ang|līþe|t=gentle, mild, pliable, limber}} ({{cog|en|lithe}}). Later misassociated with unrelated {{noncog|es|linda|t=beautiful}}. The name became known through 19th century literature and the opera ''Linda di Chamounix'' (1842). More at {{l|en|lithe}}.

The coordination language is {{named-after|en|Linda Lovelace|wplink==|nocap=1}}, a reference to the programming la
etym.Matilda: From {{inh|en|enm|Matilda}}, from {{der|en|fro|Mathilde}}, from {{der|en|goh|Mahthilt}}, {{m|goh|Mehthilt}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Mahtihild}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Mahtihildiz}}; compare {{cog|de|Mechthild}}, {{cog|ang|Mæþhild|t=Matilda}}.
etym.Rowena:
From the name of the daughter of {{w|Hengist}} and wife of {{w|Vortigern}} in {{w|Geoffrey of Monmouth}}'s 12th century [[pseudohistorical]] [[Latin]] work ''{{w|Historia regum Britanniae}}''. There have been attempts to connect it to some unattested {{cog|ang|-}} or {{w|Common Brittonic}} name, but without any real evidence. It was revived after {{w|Walter Scott}} used it in his novel ''{{w|Ivanhoe}}'' (1819).<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>
Some places are named after Lady Rowena in the novel.
etym.Rosamund: Of {{der|en|gem}} origin (probably {{der|en|frk|-}} via {{der|en|fr|Rosemonde}} or {{der|en|lng|-}} via {{der|en|it|Rosmunda}}), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*hrussą|t=horse}} and {{m|gem-pro|*mundō|t=protection}}. By medieval [[folk etymology]] interpreted as {{noncog|la|[[rosa]] [[munda]]|t=pure rose}} or {{m|la|[[rosa]] [[mundī]]|t=rose of the world}} in reference to the [[Virgin Mary]].<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 1990, p. 287.</ref>
etym.Kiana: Borrowed from {{bor|en|haw|Kiana}}, itself from {{der|en|en|Diana}}. Also used as a modern feminine form of {{m|en|Kian}}.
etym.Millicent: From the {{der|en|fro|Melisende}}, from {{der|en|goh|Amalasuntha}}, {{m|goh|Amalaswintha}}, from the {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} roots {{m|gem-pro|*amalą||hard work}} + {{m|gem-pro|*swinþaz||strong}}.
etym.Rosalind: From {{der|en|gem-pro|*hrussą|t=horse}} and {{m|gem-pro|*linþaz|t=soft; weak, tender}}, associated by medieval [[folk etymology]] with Spanish ''rosa linda'' "lovely rose".
etym.Ulrica: A feminine form of the male given name [[Ulric]] (modern German [[Ulrich]]), [[Germanic]] for "ruler of all" or "wolf[like] ruler".
etym.Trudi: In some cases, a 20th-century spelling of [[Trudy]]; in other cases borrowed from {{uder|en|de|Trudi}}.
etym.Maile: From {{bor|en|haw|Maile}}, from {{m|haw|maile|t=[[maile]], a flowering Hawaiian vine}}.
etym.Willa: Derived from {{m|en|Wilhelmina}} and recoined in the 19th century in America based on the male given names {{m|en|Will}} and {{m|en|William}}.
etym.Ricki: From [[Richard]]. As a female name also from [[Erica]].
etym.Evanthia: From {{bor|en|el|Ευανθία}} and {{bor|en|la|Evanthia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐανθία|pos=from {{af|grc|εὐ-|t1=[[good]]-, [[well]]-|άνθος|t2=[[blossom]]|-ία|t3=[[-ia]]: ''[[form]]ing [[feminine]] [[abstract noun]]s''|nocat=1}}}}. Cognate with {{m|en|Euanthe}}.
etym.Maliyah: Probably a fanciful spelling of {{m|en|Malia}}, from {{bor|en|haw|Malia}}.
etym.Rosemond:
* A variant of {{m|en|Rosamond}}; see {{m|en|Roseman}}.<ref name="DAFN">{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref>
* From {{bor|en|fr|Rosemond}}, the male equivalent of the female given name {{m|fr|Rosemonde}}; see {{m|en|Roseman}}.<ref name="DAFN"/>
etym.Kaelani: From {{der|en|haw|kaʻe|t=edge}} + {{m|haw|lani|t=sky}}, or a modern variant of {{m|en|Kailani}}.
etym.Elizabeth:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:Elizabeth<ety:der<grc:Ἐλισάβετ>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Elizabeth}}, from the {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ|}}, a transliteration of the Old Testament {{der|en|hbo|אלישבע||my [[God]] is an oath|tr=ʔĕlîšeḇaʕ}}. See {{m|en|El}} and {{m|he|שבועה}}. {{doublet|en|Elisheba|Isabel}}.
etym.Abigail: From {{bor|en|he|אֲבִיגַיִל||Abigail|lit=my Father's joy” or “fountain of joy|tr=avigáyil}}.
etym.Dina: Equivalent of the [[biblical]] name [[Dinah]] in several European languages, ultimately from {{der|en|he|דינה|דִּינָה}}.
etym.Elsie: From a Scottish diminutive of [[Alison]]/[[Alice]] and [[Elspeth]]/[[Elizabeth]].
etym.Edna:
From {{der|en|he|עֶדְנָה|t=[[pleasure]]; [[delight]]}}; a variant of [[Eden]] in the Book of Tobit.

In [[Ireland]] and [[Scotland]] it has been used as an anglicization of {{m|ga|Eithne}}.
etym.Elisabeth: The spelling of {{m|en|Elizabeth}} used in the [[Authorized Version]] of the New Testament. Borrowed from {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ}}, a transliteration of {{der|en|he|אֱלִישֶׁבַע|tr=Elishéva|t=my [[God]] is an oath}}.
etym.Debra: A spelling variant of [[Deborah]] first used in the 20th century.
etym.Beulah: A biblical name applied to the land of Israel in Isaiah 62:4, from {{bor|en|hbo|בְּעוּלָה|tr=bəʿûlâ|t=married (woman)}}, taken up as a given name by Puritans and used figuratively for the New Earth.
etym.Daniella:
{{ety|pt|Daniela|tree=1}}
:A popular alteration of {{m|pt|Daniela}}, under influence of other languages.
etym.Bathsheba: From {{der|en|he|בַּת שֶׁבַע|tr=bat shéva'|t=daughter of an oath}}, from {{af|he|בַּת|tr1=bát|t1=daughter|שֶׁבַע|tr2=shéva|t2=oath|nocat=1}}.
etym.Abiah: From {{bor|en|he|אביה}}, name of minor biblical characters.
etym.Meilani: Modern American coinage, rhyming with {{m|en|Leilani}}. Can be interpreted as {{bor|en|haw|Mei}} + {{m|haw|lani}} "heavenly May".
etym.Danna: As a surname from {{bor|en|fr|D'Anna||of {{m|fr|Anna}}}}. The given name is more probably a feminine form coined from {{m|en|Dan}} or {{m|en|Daniel}}.
etym.Hannah: From previous romanizations of {{der|en|he|חַנָּה|tr=Ḥannâ}}, chiefly for the mother of [[Samuel]], from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. As a Wren with the Royal Marines, after {{w|Hannah Snell}} (1723–1792) who disguised herself as a man to serve in the British military. {{doublet|en|Ann|Anne|Anna|Ana}}.
etym.Johan: An archaic variant of {{m|en|Joan}}, from {{der|en|fro|Johan}}, from {{der|en|la|Johanna}}. Cf. [[John]].
etym.Jessica:
First used by William Shakespeare in ''{{w|Merchant of Venice}}'' in the early 17th century, probably from {{der|en|he|יִסְכָּה|tr=yiská|5=Iscah in Genesis 11:29, Jescha in the Wycliffe version}}, a proper name meaning "he will see/behold/look for", the 3ms imperfect form of a verb ultimately {{he-root|ס|כ|ה|tr=s-k-h|nocap=1}},<ref name="klein445">{{R:CEDHL|445}}</ref> itself an alternative form of the root {{m|he|שׂ־כ־ה|tr=ś-k-h}}, both of which mean "to see, behold, look for".<ref name="klein656">{{R:CEDHL|656}}</ref>
* By folk etymology seen as an elaborate form of {{l|en|Jessie}}, from {{l|en|Jane}}.
etym.Joanna:
From {{bor|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Isabella: Latinate and Italian form of {{m|en|Isabel}}. The grape cultivar is popularly thought to have been discovered by a Mrs Isabella Gibbs of South Carolina in 1816.
etym.Isabel: From {{bor|en|es|Isabel}}, from {{der|en|pro|Elisabel}}, from {{der|en|la|Elisabeth}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ}}, from {{der|en|he|אֱלִישֶׁבַע|tr=Elishéva|t=my [[God]] is an oath}}. {{doublet|en|Elizabeth}}.
etym.Hanna: Variant spelling of {{m|en|Hannah}} or romanization of {{der|en|he|חַנָּה|tr=Ḥanâ}}, chiefly for the mother of [[Samuel]], from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥanâ}}. As an Oklahoman town, named for Hanna Bullett, one of the initial settlers. As a Polish village, named for the queen {{w|Anna Jagiellon}}.
etym.Janice:
Variant of {{m|en|Jane}} under apparent influence from {{m|en|Alice}}, {{m|en|Bernice}}, {{m|en|Eunice}}, etc.,  from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}} and earlier use of {{m|en|Joan}} in the same role.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|S
etym.Juanita:
From {{bor|en|es|Juanita}}, from {{m|es|Juana}} + {{m|es|-ita||[[-ette]]}}, from {{der|en|osp|Johanna}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Janet|Jeanette|Jeannette|Shanae|Sinead}}.
etym.Isabell: A 20th century spelling variant of {{l|de|Isabel}} and {{l|de|Isabelle}}.
etym.Jemima: From the name of a minor biblical character, from {{der|en|he|יְמִימָה||dove}}. By [[folk etymology]] also used as a feminine form of {{m|en|James}}.
etym.Juana:
From {{bor|en|es|Juana}}, from {{der|en|osp|Johanna}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Janna: A contraction of {{m|fi|Johanna}}, possibly also of {{m|fi|Juliana}} and {{m|fi|Marjaana}}.<ref>{{R:fi:Etunimet}}</ref>
etym.Jael: From the name of a minor biblical character, {{der|en|he|יעל}}.
etym.Johnna: A rare feminine form of {{l|en|John}} recorded since the 18th century.
etym.Hadassah: Borrowed from {{bor|en|he|הֲדַסָּה||myrtle}}, the Hebrew name of {{m|en|Esther}} in the [[Hebrew Bible]].
etym.Michelle: {{bor+|en|fr|Michelle}}, feminine form of {{der|en|fr|Michel||Michael}}, {{der|en|he|מִיכָאֵל||who is like God?|tr=mikhaél}}. {{doublet|en|Michaela}}.
etym.Miriam: From {{der|en|he|מִרְיָם|tr=Miryam}}, possibly from {{der|en|arc|מרים|tr=Maryām|t=bitter}}, from a root '''מר''' (''m-r'') meaning "to be bitter". The meaning of this name which is the Old Testament equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}} has been debated for centuries. Some other explanations are mutiny / rebellion / disobedience from a root '''מרי''' (''m-r-y'').
etym.Marian: A variant of [[Marion]], a medieval derivation of [[Mary]], often also interpreted as a [[contraction]] of [[Mary]] and [[Ann]], or as a variant of [[Mariana]].
etym.Marie: The {{bor|en|fr|Marie}}, equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}}; also an Early New English spelling of ''Mary'', from {{inh|en|enm|Marie}}. {{doublet|en|Mary}}.
etym.Polly: Nickname for {{m|en|Mary}}, created by rhyming with {{m|en|Molly}}.
etym.Lisa: Diminutive of [[Elisabeth]] in several European languages. The computer is named after {{w|Lisa Brennan-Jobs}}, officially explained as an acronym for “Locally Integrated Software Architecture”.
etym.Magdalene: From {{uder|en|grc|Μαγδαληνή||woman from Magdala}}, [[byname]] of the biblical {{w|Mary Magdalene}}, "Mary of [[Magdala]]", from {{m|grc|Μαγδαλά}}, the name of a village on Lake [[Galilee]] (the name of which derives from {{uder|en|he|מגדל||tower|tr=migdál}}). Generic use comes from the traditional association of Mary Magdalene with the "woman which was a sinner" mentioned in Luke 7:37. {{doublet|en|Madeleine|Magdalen|Magdalena|Maudlin}}.
etym.Michaela: From {{suffix|en|Michael|a}}. Latinate feminine form of {{m|en|Michael}}, first appearing as an [[Appendix:Glossary#anglicisation|anglicisation]] of the {{der|en|pt|Micaela|("Micaela")}} and {{der|en|es|Micaela|("Micaela")}}. {{doublet|en|Michelle}}.
etym.Lilah: Short form of {{m|en|Delilah}}; also a variant of {{m|en|Leila}}.
etym.Oprah: From {{w|Oprah Winfrey}}, a very influential [[talk show]] host, originally named {{m|en|Orpah}} after the Biblical figure, via {{metathesis|en}}. {{dercat|en|he}}
etym.Leora: Possibly a variant of the modern Israeli name transliterated as [[Liora]], from {{uder|en|he|-}}, [[ליאורה]] "my light", or an American contraction of [[Leonora]].
etym.Rachelle: 20th-century variant of [[Rachel]], from {{uder|en|fr|Rachelle}}, or possibly coined independently of it.
etym.Mehitabel: Spelling variant of {{m|en|Mehetabel}}, a name in the Old Testament of the Bible, meaning "God rejoices".
etym.Mehetabel: From {{uder|en|hbo|מהיטבאל|מְהֵיטַבְאֵל|whom God benefits|tr=m'heitav'el}}, the name of a minor biblical character mentioned in {{R:Tanach|1|36|39}}.
etym.Kizzy: From a pet form of {{m|en|Kezia}}. Explained as a {{der|en|mnk|-}} name by Alex Haley in ''Roots'' (1976).
etym.Mayim: Popularized by U.S. actress {{w|lang=en|Mayim Bialik}}, Bialik's name originated as a {{lg|diminutive}} {{contraction|en|Maryam|nocap=1}}, her grandmother's name. It has been reinterpreted as deriving from {{der|en|he|מים||water}}.
etym.Susan: English form of the biblical {{m|en|Susanna}}, from {{cog|hbo|שׁוֹשַׁנָּה||tr=šōšannā|lily}}, ultimately from {{der|en|egy|{{egy-h|z:S:n-M9}}|tr={{l|egy|zšn}}}}.
etym.Rebecca: The [[Vulgate]] ({{bor|en|la|-}}) form of biblical {{m|en|Rebekah}}, from {{der|en|he|רִבְקָה||enchantingly beautiful, captivating, snare|tr=Rivka}}.
etym.Ruth: From Ruth the [[Moabite]], {{der|en|he|רות}}, of uncertain origin, possibly meaning "[[companion]]". Also associated with the English noun {{m|en|ruth||compassion}} by Puritans.
etym.Susanna: From {{uder|en|grc|Σουσάννα|}}, the New Testament form of {{uder|en|he|שׁוֹשַׁנָּה||lily|tr=šōšannā}}.
etym.Tamara: Of [[Slavic]] origin, mainly from {{uder|en|ru|Тама́ра}}, name of a 12th-century saint in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], cognate with English biblical [[Tamar]], from {{uder|en|he|תמר|tr=tāmār||date palm}}.
etym.Siobhan:
Anglicized spelling of {{der|en|ga|Siobhán}}, from {{der|en|mga|Sibán}}, from {{der|en|xno|Jehane}} or {{m|fro|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} or {{m|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān}}, which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Selah: {{uder|en|hbo|סֶלָה|tr=selāh|}}; according to some scholars, from {{m|he|סָלָה|tr=salah||to hang”, implying “to weigh”, “to measure}}.
etym.Sinéad: From {{bor|en|ga|Sinéad}}, from {{der|en|fro-nor|Jeanette}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}} + {{m|frm|-ette}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.
etym.Yakova: From the {{uder|en|he|-}} masculine form "[[Ya'akov]]" or "[[Yakov]]" which originally refers to the Biblical character, [[Jacob]].
etym.Shavonne: Anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Siobhán}} as pronounced in modern Irish, under probable influence from {{m|en|Yvonne}}.
etym.Tirzah: Borrowed from {{bor|en|he|תִּרְצָה|tr=tirtsáh}}, meaning "pleasant" or "she is my delight".
etym.Thirza: Borrowed from the {{uder|en|de|-}} variant of [[Tirzah]] through 18th-century literature.
etym.Sian:
An anglicization of {{bor|en|cy|Siân}}, ultimately from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.
etym.Bridget:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*bʰerǵʰ-}}
English form of the {{der|en|ga|-}} saints' name ''[[Brighid]]'', ''[[Brigid]]''. {{doublet|en|Bride}}.
etym.Anya: From {{bor|en|ru,uk|А́ня|pos=informal pet form of {{m|ru|А́нна|t=Ann}}}}. Also an Anglicization of {{m|ga|Áine}}.
etym.Aoife: {{bor+|en|ga|Aoife}}. The name is unrelated to the Biblical name {{m|en|Eva}}, which was rendered as {{m|ga|Éabha}} in Irish. However, due to the lack of a more precise alternative familiar to English speakers, ''Aoife'' has often been [[anglicised]] as {{m|en|Eva}} or {{m|en|Eve}}.
etym.Ihitha: From {{bor|en|hi}}, from {{der|en|sa}} ''Iha'' (world or earth) and 'Hitha' ("who does Good, favor").
etym.Ashlyn: An anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Aisling||dream, vision}} with {{affix|en|-lyn}}.
etym.Zsa Zsa: From {{bor|en|hu|Zsazsa}}, popularized by Hungarian–American actress {{w|Zsa Zsa Gabor}}.
etym.Attracta: {{bor|en|la|-}}, from {{der|en|ga|Athracht}}, patron saint of [[Locha Techet]] and [[Tourlestrane]].
etym.Eileen: From Anglicized forms of {{bor|en|ga|Eibhlín}}, {{m|ga|Eilín}} or {{m|ga|Aibhilín}} in {{inh|en|enm|-}} and Modern English, all cognates of {{doublet|en|Evelyn|notext=1}} from {{der|en|fro|Aveline}}. Sometimes also used for the Irish name {{m|ga|Éibhleann}}, possibly from {{der|en|sga|oíph||radiance, beauty}}.
etym.Maureen: Anglicized from {{bor|en|ga|Máirín}}, diminutive of {{m|ga|Máire}}, an Irish equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}}. {{surf|en|Maura|-een}}.
etym.Kathleen: Anglicization of {{m|ga|Caitlín}}, an {{der|en|ga|-}} equivalent of the English [[Catherine]].
etym.Kira: Variant of {{m|en|Kyra}} or {{bor+|en|ru|Ки́ра|nocap=1}}, ultimately from {{der|en|fa|کوروش|tr=Kūrūš}}. Also used as a respelling of {{m|en|Ciara}}, from {{bor|en|ga}}.
etym.Keavy: Anglicised form of the {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gd|Caoimhe|t=beautiful, precious}}.
etym.Maeve: Anglicized form of the {{bor|en|ga|Méabh}}, from {{der|en|mga|Medb|lit=intoxicating}} and {{l|en|Meadhbh}} in Medieval irish. The name of a legendary queen of [[Connacht]] in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology.
etym.Maura: Either from {{bor|en|ga|Máire}} and {{bor|en|gd|Màiri}}, or from {{bor|en|it|Maura}}. When borrowed from Irish, a {{doublet|en|Moira|nocap=1}}.
etym.Keira: A modern feminine form of [[Kieran]], from {{der|en|ga|ciar|t=black, dark, little dark one}}.
etym.Shauna: From {{suffix|en|Shaun|a}}, variant of {{der|en|ga|Seán}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehan}}, from {{der|en|la|Johannes}}, variant of {{m|la|Ioannes}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Sheena}}.
etym.Etna: From the {{der|en|la|Aetna}}, perhaps via the {{bor|en|it|Etna}}. From either {{der|en|grc|Αἴτνη||Aetna}} or {{m|grc|αἴθω||to burn}}, or from a {{der|en|sxc|-}} dialect {{der|en|itc|-}} base {{m|itc-pro|*aið-na||fiery one}}, all from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂eydʰ-||burn; fire}}. {{doublet|en|Aetna}}.
etym.Shanae:
Anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Sinéad}} q.v. based on its modern Irish pronunciation.

{{doublet|en|Janet|Jeanette|Jeannette|Juanita|Sinead}}.
etym.Sadhbh: From {{inh|ga|mga|Sadb}}, from {{der|ga|sga|Sadb}}, from {{der|ga|cel-pro||*swadwā}}, feminine derivative of {{m|cel-pro|*swādus||sweet}}.<ref>{{R:cel:Zair:2012|pages=155, 160}}</ref>
etym.Myrna: An anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Muirne||beloved}}. Popularized by the American actress {{w|Myrna Loy}}.
etym.Kerrigan: Reduced Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Ó Ciaragáin||grandson/descendant of Ciaragán}}, a byname from a double diminutive of {{m|ga|ciar||black}}.
etym.Nuala: From {{der|en|ga|-}}: either a shortened form of {{m|ga|Fionnuala}}, alternative form of {{m|ga|Fionnghuala}}, or an alternative form of {{m|ga|Úna}}.
etym.Donna: A 19th-century invention from the {{der|en|it|-}} noun {{m|it|donna}}; also interpreted as a feminine form of [[Donald]].
etym.Madonna: From {{uder|en|it|madonna}}, from Old {{uder|en|it|ma||my}} + {{m|it|donna||lady}}. The given name is derived from the English term, not used as a given name in Italy. {{doublet|en|madam}}.
etym.Clarissa: {{bor+|en|it|Clarissa}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Clarissa}}; see there for more. Popularized in English by {{w|Samuel Richardson}}'s 1748 novel ''{{w|Clarissa (novel)|Clarissa}}''. {{doublet|en|Clarisse}}.
etym.Angelica: {{der|mul|la-new|-}}, feminine nominative singular of {{der|mul|la-lat|angelicus}}, alluding to the supposed magical properties of the plant.
etym.Sinead:
Anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Sinéad}}, from {{der|en|fro-nor|Jeanette}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}} + {{m|frm|-ette}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Janet|Jeanette|Jeannette|Juanita|Shanae}}.
etym.Lorena: From {{uder|en|it|-}} and {{uder|en|es|-}}, by [[folk etymology]] associated with [[Laura]]. Henry Webster's title for his song was inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's [[Lenore]].
etym.Francesca: Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Francesca||Frances}}, the feminine form of {{m|it|Francesco||Francis}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Franciscus}}, from {{af|la|Francia|t1=France|-iscus|t2=-ish|nocat=1}}. {{doublet|en|Frances|Francisca}}.
etym.Rosina: An {{uder|en|it|-}} pet form of [[Rosa]] borrowed in the nineteenth century, particularly from the character in Rossini's opera ''The Barber of Seville'' (1816).
etym.Valentina: From {{bor|en|es|-}}, {{bor|en|it|-}}, and {{bor|en|la|Valentīna}}, feminine forms of {{der|en|es|-}} and {{der|en|it|Valentino}}, and {{der|en|la|Valentīnus<id:cognomen>}}. {{doublet|en|Valentine|Valentinus|Valentino|Valentini}}.
etym.Leonora: From the {{uder|en|it|-}} short form of [[Eleonora]], cognate to [[Eleanor]].
etym.Allegra: Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Allegra}}, from {{m|it|allegra||cheerful}}, inspired by the musical term {{m|it|allegro}}.
etym.Sheilagh: Rare spelling variant of {{m|en|Sheila}}, anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Síle}}.
etym.Caramella: From {{bor|en|it|Caramella}}, a variant of the {{der|en|fr|-}} surname {{m|fr|Caramelle}}, from {{der|en|fro|calamel|t=[[chalumeau]]}}.
etym.Airi: Variant of {{m|et|Aili}}, itself from {{der|et|fi|-}}, or directly from {{bor|et|fi|Airi}}.
etym.Isuzu: From {{der|en|ja|-}}. The automotive manufacturer is named after the {{m|ja|五十鈴川|tr=Isuzu-gawa||{{w|Isuzu River}}}}.
etym.Hata: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ja|畑|tr=Hata}}, {{m|ja|秦|tr=Hata}}, {{m|ja|羽田|tr=Hata}} or {{m|ja|はた|tr=Hata}}.
etym.Mari: From {{der|en|akk|𒈠𒌷𒆠|tr=ma-ri<sup>ki</sup>}}, from {{m|und|Mer}}, an ancient storm/{{w|patron deity}} of [[Mesopotamia]] and Syria.<ref>Tinney, Steve; Novotny, Jamie; Robson, Eleanor; Veldhuis, Niek, eds. (2020). "Mari [1] (SN)". Oracc (Open Richly Annotated Cuneiform Corpus). Oracc Steering Committee.</ref><ref>Green, Alberto Ravinell Whitney (2003). The Storm-god in the Ancient Near East. Biblical and Judaic studies from the University of California, San Diego. 8. Eisenbrauns. </ref><ref>Oldenburg, Ulf (1969). The Conflict between El and Ba'al in Canaanite Religion. Dissertationes ad Historiam Religionum Pertinentes. 3.</ref> Also see {{w|Nûr-Mêr}}.
etym.Uno:
[[File:UNO Logo.svg|thumb|Logo]]

{{bor+|en|it,es|uno||one}}; players must call "uno" when down to their last card. {{doublet|en|an|one}}.
etym.Albina: From {{bor|en|la|Albina}} (name of a third-century martyr), feminine form of the Roman [[cognomen]] {{m|la|Albīnus}}, derivative of {{der|en|la|albus||white}}.
etym.Waka: From the {{bor|yo|ha|waƙa}} ''(song)''. Entered Yorùbá through Islamic influence from the Hausa, with the first literary usage of the word being written in an [[Ajami]] manuscript written by Salihu Apomu from the center of Islamic learning of Yorubaland, Ìlọrin. In his manuscript the word simply meant song, which is the same as the original Hausa definition.
etym.Amy:
Anglicized form of {{der|en|fro|Amee}} (modern French [[Aimée]]),
which was both a nickname and a form of the {{der|en|la|-}} name {{m|la|Amata||beloved}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of Given Names.Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>
etym.Clara: {{lbor|en|la|clāra}}, feminine of {{m|la|clārus|t=bright, shining, clear}}, a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara ([[Clare]]) of Assisi. {{dbt|en|Clare|Claire}}.
etym.Barbara:
* From {{der|en|la|Barbara}}, the name of {{w|Saint Barbara}}, feminine form of {{m|la|barbarus}}, from {{der|en|grc|βάρβαρος|t=strange, foreign}}. {{doublet|en|Varvara}}.
* {{sense|logic}} From the given name; chosen because it has three A's in it representing universal affirmatives.
etym.Amanda: {{der+|en|la|Amanda}}, feminine form of the saint's name {{taxfmt|Amandus|genus}}, from {{m|la|amandus}}, future passive participle of {{m|la|amāre||to love}}: thus meaning "who/which is to be loved". Taken into regular use as an English given name from 18th-century literature. {{doublet|en|Aimee}}.
etym.Alma: Usually explained as {{der|en|la|alma||nourishing, kind}}. It has also been used as a short form of {{der|en|gem}} compound names beginning with the element ''Amal''-, as in [[Amelia]].
etym.Aura: The name of the deity is from {{der|en|grc|Αὔρα}}, from {{m|grc|αὔρα||breeze}}.
etym.Aurora:
{{ety|en|:der|la:Aurōra}}
Ultimately from {{der|en|la|Aurōra}}. The Philippine placenames were {{named-after|en|occ=First Lady|Aurora Quezon|wplink=Aurora Quezon|nocap=1}}, the wife of Pres. {{w|Manuel Quezon}}, the 2nd president of the [[Philippines]].
etym.Camilla: From {{der|en|la|Camilla}}, feminine form of old Roman family name [[Camillus]], of obscure and probably non-Latin origin.
etym.Candida: Feminine singular of {{der|mul|la|candidus||of a shining, dazzling white}}.
etym.Cecilia: From {{der|en|la|Caecilia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Caecilius}}, a Roman family name possibly derived from the byname {{m|la|caecus|t=blind}}. Popularized by Saint Cecilia, third century Roman martyr, the patron saint of music. {{doublet|en|Sheila}}.
etym.Celia: {{bor+|en|la|Caelia}}, feminine of Roman family name {{m|la|Caelius}}, probably from {{m|la|caelum||heaven}}. Introduced into English by [[w:William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]] in ''As You Like It''.
etym.Carina:
{{wp|+ (constellation)}}
Named by the French [[astronomer]] [[w:Nicolas Louis de Lacaille|Nicolas Louis de Lacaille]] in 1763. From {{der|en|la|carīna||the [[keel]] of a ship}}
etym.Beatrice: Either 1) from the {{der|en|la|Beatrix}}, name of early Christian saints, from {{m|la|beatrix||she who makes happy}}, or 2) from {{m|la|beata}}, influenced by {{m|la|viātrīx|viatrix}} (“female wayfarer, traveller”).
etym.Annabel: Originally a mishearing or misreading of {{der|en|la|amabilis||lovable}} (= {{m|en|Amabel}}, {{m|en|Mabel}}), used since the 12th century and by [[folk etymology]] interpreted as {{m|en|Anna}} + {{m|en|belle}}, "beautiful Anna".
etym.Arabella: {{unc|en}}, used in Scotland since the sixteenth century; possibly from {{der|en|la|orabilis|t=yielding to prayer}} or a variant of [[Annabel]].
etym.Beatrix: A Latinate variant of the standard English {{l|en|Beatrice}}.
etym.Aurelia: From {{der|mul|la|Aurēlia}}, feminine form of the Roman gens name {{m|la|Aurēlius}}, from {{m|la|aureus|t=golden}}.
etym.Celine: From {{bor|en|fr|Céline}}, from {{der|en|la|Caelīna}}, derived from the Roman gens name {{m|la|Caelius}}, from {{m|la|caelum||heaven}}. Also a short form of {{m|fr|Marceline}}, feminine diminutive of {{m|fr|Marcel}}.
etym.Amabel: Medieval English name apparently based on {{der|en|la|amabilis||lovable}}.
etym.Claribel: A fanciful variant of {{m|en|Clara}}, inspired by names like {{m|en|Annabel}}, {{m|en|Christabel}}{{,}} and {{m|en|Isabel}}.
etym.Antonina:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|Antōnīna}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Antōnīnus}}, derivative of {{m|la|Antōnius}}.
Name of obscure early martyrs venerated in the [[Eastern Orthodox]] Church.
etym.Celestia: From {{der|en|la|caelestis|t=heavenly}}, perhaps influenced by {{m|en|celestial}}. In {{senseno|en|Fredericton|t=Fredericton}}, after {{m|en|Celestial City}}.
etym.Juliet: {{bor+|en|it|Giulietta}}, diminutive of {{m|it|Giulia}}, from {{der|en|la|Iūlia}}, feminine of {{m|la|Iūlius}}, a Roman family name. Cognate with {{cog|fr|Juliette}}.
etym.Jill: A variant of {{m|en|Gill}}, diminutive of {{m|en|Gillian}}, a medieval form of {{m|en|Juliana}}, ultimately from {{uder|en|la|-}}.
etym.Fauna:
Feminine form of {{m|la|Faunus}}.

Some refer it to {{der|en|ine-pro|*dʰeh₂w-}}, whence {{cog|grc|θαῦνον||beast}}, Illyrian-related Daunus. Some refer it to {{m|la|faveō}}.
etym.Gloria: From {{der|en|la|gloria||glory}}, first used as a name in 19th-century literature.
etym.Emily: English form of {{uder|en|la|Aemilia}}, a gens name from {{m|la|aemulus||[[rival]], [[emulator]]}}.
etym.Juliett: {{bor+|mul|en|Juliet}}, spelled so as to make the final /t/ clear to non-English speakers.
etym.Julianna: Modern combination of {{compound|en|Julie|Anna}}, perhaps sometimes intended as a form of {{m|en|Juliana}}.<ref>{{R:en:DFN|page=151|column=1}}</ref>
etym.Johanna:
From {{bor|en|la|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena|Zhanna}}.
etym.Honora: Medieval variant of {{m|en|Honoria}}, feminine form of {{m|en|Honorius}}.
etym.Cornelia: From {{bor|en|la|Cornēlia}}, name of a famous Roman matron, feminine form of the gens name [[Cornelius]]; in continental Europe, also a feminine form of the saint's name Cornelius.
etym.Ina: Short form of given names ending in -ina, e.g. [[Georgina]], [[Christina]], [[Wilhelmina]].
etym.Clementine: From {{bor|en|la|clēmentīnus}},<ref>{{R:OED Online|pos=''adj.'' and ''n.''<sup>1</sup>|noformat=1|id=4570281323}}</ref> from {{der|en|la-lat|Clēmens|t=[[Clement]]}} (genitive {{m|la|Clēmentis}}) + {{m|la|-īnus|t=of or pertaining to}}, from {{m|la|clēmens||merciful}}. {{surf|en|Clement|-ine<pos:adjectival suffix>}}.
etym.Drusilla: {{bor+|en|la|Drūsilla}}, feminine diminutive form of the cognomen {{m|la|Drūsus}}.
etym.Flavia: {{uder|en|la|Flavia}}, feminine form of the gens name {{m|la|Flavius}}, probably from {{m|la|flavus||yellow}}.
etym.Cordelia: Shakespeare's spelling of a historical British name appearing as ''Cordeilla'', etc., possibly derived from the {{bor|en|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Cordula}}.
etym.Julianne: A 19th/20th century variant of [[Juliana]]. Can also be interpreted as a combination of {{com|en|Julia|Anne}}.
etym.Dulcie: From {{uder|en|la|dulcis||sweet}} in the 19th century, probably inspired by earlier names like [[Dowsabel]] and Spanish {{m|es|Dulcinea}}.
etym.Juliann: A variant of [[Julian]], [[Juliana]] or [[Julianne]]. Can also be interpreted as a combination of [[Julia]] + [[Ann]].
etym.Judayah: Respelling of {{m|en|Judea}}, from {{bor|en|la|Iudaea}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰουδαία}}, from Biblical {{der|en|hbo|יְהוּדָה|tr=yehudá}}.
etym.Emerentia: {{lbor|en|la|Ēmerentia}}, feminine of {{m|la|Ēmerentius}}, from {{m|la|ēmereō|t=to earn, merit, gain by service}}.
etym.Emerentiana: {{lbor|en|la|Ēmerentiāna}}, feminine of {{m|la|Ēmerentiānus}}, from {{m|la|Ēmerentius}} + {{m|la|-ānus}}, from {{m|la|ēmereō|t=to earn, merit, gain by service}}. {{surf|en|Emerentia|-ana<id:female given name>}}.
etym.Laura: From Late {{der|en|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Laura}}, from the feminine form of {{m|la|laurus||laurel tree}}. A post-classical name made famous by [[Petrarch]]'s sonnets to Laura in the fourteenth century.
etym.Lillian: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of [[Elizabeth]], but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin {{m|la|lilium||lily}}.
etym.Lucia: [[Latinate]] variant of {{m|en|Lucy}}, or today borrowed from modern Italian. Name of a Sicilian martyr, {{uder|en|la|Lūcia}}, feminine form of the Roman [[praenomen]] {{m|la|Lūcius}}.
etym.Lucy:
From {{inh|en|enm|Lucy}}, from {{der|en|fro|Lucie}} (notably after the Christian martyr {{w|Saint Lucy|Lucia of Syracuse}}), from {{der|en|la|Lucia}} (feminine of {{m|la|Lucius}}, a Roman [[praenomen]]), from {{m|la|lux||light}}.

The name of the {{taxfmt|Australopithecus|genus}} skeleton came from the [[Beatles]] song “{{w|Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds}}”, which was being played repeatedly at the dig site camp at the time of the discovery. The slang term for LSD also derives from the song name, which many believe is essentially a reference to the drug.<ref>{{R:Greens|id=ihjkiki|head=lucy in the sky with diamonds|pos=n}}</ref>
etym.Justine: From {{uder|en|fr|Justine}}, from {{uder|en|la|Iūstīna}}, name of early saints, feminine of {{m|la|Iūstīnus}}, derivative of {{m|la|Iūstus}}, from {{m|la|iūstus||just}}. The feminine equivalent of [[Justin]].
etym.Lilian: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of [[Elizabeth]], but generally accepted as a variant of {{der|en|la-lat|lilium||lily}}.
etym.Leonie: From {{bor|en|fr|Léonie}}, from {{der|en|la|Leonia}}, feminine of {{m|la|Leonius}}, derived from {{m|la|leo||lion}}.
etym.Lucile: Alternative spelling of [[Lucille]], from {{uder|fr|la|Lucilla}}. Variant of {{m|fr|Lucie||[[Lucy]]}}.
etym.Lucinda: Derived from {{m|en|Lucia}} with the suffix {{af|en|-inda}}, first used by [[w:Miguel de Cervantes|Cervantes]] in ''[[w:Don Quixote|Don Quixote]]'' (1605).
etym.Lucretia: Originally from {{uder|en|la|lucrum||gain, profit}}. Many people with the given name have no doubt been named after others so named, not necessarily after the 6th-century-BC Roman noblewoman.
etym.Letitia: Name of an obscure {{uder|en|es|-}} saint, {{m|es|Leticia}}, from {{uder|en|la|laetitia}} "gladness".
etym.Lavinia: {{uder|en|la|Lavinia}}, of obscure meaning. {{m|la|Lavinium}} was a town in ancient [[Latium]].
etym.Lauretta: An {{uder|en|it|-}} pet form of {{m|it|Laura}}; first introduced into English as the name of one of the [[narrator]]s in the [[Decameron]].
etym.Lilias: First recorded in 16th-century Scotland, a variant of {{m|en|Lilian}} or possibly from the {{uder|en|es|Liliosa}}, name of a 9th-century saint, both ultimately from {{uder|en|la-lat|lilium||lily}}.
etym.Lilia: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|lilia}}, plural of {{m|la|lilium||lily}}, or a Latinization of the English [[Lily]].
etym.Luci: A modern [[nonstandard]] spelling of [[Lucy]], from [[Lucia]], from the {{uder|en|la|-}} feminine form of the Latin [[praenomen]] [[Lucius]], from {{m|la|lux}} "light".
etym.Livia: From {{bor|en|la|Līvia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Līvius}}, name of a plebeian Roman gens.
etym.Lucilla: From {{uder|en|la|Lūcilla}}, feminine diminutive form of the [[praenomen]] {{m|la|Lūcius}}.
etym.Monica: From {{der|en|la|Monica}}, name of the mother of [[w:Augustine of Hippo|St. Augustine]], of uncertain meaning but probably {{der|en|ber}} or {{der|en|phn|-}} origin.
etym.Ora:
* {{sense|given name}} First appeared in the 19th century when similar sounding names like {{m|en|Cora}}, {{m|en|Dora}} and {{m|en|Nora}} were in fashion. Possibly shortened from {{m|en|Aurelia}}, sometimes spelled {{m|en|Ora Lee}}, or, {{m|en|Aura Lea}}, in the American civil war song.
* {{sense|Italian commune}} Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Ora}}
etym.Patricia: From {{uder|en|la|patricia||noble}}; later also seen as the feminine form of the saint's name [[Patrick]].
etym.Olivia:
{{ety|en|:der|la:Olīva<ety:der<la:olīva>>|tree=++}}
From {{der|en|la|Olīva}}, an early saints’ name from {{m|la|olīva||olive; olive branch}}. First popularized by Shakespeare's ''{{w|Twelfth Night}}''.
etym.Priscilla:
Feminine diminutive form of a Roman cognomen [[Prīscus]], from {{der|en|la|prīscus||former, ancient, old-fashioned}}.

Compare typologically {{m|en|Seneca}} (< {{m+|la|Seneca}} < {{m|la|senex}}).
etym.Martina: Usually interpreted as the feminine form of the saints' name {{m|en|Martin}}, though there was an identical Roman name, likewise derived from {{uder|en|la|Martinus}}.
etym.Natalie: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} form of the {{der|en|la-lat|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Natalia}}, from {{m|la|[[nātālis]] ([[diēs]])|t=birthday [of Christ], Christmas}}. {{doublet|en|Natalya}}.
etym.Marcia: From {{bor|en|la|Marcia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Marcius}}, a derivative of {{m|la|Marcus}}, ultimately from {{m|la|Mārs}}, the god of war.
etym.Renata: Feminine form of {{uder|en|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Renatus}}, from {{m|la|renatus||reborn}}
etym.Monika: A less common spelling of [[Monica]], used since the twentieth century.
etym.Maxine: From {{suffix|en|Max|-ine<id:female>}}. An English feminine form of [[Max]] coined at the end of the nineteenth century. {{piecewise doublet|en|Maxina}}.
etym.Natalia: {{uder|en|la|natale||birthday (of the Lord)}}, referring to birth on Christmas Day, name of an early martyr.
etym.Petronella: From {{bor|en|la|Petronella}}, feminine diminutive of [[Petronius]], a Roman family name possibly derived from ''[[petra]]'' "rock". Name of an obscure early saint; because of similarity of sound, used as a feminine form of [[Peter]].
etym.Paulina: From {{der|en|la|Paulīna}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Paulīnus}}, derivative of {{m|la|Paulus}}, from {{m|la|paulus||small}}. Name of a third-century saint.
etym.Roma:
[[File:Musical instrument, music, violin, double bass, gypsy, Gypsy music Fortepan 1714.jpg|right|thumb|A group of '''Roma''' playing musical instruments.]]

{{bor+|en|rom|roma}}, plural of {{m|rom|rom|t=man, husband, Romani man}}. The latter probably comes from {{der|en|sa|डोम्ब||lower-caste person working as a wandering musician}}, from {{der|en|sa|डमरु||drum}}, which may have been borrowed from a Dravidian language.<ref>{{R:OED Online|entry=Rom|pos=n|id=1117377491|date=September 2024}}</ref> [[folk etymology|Folk etymology]] pointed to a legend that the ethnic group were an exiled people from [[Roman]] Imperial times.

The other major categories of words for the Roma are cognates of ''[[G
etym.Rosaline: An elaborate form of [[Rosalie]], or a simplified form of [[Rosalind]].
etym.Prisca: {{uder|en|la|-}} feminine form of the cognomen {{m|la|Prīscus}}, from {{m|la|prīscus||former, ancient, old-fashioned}}.
etym.Octavia: From {{uder|en|la|Octāvia}}, feminine form of the gens name {{m|la|Octāvius}}, from {{m|la|octavus||the eighth}}.
etym.Natali: Patronymic surname from the personal name {{m|it|Natale}}.
etym.Marciana: From {{bor|en|pt,es|Marciana}} and their etymon {{bor|en|la|Mārciāna}}, feminine of {{m|la|Mārciānus}}.
etym.Ursula:
{{word|en|ine|h₂ŕ̥tḱos}}
From {{bor|en|la|Ursula}}, the name of a fourth century saint. Via {{m+|ine-pro|*h₂ŕ̥tḱos}} cognate with {{m|en|Arcady}}.
etym.Vesta:
From {{inh|en|enm|Vesta}}, from {{der|en|la|Vesta}}, related to {{cog|grc|ἑστία||to dwell}} and {{m|grc|Ἑστία||Hestia}}, all from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂wes-}}; see also {{cog|goh|-}} and {{cog|ang|wesan||to be}}, {{cog|got|wisan|}}, {{cog|sa|वसति||abide dwell}}.

''Vesta'' itself came to mean chaste, pure, or virgin, based from this goddess.
etym.Stella:
From {{der|en|la|stēlla||star}}.

{{senseno|en|black woman who visits Jamaica as a sex tourist|cap=1}} is after the protagonist of ''{{w|How Stella Got Her Groove Back}}'' (1998).
etym.Silvia: Feminine form of [[Silvius]], from {{uder|en|la|silva||forest}}. In myths, Rhea Silvia was the mother of famous twins [[Romulus]] and [[Remus]], the founders of [[Rome]]. 6th-century saint Silvia was the mother of the [[pope]] Gregory the Great.
etym.Tatiana: Popular saints' name in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], feminine of {{der|en|la|Tatiānus}}, from {{m|la|Tatius}} (a Roman family name of obscure origin) + {{m|la|-ānus}}. Modern English usage is derived from {{bor|en|ru|Татья́на}}.
etym.Serena: From the name of an early Christian saint, {{uder|en|la|serena||serene}}.
etym.Selina: First recorded in England in the 17th century, possibly from {{uder|en|la|Caelīna||heavenly}}, or a variant of {{m|en|Selene}}, the {{uder|en|grc|-}} goddess of the moon.
etym.Sini: Originally a short or pet form of {{m|fi|Sinikka}},<ref>{{R:fi:Etunimet}}</ref> with formal name status since the 1960s. Identical with {{m|fi|sini|id=blue}}, the poetic word for [[blue]], but with a different declension.
etym.Valeria: Feminine form of [[Roman]] family name {{m|la|Valerius}}, from {{der|en|la|valere|t=to be healthy, to be strong}}. {{doublet|en|Valerie}}.
etym.Tiana: Modern contraction of [[Tatiana]] and [[Christiana]]. In the USA it is also explained as a form of [[Diana]] in such unrelated languages as [[Samoan]] and [[Cherokee]] (but the author Tiana Bighorse is a [[Navajo]]).
etym.Verna: Coined in the 19th century, from {{der|en|la|vernus||spring-like}} or as a feminine of {{m|en|Vernon}}.
etym.Roslyn: A variant of [[Rosaline]] inspired by the Scottish place name [[Roslin]] or [[Rosslyn]].
etym.Mei: From {{der|mul|cmn|-}} {{zh-l|寐||sleep}} (such that the name of the type species means "sleeping dragon").
etym.Seraphina: From Late {{der|en|la|Seraphina}}, name of obscure early martyrs, from biblical {{m|la|seraphim}}. {{surf|en|Seraphin|-a}}.
etym.Undine: From {{bor|en|de|Undine||[[undine]]}}, first used as a given name in the novel ''[[w:Undine (novella)|Undine]]'' by {{w|Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué}} and in 19th-century operas based on the book.
etym.Tetyana: Popular saints' name in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], feminine of {{der|en|la|Tatiānus}}, from {{m|la|Tatius}} (a Roman family name of obscure origin) + {{m|la|-ānus}}. Modern English usage is derived from {{bor|en|uk|Тетя́на}}.
etym.Edith: {{inh+|en|ang|Ēadġȳþ}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*audaz||wealth, riches}} + {{m|gem-pro|*gunþiz||battle}}. Name of a 10th century English saint.
etym.Averil: A rare variant of the 7th century saint's name [[Everild]], from {{inh|en|ang|eofor|t=boar}} + {{m|ang|hild|t=battle}}.
etym.Ethel: Short form of names of {{der|en|ang|-}} origin beginning with Ethel-, {{m|ang|æþele||noble}}. First used in the 19th century. Cognate to the Germanic [[Adela]] and [[Adele]].
etym.Jasmine: From {{bor|en|fr|jasmin}}, from {{der|en|ar|يَاسَمِين}}, from {{der|en|fa-cls|یاسمین|tr=yāsamīn}}, from earlier {{m|fa-cls|یاسمن|tr=yāsaman}}, from {{der|en|pal|yʾsmn'|tr=yāsaman|sc=Latn}}.
etym.Esther:
{{etymon|en|:der|grc:Ἐσθήρ}}
From {{der|en|grc|Ἐσθήρ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|אֶסְתֵּר|tr=ʾestēr}}. Has been connected to {{der|en|peo|𐎠𐎿𐎫𐎼|ts=star-|t=star}} (whence {{cog|pal|𐭮𐭲𐭫|ts=star|t=star}}, {{m|pal|𐭮𐭲𐭠𐭫𐭪|ts=stārag|t=star}}, {{cog|fa|ستاره||star|tr={{fa-xlit|سِتَارَه}}}}), from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂stḗr}} (if so, a distant {{doublet|en|star|nocap=1}}); or else to {{cog|akk|Ištar|𒀭𒈹|tr=Ištar|t=[[Ishtar]]}} ({{cog|he|עִשְׁתָּר||tr=ʿištār}}).
etym.Daria: Feminine form of {{m|en|Darius}}, of {{der|en|peo|-}} origin. Name of an early Christian saint.
etym.Mildred: From the name of an 8th-century English saint, {{inh|en|ang|Mildþrȳþ|pos=from {{af|ang|milde|t1=mild|þrȳþ|t2=strength|nocat=1}}}}.
etym.Inga:
[[File:Inga Vera, flower of the Guabo tree (10108387095).jpg|thumb|{{taxlink|Inga vera|species|'''Inga''' vera}} ({{taxfmt|Fabaceae|family}})]]
Of South American origin
etym.Edwina: Female form of {{m|en|Edwin}} from {{inh|en|ang|-}}, equivalent to {{suffix|en|Edwin|a}}.
etym.Helga: From {{der|en|non|Helga|t=holy}}, a pre-Christian term, feminine form of {{m|non|Helgi}}. {{doublet|en|Olga}}.
etym.Thora: Short form of {{der|en|non|-}} female given names beginning with {{m|non|Þórr||Thor}}.
etym.Alfreda: Originally a variant of {{m|en|Elfreda}}, used as a feminine form of {{m|en|Alfred}} since the 19th century.
etym.Roxana: From {{uder|en|grc|Ῥωξᾱ́νη}} of {{uder|en|peo|-}} or {{uder|en|xbc|-}} origin. Akin to {{cog|fa|روشن|tr=rowšan}}.
etym.Ermengarde: From the {{inh|en|ang|-}} name reinforced by its Norman cognate, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*ermunaz||all,whole}} + {{m|gem-pro|*gardaz||enclosure}}, "strong protection". Cognate with the German saint's name {{m|de|Irmgard}}.
etym.Kymber: A very rare spelling variant of [[Kimber]].
etym.Kimber:
* From the name of a 7th-century English female saint, [[Kyneburga]] or {{m|ang|Cyneburg}}, from {{inh|en|ang|cyne-||royal}} + {{m|ang|burh||fortress}}.
* English: probably a habitational name from East and West Kimber in the parish of Northlew in [[Devon]], so named from Old English {{m|ang|cempa||warrior}} (or the Old English personal name Cempa) + {{m|ang|bearn||grove/wood}}. It may also be an altered form of Kimbrough. Jewish (Ashkenazic): variant of Kinberg.<ref name="Kimber Family History">[https://www.ancestry.com/name-origin?surname=kimber Kimber Family History]Ancestry.com and ''Dictionary of American Family Names ©2013, Oxford University Press''</ref>
etym.Eda: From {{der|en|ang|ead||riches}}, also short for compound given names beginning thus, particularly [[Edith]].
etym.Sifan:
{{rfe|en}}<!--needs templating-->
From [[Oromo]] [[Siifan]], Siif (for you) + an (I am, me) = (I am for you).
<!--===Pronunciation===
* {{audio|en|Siifan.wav|Audio (Oromo)}} not English
-->
etym.Bahazhoni:
From {{bor|en|nv|[[baa]] [[hózhǫ́|hózhónii]]}} or similar, meaning "pleasant one".

{{rfe|nv|Almost certainly related to [[hózhǫ́]], but someone who knows Navajo grammar should check that "baa" and the form "hózhónii" are right.}}
etym.Misha:
A transliteration of the {{der|en|ru|Ми́ша}}, a [[hypocoristic]] for {{m|ru|Михаи́л}}, the Russian equivalent of {{m|en|Michael}}, from {{der|en|he|מיכאל}}.

Also a female name, presumably analogous to {{m|en|Michelle}}.
etym.Vera: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from the {{der|en|ru|-}} virtue name {{m|ru|Ве́ра||faith}}. By folk etymology it has also been explained as Latin {{m|la|vera||true}}.
etym.Wanda: {{bor+|en|pl|Wanda}}, possibly derived from an ethnic term for “a [[Wend]]”.
etym.Sonya: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ru,uk|Со́ня}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Со́фья}}, {{m|uk|Софі́я}} or {{m|ru|Софи́я||Sofia, Sophia}}, from the {{der|en|grc|σοφία||wisdom}}. It was introduced into English through 19th century Russian literature and taken into general use in early twentieth century.
etym.Scheherazade:
Borrowed from {{bor|en|de|Scheherazade}}, from {{der|en|ru|Шехераза́да}}, from {{der|en|fa-cls|شَهْرَازَاد}}, alternative form of {{m|fa-cls|شَهْرْزَاد}}; either a reborrowing from {{der|en|ar|شَهْرْزَاد}} from {{der|en|pal|*čihrāzād⁠}}, equivalent to {{l|en|New Persian}} {{compound|fa|چهر|آزاد|tr1={{fa-xlit|چِهْر}}|t1=lineage|tr2={{fa-xlit|آزَاد}}|t2=noble|nocat=1}}, or a compound of {{af|fa|شهر|tr1=šahr|t1=city|زاد|tr2={{fa-xlit|زَاد}}|t2=child of|nocat=1}}, in which case there was likely no {{l|en|reborrowing}} through Arabic involved.
Given name popularized by the fictional character below.
etym.Lara: Anglicized from {{der|en|ru|Ла́ра}}, a {{uder|en|ru|-}} pet form of [[Larissa]], known from the novel (1957) and film (1965) ''Dr Zhivago''.
etym.Tonya: Phonetic rendering of {{uder|en|ru|То́ня}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Антони́на||[[Antonina]]}}.
etym.Ronja:
* {{bor+|en|sv|Ronja}}, from [[w:Ronja, the Robber's Daughter|the book]] of [[w:Astrid Lindgren|Lindgren]].
* {{translit|en|ru|Роня}}, diminutive of {{m|ru|Вероника}}.
etym.Lana:
From {{der|mul|en|Lanna}} or {{der|mul|fr|lanna}}.

The letter "n" was trimmed from "Lanna", in accordance with the four-letter format in {{w|ISO 15924}}.
etym.Sveta: From {{bor|en|ru|Све́та}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Светла́на||Svetlana}}.
etym.Nila:
{{wp|en:Nila (Ramayana)}}
From {{der|en|sa|नील||of a dark colour; blue; black}}, {{der|en|bn|নীলা||blue}}, or related words in other Indian subcontinent languages.
etym.Ruslana: A transliteration of the female given name {{noncog|ru,uk|Русла́на}}
etym.Ronia:
* {{bor+|en|sv|Ronja}}, from [[w:Ronja, the Robber's Daughter|the book]] of [[w:Astrid Lindgren|Lindgren]].
* {{translit|en|ru|Роня}}, diminutive of {{m|ru|Вероника}}.
etym.Asha: {{bor+|en|sa|आशा||[[hope]], [[wish]]}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>
etym.Kanak: First attested in 1910, borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|canaque}}, from {{der|en|en|kanaka||Pacific islander}}, from {{der|en|haw|kanaka||person}}.
etym.Kumari: From {{bor|en|sa|कुमारी||a young girl, one from ten to twelve years old, maiden, daughter}}.
etym.Meena: {{bor+|en|hi|मीना}}, from {{der|en|sa|मीन|gloss=fish, synonym of the patron deity [[Matsya]]}}.
etym.Rama:
{{bor+|en|sa|राम}}.
* {{sense|Oumuamua}} The nickname derives from the similarity of {{m|mul|Oumuamua}} to the fictional object "Rama" in the story {{w|lang=en|Rendezvous with Rama}}, where that fictional object is named for the god.
etym.Padma: {{bor+|en|sa|पद्म||lotus}}, which the river was named for. {{doublet|en|Pema}}.
etym.Padmini: {{bor+|en|sa|पद्मिनी||a lotus, a multitude of lotuses or a lotus-pond}}.
etym.Samatha: From {{der|en|sa|समाधान}} (śamatha) meaning "tranquility" and "concentration" (referring to [[Buddhist]] meditation) or "equality".
etym.Rani: From {{uder|en|sa|राज्ञी||a queen, princess, the wife of a king}}, through {{der|en|hi|रानी}}.
etym.Roopa: Borrowed from {{bor|en|sa|रूप||any outward appearance or phenomenon or colour, form, shape, figure}}.
etym.Sasikala: From {{bor|en|sa|शशिकला||a digit or sickle of the moon}}; ultimately {{m|sa|शशि}} + {{m|sa|कला}}.
etym.Tara: {{bor+|en|ga|Teamhrach}}, genitive of {{m|ga|Teamhair}}, from {{der|en|sga|Temair|lit=high place}}. The female given name is derived from the name of [[w:Tara (plantation)|the plantation]] in ''{{w|Gone with the Wind}}'', named for the place in Ireland.
etym.Srimati: From {{uder|en|sa|श्रीमत्||beautiful, charming, lovely, pleasant, splendid, glorious}}.
etym.Mhairi: From {{der|en|gd|Màiri||Mary}}, which in the [[vocative case]] becomes {{m|gd|[[a]] [[Mhàiri]]}}.
etym.Lorna: {{coin|en|R. D. Blackmore|nat=English|occ=novelist|in=1869}} for his novel ''{{w|lang=en|Lorna Doone}}'', possibly from the Scottish place name {{w|lang=en|Lorne, Scotland|''Lorn(e)''}} in {{l|en|Argyll}}.
etym.Muriel: Anglicized form of {{der|en|gd|Muireall}}, from {{m|gd|muir||sea}}, from {{der|en|sga|muir}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*mori}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*móri}}; + {{m|gd|geal||white, bright}}, from {{der|en|sga|gel}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*gelos||yellow, white}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*ǵʰelh₃-||green, yellow}}.
etym.Sheena:
Anglicization of {{bor|en|gd|Sìne}} and {{m|ga|Síne}}, ultimately from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna}}.
etym.Danica: From {{bor|en|sla}} female given name, from the {{der|en|sla}} name for the {{l|en|Morning Star}} {{gloss| an aspect of the planet {{l|en|Venus}} }}.
etym.Kenna:
* As a Scottish surname, shortened from {{m|en|McKenna}}.
* As a {{der|en|gv|-}} and {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Cionaodha//Ó Cionaoith||descendant of [[Cionaodh]]}}, a name usually Anglicized as {{m|en|Kenneth}}.
etym.Danika: A spelling variant of [[Danica]], a female given name of Slavic origin.
etym.Morven: A variant of the place name [[Morvern]], from Scottish Gaelic ''A' Mhorbhairne'', meaning "the sea gap" or "the big gap".
etym.Mercedes:
From {{bor|en|es|Mercedes}} {{gloss|{{l|en|Mary}}, Our Lady of Mercy}}. The car was named for {{w|Mercédès Jellinek}}, the daughter of Austrian businessman {{w|Emil Jellinek}} who ordered 36 cars from Gottlieb Daimler.<ref>{{cite-web
|date=2001-10-19
|title=Her Name Still Rings A Bell
|author=Michelle Krebs
|work=New York Times
|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/10/19/automobiles/her-name-still-rings-a-bell.html
|passage=Jellinek agreed to order 36 cars if they bore the name of his daughter -- and if the factory gave him an exclusive sales agency for America and parts of Europe. Daimler agreed.
}}</ref>
etym.Lourdes:
From {{bor|en|fr|Lourdes}}, corruption of {{der|en|la-med|Lorus}} (778), the baptismal name taken by a Moorish leader who converted to Christianity, though of unknown ultimate meaning.

The town in Newfoundland is named after the town in France.
etym.Yana: Cognate to English [[Jane]], ultimately from {{uder|en|he|-}}, feminine form of [[Ioannes]] ( =[[John]]).{{rfv-etym|en}}
etym.Yolanda: From {{bor|en|es|Yolanda}}, the form of a medieval royal name of obscure, probably {{der|en|gem}}, origin. It has been identified with {{cog|la|Violante}} and with {{cog|grc|ἴον|t=violet}} + {{m|grc|ἄνθος|t=flower}}. {{doublet|en|Yolande}}.
etym.Inez:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₁yaǵ-}}
Anglicised form of {{bor|en|es|Inés}} and {{bor|en|pt|Inês}}, both from  {{der|en|la|Agnes}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἁγνή}}. First used in 18th century English poetry and plays referring to [[w:Inês de Castro|Inês de Castro]]. {{dbt|en|Agnes}}.
etym.Amaya: Heroine of a {{der|en|es|-}} historical novel ''Amaya o los vascos del siglo VIII'' (1877) by F. Navarro Villoslada, explained as {{der|en|eu|amai||the end}}.
etym.Esmeralda: From {{der|en|es|esmeralda||emerald}}, as first used in the novel ''[[w:The Hunchback of Notre Dame|Notre-Dame de Paris]]'' (1831) by [[w:Victor Hugo|Victor Hugo]].
etym.Elvira: {{der|mul|la-new|-}}, from {{der|mul|fr|Elvire}}, after the female subject of "A Elvire" by {{w|Alphonse de Lamartine}}. {{etydate|1866}}.
etym.Zenaida: A {{der|mul|la-new|-}} form of {{der|mul|fr|Zénaïde}}; the genus was named in honor of {{w|Zénaïde Bonaparte}}.
etym.Mila: From a diminutive in many {{der|en|sla}} languages {{der|en|bg,mk,ru,sh|-}}, etc.) of female given names containing the element Mil-, -mila ("grace, beloved"), such as [[Ludmila]], [[Milena]], {{m|sh|Milica}}, and of the cognates of [[Emily]]. Also from {{bor|en|es|Mila}}.
etym.Isabela: {{bor+|en|es|Isabela}}. The province is named after {{m|en|w:Isabella II of Spain|Isabella II of Spain}}. {{doublet|en|Isabelle}}.
etym.Vanna:
From {{bor|en|sla}} ''Vanna'', from ''[[Ivana]]'' ([[Ѝвана]]) and ''[[Ivanna]]'' ([[Ива́нна]]), ultimately from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets.

{{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead}}.
etym.Gladys: Anglicized from {{bor|en|cy|Gwladus}}, of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with {{m|cy|gwlad||country}}.
etym.Gwen:
A female given name from {{der|en|cy|-}}. 
* {{bor+|en|cy|Gwen}}.
* {{clipping of|en|Gwendolen}}. {{doublet|en|Wendy}}. 
* {{clipping of|en|Guinevere}}. {{doublet|en|Jen}}.
etym.Enid: From {{der|en|wlm|eneit|t=spirit, life; purity}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*anatyom}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂enh₁-|t=to breathe, blow}}. Cognate with {{cog|cel-gau|anatia||souls (?)}} attested on the [[w:Larzac tablet|Larzac tablet]]; see also the modern {{cog|cy|anadl|t=breath, wind}}, from {{cog|cel-pro|*anatlā|t=breath, breathing}}.<ref>{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary}}</ref>
etym.Gwendolen: From {{bor|en|cy|Gwendolen}}, from {{compound|cy|gwen|t1=white, fair, blessed|dolen|t2=ring, bow, hair, brow|nocat=1}}.
etym.Glenda: Coined in the twentieth century from {{der|en|cy|glân||holy, fair}} and {{m|cy|da||good}}.
etym.Lynette: Anglicized form of {{der|en|cy|Eluned}}, first used by Tennyson in the ''Idylls of the King''(1859-85), altered by folk etymology to be {{af|en|Lynn|-ette}}.
etym.Glenys: A twentieth century coinage from {{der|en|cy|glân||clean, holy}} + {{m|cy|-ys}}.
etym.Tyra: A Latinized form of {{der|sv|gmq-oda|Thyrvi}}, from {{der|sv|non|Þórr||Thor}} and a second element of debated meaning.
etym.Linette: In modern use a spelling variant of {{m|en|Lynette}}, though it is also identical with a rare {{der|en|fr|-}} name, diminutive of {{m|fr|Line}}, from {{m|fr|Caroline}}, {{m|fr|Pauline}} and other female names ending in ''-line''.
etym.Andal:
Two main origins:
* Borrowed from {{bor|en|gl|Andal}}, a surname predominantly established in the [[Philippines]].
* Borrowed from {{bor|en|no|Andal}}, probably a compound of {{m|no|ahn||elm}} and {{m|no|dal||valley}}.
etym.Megan: {{bor+|en|cy|Megan}}, cognate with {{cog|en|Margaret}}, ultimately from an [[Indo-Iranian]] source.
etym.Belinda: From {{suffix|en|Belle|inda}}, base from various Romance sources such as {{cog|fr|belle}}, {{cog|it|bella||beautiful}}, suffix Latinate form of {{cog|de|linde||soft}} (English {{m|en|linden}}, {{m|en|lithe}}). Popularised by {{w|Alexander Pope}} in his poem ''{{w|The Rape of the Lock}}'' (1714). The moon is named after a character in Pope's poem.
etym.Shana: Anglicized variant of the {{uder|en|cy|-}} name [[Siân]] (pet form [[Siana]]) - or a version of the {{uder|en|fr|-}} name [[Jeanne]].
etym.Amara: Borrowed from the feminine inflection of {{bor|mul|la|amārus|t=bitter, sour, distasteful}}.
etym.Arlene: A nineteenth-century coinage probably based on similar-sounding names such as [[Charlene]] and [[Arlette]].
etym.Almira: Coined name, possibly inspired by {{m|en|Elmira}}, of a queen of [[Castile]] in C. F. Handel's opera ''Almira'' (1705) to an {{bor|en|it}} libretto.
etym.Kaila: From {{bor|en|yi|קיילה|tr=kaila}}), In modern use a spelling variant of [[Kayla]] or [[Kyla]].
etym.Rhiannon: From {{inh|cy|wlm|Rhiannon}}, from {{m|wlm|riein|t=maiden}} (modern {{m|cy|rhiain}}), first used in fiction.
etym.Abrielle: Modern coinage possibly shortened from {{m|en|Gabrielle}}. Compare {{m|en|Brielle}}, {{m|en|Aubrielle}}.
etym.Cinderella: From {{com|en|cinder|it:-ella}}, as in ''little cinder girl''. Compare {{cog|fr|Cendrillon}}.
etym.Cheryl: Coined in the early 20th century, possibly a blend of {{m|en|Cherie}} or {{m|en|Cherry}} and {{m|en|Beryl}}. (See {{l|fr|cher}} for the etymology of Cherie.)
etym.Elma: A 19th-century creation, usually explained as a form of {{m|en|Wilhelmina}} or {{der|en|it|Guglielma}}. It has also been recorded as a blend of {{m|en|Elizabeth}} and {{m|en|Mary}}.
etym.Della: Possibly a variant of {{m|en|Adela}} or {{m|en|Delia}}. First appeared in the 19th century.
etym.Evangeline: Invented by the poet {{w|Henry Wadsworth Longfellow}} when he began research on his epic poem ''Evangeline'' about [[Acadian]] lovers deported from French-Canada. From {{der|en|grc|εὐαγγέλιον||good news}}.
etym.Glenna: From male given name {{m|en|Glen}}, from Scottish {{m|en|glen||secluded valley}}.
etym.Charmaine: 20th century variant of {{m|en|Charmian}}, or coinage from the noun {{m|en|charm}} with the {{m|en||-aine}} ending as in {{m|en|Elaine}} and {{m|en|Germaine}}.
etym.Haidée: Lord Byron's transliteration of the Greek name ''Χάϊδι'' ("caress") for his 1819 "Translation of the Romaic Song."<ref>https://www.ascsa.edu.gr/uploads/media/hesperia/146751.pdf</ref> The name would become popularized in English when he used the name again in 1824 in ''Don Juan''.
etym.Daenerys: {{coin|en|Q181677}}. From the name of a character in George R. R. Martin's ''{{w|A Song of Ice and Fire}}'' novels; popularised by the later television adaptation ''{{w|Game of Thrones}}''.<ref>{{cite-av|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nTBQZBMQtOw|title=George R. R. Martin on how he comes up with his characters' names.|year=2014}}</ref> {{bor+|en|art-vlh|Daenerys}}.
etym.Eartha: 19th-century coinage from {{suffix|en|earth|a}}. Best known for the American singer {{w|Eartha Kitt}}.
etym.Coraline: An elaborate form of {{m|fr|Coralie}}, itself derived from ''[[coral]]''. Name of a character in Adolphe Adam's opera {{w|Le toréador}}.
etym.Deangela: {{prefix|en|De|Angela}}. Of African-American coinage using the prefix ''De''
etym.Kylie: {{unc|en}}, possibly from {{m|en|kylie||boomerang}}. Originally popular in [[Australia]], the name has gained popularity elsewhere in the English-speaking world due to the fame of {{w|Kylie Minogue}}. Unrelated to {{m|en|Kyle}}, though often seen as its feminine equivalent.
etym.Kendra: Coined in the latter half of the twentieth century, presumably a {{blend|en|Kenneth|Sandra|nocap=1}}.
etym.Jolene: A [[blend]] of the element {{m|en|Jo}}... in common anglicized forms of various {{der|en|he|-}} names and the ending {{m|en|Lene|...lene}} shared by the {{der|en|de|-}} names {{m|en|Helene}} and {{m|en|Magdalene}}. [[cognate|Cognate]] with {{m|en|Charlene}}, {{m|en|Darlene}}, and {{m|en|Marlene}}, which were constructed in similar manner from the names {{m|en|Charles}}, {{m|en|darling}}, and {{m|en|Maria}}.
etym.Kyla: Modern invention that can be explained as a feminine form of {{m|en|Kyle}} with {{affix|en|-a}}.
etym.Lakeisha: An African-American creation from the 1970s, possibly {{prefix|en|La|Keisha}}.
etym.Joelyn: Coined from {{m|en|Jo}} or {{m|en|Joe}} + the suffix {{af|en|-lyn}} in the 20th century.
etym.Khaleesi: {{bor+|en|art-dtk|khaleesi|t=queen}}, feminine of {{m|art-dtk|khal|t=king}}. {{coin|en|Q181677}} for the title of the character {{w|Daenerys Targaryen}} in his book ''{{w|A Song of Ice and Fire}}'' (1996) novels. Popularised by the later television adaptation ''{{w|Game of Thrones}}'' (2011).
etym.Jaylene: 20th-century coinage from {{m|en|Jay}} + -lene ending as in {{m|en|Charlene}}, {{m|en|Jolene}}, etc.
etym.Norma: Coined name of an imaginary [[Celtic]] priestess in Bellini's opera [[w:Norma (opera)|Norma]] (1831). Sometimes explained as {{uder|en|la|norma||pattern, model}}, or as a feminine form of {{m|en|Norman}}.
etym.Melinda: Coined in the eighteenth century from names such as {{m|en|Melanie}} and {{af|en|Melissa|-inda}}.
etym.Pamela: Invented by Sir {{w|Philip Sidney}} for his pastoral poem ''{{w|The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia}}'' (c 1593).
