Seemingly created from scratch;<ref>Patrick Hanks, Kate Hardcastle, Flavia Hodges. ''A Dictionary of First Names'', Oxford University Press, 2006</ref> some imagine an analysis as {{cog|grc|πᾶς||all}} + {{m|grc|μέλι||honey}} but there is no evidence that this was intended.
etym.Nevaeh: From {{m|en|heaven}}, spelled backwards. Popular since 2000 when the rock singer {{w|Sonny Sandoval}} gave the name to his baby daughter.
etym.Senga: The name was relatively common in West Central Scotland until the 1980s, and is sometimes said to derive from {{m|en|Agnes}}.
etym.Myra: First used by the poet Fulke Greville, possibly as an [[anagram]] of [[Mary]].
etym.Malinda: Variant of {{m|en|Melinda}}, used since the eighteenth century.
etym.Luana: American 18th/19th century coinage, a fanciful spelling of [[Louanna]], from [[Lou]] + [[Anna]].
etym.Leia: From the name of a princess in the American fantasy film ''Star Wars'' (1977).
etym.Porscha: Probably from the luxury car brand {{m|en|Porsche}}.
etym.La Toya: Possibly a combination of the prefix '''La-''' + [[Toya]], a Spanish pet form of [[Victoria]].
etym.Merida: {{unc|en}}. Possibly a coinage based on {{m|en|Mary}}, or transferred from the {{uder|en|es|-}} place name {{m|es|Mérida}}.
etym.Sariah: Name of a character in the {{w|Book of Mormon}}. Compare {{m|en|Sarah}} and {{m|en|Maria}}.
etym.Pearline: Coined at the end of the 19th century from {{suffix|en|Pearl|ine}}. Compare {{m|en|Pauline}}, {{m|en|Earline}}.
etym.Renesmee: {{coinage|en|occ=the American novelist and film producer|Stephenie Meyer|nobycat=1}} as the name of [[w:List of Twilight characters#Renesmee Cullen|Renesmee Cullen]] (a character in her novel ''{{w|Breaking Dawn}}'' (2008), the fourth in the ''[[w:Twilight (novel series)|Twilight]]'' series, who also appeared in ''[[w:The Twilight Saga (film series)|The Twilight Saga]]'', a film series based on the novels). She is given this name by her mother ({{w|Bella Swan}}) as a {{blend|en|Renée|Esme|nocap=1}}, the names of [[w:List of Twilight characters#Renée Dwyer|Renée Dwyer]] (Bella Swan’s mother) and [[w:List of Twilight characters#Esme Cullen|Esme Cullen]] (her father’s adoptive mother).
etym.Thelma:
A literary invention, first appeared in the {{uder|en|sv|-}} novel ''Kyrkoinvigningen i Hammarby'' (1840-1841) by [[w:Emilie Flygare-Carlén|Emilie Flygare-Carlén]], <ref> '''1841''' [[w:Emilie Flygare-Carlén|Emilie Flygare]], ''Kyrkoinvigningen i Hammarby'', Andra delen, N.H.Thomson, Stockholm 1841, page 468:
: - - - och följande söndagen förkunnades högtidligt från predikstolen i Hammarby kyrka, att grefve Albano v. H. skulle trädä i äktenskap med högvälborna fröken '''Thelma''' v. Rawenstein.</ref> translated into English as "The Magic Goblet" (1845). Similar names of ambiguous origin, [[Elma]], [[Selma]], [[Velma]], appeared in the 19th century.

By [[folk etymology]] explained as Ancient
etym.Velma: Coined at the end of the 19th century, by analogy with {{m|en|Thelma}} and {{m|en|Wilma}}.
etym.Shaniqua:
{{rfv-etym|en}}
Popularized in the 1970s among African Americans, possibly influenced by {{m+|sw|shani||novelty}} or {{m+|cy|Siân}} ([[Joanna]], "God is gracious");<ref>[https://www.blacknamesproject.com/names/shanequa Shaniqua], The Black Names Project</ref> compare other names starting with ''Shan-'' like ''[[Shanice]]'', ''[[Shanika]]'', ''[[Shanita]]''.
etym.Taryn: A 20th-century coinage, apparently from {{m|en|Tara}} combined with names like {{m|en|Karen}}. In the case of the American actress {{w|Taryn Power}}, derived from her father's given name {{m|en|Tyrone}}.
etym.Tamia: A 20th-century coinage popularized by the Canadian singer {{w|Tamia Hill}}.
etym.Stellaluna: From {{m|en|Stella|t= star}} + {{m|en|Luna|t= moon}}, or possibly more directly from Italian.
etym.October:
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:<ety:bor<fro:octobre>>}}
From {{inh|en|enm|-}}, borrowed from {{der|en|fro|octobre}}, from {{der|en|la|Octōber||eighth month}}, from {{der|en|la|octō||eight}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*oḱtṓw||twice four}}; + {{der|en|la|-ber}}, from {{m|la|-bris}}, an adjectival suffix; October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.
etym.Asia: From {{inh|en|enm|Asia}}, {{m|enm|Asie}}, from {{der|en|fro|Asie}} and {{der|en|la|Asia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ᾰ̓σῐ́ᾱ}}, from {{der|en|gmy|𐀀𐀯𐀹𐀊|ts=aswijaː}}, in turn probably from {{der|en|hit|𒀸𒋗𒉿|tr=aš-šu-wa|ts=Aššuwa|t=northwest Anatolia}} of uncertain origin. Potentially from an [[w:Tyrsenian_languages#Aegean_language_family|Aegean language family]] substrate or {{der|en|akk|-}}. Possibly a {{dbt|en|Assuwa|nocap=1}}.
etym.Brittany:
{{root|en|ine-pro|*kʷer-}}
{{inh+|en|enm|Bretany}}, {{m|enm|Brytany}}, itself borrowed from {{der|en|la-med|Britannia}}, applied to Brittany from at least the 6th century, and reinforced by {{der|en|frm|Bretagne}}. See {{m|la|Britannia}} for more. {{doublet|en|Britain|Britannia}}.
etym.Geneva:
[[File:Karte Lage Kanton Genf 2026.png|thumb|canton of '''Geneva''' (''sense 2'')]]
Mentioned in {{der|en|la|-}} texts as {{m|la|Genava}}. Probably via a {{der|en|cel-pro|*genwā}} from {{der|en|ine-pro|*ǵénw-eh₂|t=knee}}, a derivative of {{m|ine-pro|*ǵónu}} in the sense of a bending river or estuary, possibly akin to {{m|en|Genoa}}.
etym.Savannah: The cities are named after the {{m|en|Savannah River}}, possibly derived from {{uder|en|sjw|-}} or {{uder|en|alg|-}}.
etym.Brooke: A [[topographic]] surname for someone who lived near a [[brook]].
etym.Dixie: {{etydate|1859}}. {{unk|en}}, but may come from the [[Mason-Dixon line|Mason-'''Dixon''' line]], the boundary between the northern states and the southern states, or from the slang term {{m|en|dixie}} for a Louisiana $10 bill (equivalent to English ''[[tenner]]''), in turn from French {{m|fr|dix}} (ten).<ref>Funk, W. J., ''Word origins and their romantic stories'', New York, Wilfred Funk, Inc.</ref>
etym.Skye: Derived from {{der|en|gd|Eilean Sgitheanach|An t-Eilean Sgitheanach}}, of long disputed (probably non-Indo-European {{der|en|qfa-sub|-}}) origin, with several theories proposed and none widely accepted; see {{w|Etymology of Skye}}.
etym.Delaney: From a {{der|en|nrf|-}} baronial surname, from a place in France, {{der|en|fro|del}} {{m|fro|aunaie||from the alder grove}}. In Ireland an anglicization of {{bor|en|ga|Ó Dubhshláine}} (descendant of Black ([[dubh]]) + Challenge ([[slán]])).
etym.Iona: Probably a misreading of {{cog|la|Ioua}}, an attempt to Latinize {{cog|sga|Í}}.
etym.Beyoncé: The recent use of this name is due to the American singer [[w:Beyoncé Knowles|Beyoncé Knowles]] (born 1981), after her mother's maiden name, which was different from her own parents' surname, Beyincé, due to a clerical error on her birth certificate. It is probably derived from the French surname {{m|fr|Boyancé}}.
etym.Blythe: English surname, from {{inh|en|ang|blīþe||merry}}. Many senses are derived from placenames, such as the {{w|River Blythe}}, all from the Old English adjective.
etym.Rochelle: Habitational or topographic name from places in France, {{m|en|La Rochelle}}, from {{der|en|fro|rochelle}} diminutive form of {{m|fro|roche||rock}}.
etym.Cagney: Reduced Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Ó Caingnigh||descendant of Caingneach}}, a byname from {{m|ga|caingneach||troublesome}}.
etym.Anslee: Modern spelling variant of {{m|en|Ansley}}. Possibly of {{l|en|Scottish}} origin, related to {{m|en|Ainsley}}.
etym.Chanel: From {{bor|en|fr|Chanel}}. As a given name, principally after {{w|lang=en|Coco Chanel}}.
etym.Everleigh: From {{inh|en|ang|eofor||wild boar}} + {{m|ang|leah|lēah|woodland clearing}}. Compare the {{cog|nl|-}} toponym {{m|nl|Everlo}}.
etym.Aubrie: Modern altered spelling of {{m|en|Aubrey}} as a feminine name.
etym.Everly: Habitational surname, from a variant of {{m|en|Everleigh}}.
etym.Anniston:
The city in Alabama, originally Woodstock, was renamed by town officials in 1873 (after realizing there was another village named Woodstock in central Alabama) in honor of Annie Eliza Scott Tyler (1838–1914), daughter-in-law of {{w|Daniel Tyler}}, one of the two organizers of the Woodstock Iron Company, which started the then planned community. Equivalent to {{affix|en|Annie|-s-|-ton}} (“Annie’s town”).

The name of the city in Missouri was changed in 1894—a transfer from the city in Alabama.
etym.Greenlee: Habitational surname from several minor places in [[England]], named from {{der|en|ang|grēne||green}} + {{m|ang|lēah||clearing, glade}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|green|-leigh|alt2=-lee|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}; compare {{m|en|Green}} and {{m|en|Greene}}.
etym.Mackenzie: {{cln|en|spelling pronunciations}} {{glossary|spelling pronunciation|Spelling pronunciation}} of {{bor|en|sco|MacKenȝie}} with the letter ⟨[[ȝ]]⟩ confused with ⟨[[z]]⟩. Ultimately from {{der|en|gd|MacCoinnich}}, itself from {{compound|gd|mac<t:son, descendant>|Coinneach<alt:Coinnich><t:of Coinneach>|nocat=1}}.
etym.Lyndsey: Spelling variant. A less common spelling of {{m|en|Lindsay}} or {{m|en|Lindsey}}.
etym.Kaylee:
Coined toward the end of the 20th century
* A combination of {{compound|en|Kay|Lee}}.
* A variant of the surname {{m|en|Cayley}} or {{m|en|Keeley}}.
etym.Kelli: Contraction of {{m|et|Gertrud||[[Gertrude]]}} or {{m|et|Kerli}}, or borrowed from the {{der|et|en|Kelly}}.
etym.Laverne: 19th-century invention, possibly from the Californian town [[La Verne]], named in the belief that it means "the green" in French. Laverne is a genuine French surname, from [[Gaulish]] ''la verne'' "the alder (tree place)" but - as in the case of [[Leroy]] - there is no apparent reason to turn it into an American given name.
etym.Macy: [[Norman]] baronial surname from places named ''Massy'' in France, derived from a [[Gallo]]-[[Roman]] personal name ''[[Maccius]]''.
etym.McKenna: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gd|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|McKinney}}.
etym.Makenna: A variant of {{m|en|McKenna}} invented in the 1980s.
etym.Kenley:
* Shortened from {{m|en|McKenley}}, variant of {{m|en|McKinley}}
* Habitational from {{der|en|ang|Cena||a man's name}} + {{m|ang|leah|lēah|woodland clearing}}.
etym.Macey:
* As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Massey}}.
* As a {{der|en|sla|-}} surname, Americanized from {{der|en|sk|Macej}}, {{der|en|rue|tr=Mačej}}, {{der|en|pl|Maciej}}, all variants of {{m|en|Matthew}}.
etym.McCamey: Anglicized form of {{der|en|gd|Mac Shimidh||son of Jamie}}.
etym.Medina: From {{bor|en|ar|اَلْمَدِينَة||the city}}. {{root|en|ar|م د ن}} {{rfe|en|This spelling influenced by Ottoman Turkish?}} {{doublet|en|Mdina}}.
etym.Tiffany:
From {{der|en|fro|Tifinie}}, {{m|fro|Tiphanie}}, from {{der|en|la|Theophania||Epiphany}}, from {{der|en|grc|θεο-||god}} (combining form of {{m|grc|θεός||god}}) + {{m|grc|φαίνω||to shine, appear}}. {{doublet|en|theophany}}.

The given name (from circa 12th century) was usually given to girls born at [[Epiphany]]. The surname (from late 13th century) is a dialectal variant of the surname {{m|en|Tiffin}}, which derives from the given name variant {{m|en|Tiffania}}.<ref>"[https://www.surnamedb.com/Surname/Tiffany Last name: Tiffany]" on [https://www.surnamedb.com/ The Internet Surname Database].</ref>

etym.Whitney: From {{der|en|ang|hwītan}}, dative of {{m|ang|hwīt||white}} + {{m|ang|īeġ||island}}, "white island".<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: ''The Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names''. Cambridge University Press, 2004.</ref>
etym.Reese:
* As a given name and British surname generally from {{der|en|cy|Rhys|lit=ardor}}.
* Chiefly in North America, the surname may also be from unrelated {{der|en|de|Reese|lit=giant}}.
etym.Sidnee: A very rare spelling variant of {{l|en|Sidney}}.
etym.Tenley: From {{m|en|Tineley}} in Northumberland or {{m|en|Teenley}} in West Yorkshire.
etym.Mckenzie: Rare spelling variant of the surname {{m|en|MacKenzie}}.
etym.Tinsley: From the unattested {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|*Tynni}} + {{m|en|-s-}} + {{m|ang|lēah||woodland clearing, glade}} {{cln|en|terms suffixed with -leigh}}.
etym.Shealy: Reduced form of {{m|en|O'Shealy}}, an Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Ó Sealbhaig||descendant of Sealbhach}}, a byname from the adjective {{m|ga|sealbhach||wealthy}}.
etym.Nolette: Further anglicization of {{m|en|Nolet}} based on its usual English pronunciation, from {{der|en|fr|Nolet}}, an apheretic form of personal names like {{m|fr|Renolet}}, diminutive form of {{m|fr|Renaud}}.
